# A THEOLOGICAL-POLITICAL TREATISE

<note>original: "Tractatus Theologico-Politicus"</note>

<note>This work is a cornerstone of Enlightenment philosophy. In it, Baruch Spinoza argues for the "freedom to philosophize," suggesting that such liberty is not only compatible with religious piety and the peace of the state but is actually essential for protecting them. It was a highly controversial text in its time, leading to its eventual ban by both religious and civil authorities.</note>

# INTRODUCTION.

### THE EDITOR TO THE READER.

The theological and political Treatise (*Tractatus Theologico-politicus* <note>original: "Tractatus Theologico-politicus" — Latin for "Theological-Political Treatise"</note>) of Benedict de Spinoza, now presented to the English reader, is the most generally interesting of the works of this celebrated writer. We say *celebrated*, because there is no person of any culture who has not heard of Spinoza, though it must be admitted that few know more of the man than his name. 

Nevertheless, Spinoza left his mark on the path of human progress, and no history of Philosophy would be complete without a chapter devoted to the consideration of his metaphysical <note>Metaphysics: the branch of philosophy dealing with the fundamental nature of reality, including the relationship between mind and matter, substance, and cause.</note> views and conclusions. 

The common people <note>original: "The vulgar"</note>, however, and their ministers—the theologians—have until now been the primary judges in matters concerning the mysteries of God, the soul, and the religious and moral nature of humanity. Spinoza was opposed to these theologians and felt contempt for common prejudices. Having no reverence for antiquity for its own sake and no respect for established tradition <note>original: "prescription"</note>, he dared to think independently. Above all, because he dared to give voice to his thoughts, he has been denounced as a dangerous person and labeled an atheist as a matter of course. His writings were banned <note>original: "proscribed"</note>, and his truly spotless reputation has been vilified and condemned.

<summary>The editor introduces Spinoza's "Theological-Political Treatise," noting that while Spinoza is famous, he is often misunderstood or unfairly slandered by theologians and the public for his independent thought.</summary>
<keywords>Benedict de Spinoza, Tractatus Theologico-politicus, Metaphysics, Theologians, Censorship, Atheism, Philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Editor's Introduction, moving from a general description of Spinoza’s reputation to the specific origins and goals of the "Theological-Political Treatise."</meta>

# INTRODUCTION.

In the explanatory and critical treatise <note>original: "exegetical" — relating to the interpretation of texts, especially scripture</note> that follows, it is easy to see the reasons for all the theological hatred that has so long been attached to the name of Spinoza. Purely philosophical and theoretical writings rarely catch the attention of the general public; they only provide topics for discussion among philosophers and scholars, whose interests usually align with those of society as a whole. However, critical investigations—no matter how they are intended—almost inevitably clash with the opinions and prejudices of individuals. They may even be found to oppose the interests of large and influential groups in society, who immediately unite to wage a bitter war against the researcher. This was the case with Spinoza.

As a young man, he was brought into close contact with the Hebrew Scriptures, the Talmud <note>Talmud: the collection of ancient writings constituting the basis of religious authority in Orthodox Judaism</note>, and the explanatory writings of the Jewish Rabbis. He was particularly influenced, it seems, by the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "Moré Nebouchim" — a 12th-century work of Jewish philosophy by Maimonides</note> by the famous Rabbi Moses Maimonides of Cordova. However, Spinoza was unsatisfied with the officially accepted and traditional <note>original: "orthodox"</note> ways of explaining away the many difficulties found in the Old Testament. Driven by his own natural curiosity, he decided to examine the ancient records of his ancestors' faith for himself. Bringing great talent, extensive learning, a total lack of prejudice, and a fearless spirit to the task, he gradually reached conclusions that were very different from those commonly held.

He recorded the results of his research in the work now presented in this English translation <note>original: "dress"</note>. Beyond its critical and explanatory components, the purpose of this book is to show that the free discussion of both religious and political principles is not only consistent with true devotion <note>original: "piety"</note> and the safety of the State, but that such freedom cannot be forbidden without causing harm and danger to both.*

It is not surprising that the publication of this remarkable work immediately caused a great stir in the world of theology. Nor is it surprising that it was viewed as a very serious attack on the established systems of religious tradition <note>original: "prescription"</note> and belief in the Christian world <note>original: "Christendom"</note>.

\* For the original full title <note>original: "in extenso"</note>, see <note>original: "vide"</note> page 16.

# INTRODUCTION.

Yet this book, or one like it, was almost a necessity for the advancing European Enlightenment. It is, in fact, the first fruits of religious criticism produced by the spirit of debate sparked by the Reformation—or rather, the spirit of free inquiry that the Reformation itself expressed. Once the chains of tradition had been cast off, and the prison of blind obedience to unaccountable authority had been broken, the Bible was made accessible to everyone in their own language <note>original: "vulgar tongue" — the common language spoken by ordinary people, such as English or German, rather than Latin</note>. As the sole record of the Christian religious system, this accessibility marked the first major step in the remarkable history of European progress. 

However, it was only the first step. The same spirit of inquiry, born from doubt, which had challenged the *Old* way and led to the *New*, eventually attacked the new system in its turn. Before long, people began to ask if what had been gained was truly the *End* and the *Ultimate Goal*. Benedict de Spinoza’s *Theological-Political Treatise* <note>original: "Tractatus Theologico-politicus"</note> was the philosophical answer to this question. Nevertheless, the work should be seen as the result of the author's own private reflections and research, rather than as a reflection of any specific skeptical or critical mood common during his time. 

With the Reformation, the world had merely shifted its loyalty from one system of rigid religious doctrine <note>original: "dogmatic theology"</note> to another. Although it was no longer necessary to pledge total obedience to the Church of Rome, and individuals were now considered significant within the structure of Christian society, it was still nearly as dangerous to hold what every era labels as unorthodox <note>original: "heterodox" — beliefs that conflict with official church teachings</note> opinions. Taking a more elevated view of God’s divine plan <note>original: "providence"</note> remained a risk, just as it had been in the time of Socrates, or for Jesus <note>original: "One much greater than Socrates"</note>, for the long line of Christian martyrs, and for all those persecuted for their religious opinions up to the present hour. Although Spinoza's remarkable work was fundamentally a product of its era, it did not appear without warning. The minds of scholars and philosophers were not entirely unprepared for it, even though the information it provided and the views it proclaimed were strikingly new...

Copernicus and Galileo, however, had already come into open conflict with the literal text of Scripture and the official pronouncements <note>original: "dicta"</note> of rigid religious doctrine <note>original: "dogmatic theology"</note> in the field of physical science; meanwhile, Bacon and Descartes had successfully asserted humanity's right to freedom of opinion in the realm of philosophy. Spinoza's work, consequently, however poorly it was received by professional theologians, appears to have found enough support <note>original: "countenance"</note> in the world of science and letters. Copernicus, Luther, Galileo, Bacon, Descartes, Leibniz, and, though last certainly not least, Spinoza—these are the mighty names to whom we owe the intellectual freedom we now enjoy. Spinoza is not the least in this illustrious list, we say, because—though he was behind <note>original: "in arrear"</note> our own great writers and activists from the time of King Charles I regarding political principles—as the true founder of the school of biblical criticism, he continues to influence the religious opinions of Europe to a greater degree, perhaps, than any other man of modern times.

In these our own days of freer individual thought and greater general enlightenment, when authority and tradition in matters of faith—no less than in subjects of science—are ignored by the truly educated in all classes of society, an English version of the *Treatise* <note>original: "Tractatus"</note> of Spinoza appears to be a need that ought to be supplied. In this favored land, we have long held a beneficial conviction regarding the clear advantages that come from the open discussion of political and social questions. However, in regard to subjects of faith and religion, it must be confessed that public opinion is less advanced. Many people still fear to involve themselves here; from the pulpit, we are anxiously cautioned against too much "curious inquiry" and told simply to believe. Nevertheless, and in spite of all advice to the contrary, mankind will inquire. Lately, there are unmistakable signs of greater freedom and of some progress in considering the "subject of subjects"—the relationship of man to his Creator. A ray of the light that has long illuminated the scholars of Germany and the North has at length broken in upon the stagnant theological atmo-

Although it has so dazzled our official religious leaders <note>original: "accredited spiritual chiefs"</note> that they now seem inclined to turn their backs on this enlightenment—even at the risk of being left behind by the science and general intelligence of the country—they will eventually learn to accept it. England cannot afford to fall behind the rest of the world in her religious philosophy <note>original: "speculative theology"</note> any more than she would dare to lag behind in science or the industrial arts. Given the fortunate character <note>original: "constitution"</note> of her people, she ought to lead in this field, just as she has already led in everything that contributes to physical well-being and defines true civilization: respect for the law, regard for the rights of others, and the defense of civil and religious liberty. 

Religion is indeed a permanent part of human nature. Outcries against the free discussion of its elements—and against investigating the value and authenticity of the ancient records of religions that existed among the earliest civilized societies <note>original: "policied races"</note>—really only mean one thing: that current religious teachers <note>original: "professors"</note> prefer to be left alone in their faith, whatever it may happen to be. But just as surely as there has been an *Old Covenant* and a *New*, there will certainly be another and another even newer still, each one more in harmony with the knowledge and aspirations of a constantly advancing humanity than the last. 

The fearsome Jehovah of the Pentateuch <note>the first five books of the Hebrew Bible</note>—who demanded every first-born male, whether human or animal, as a burnt offering for himself, and whose altar smelled of the blood of victims every morning and evening—gave way to the gentler concept of later ages. This later God "took no pleasure in the blood of bulls or rams," and "did not require from his people their first-born for their sins, the fruit of their body for the sin of their soul." Instead, he only asked of his worshippers that "they should act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with their God." The entire exclusive, physical, and blood-stained ritual of the ancient Hebrew people had therefore given way to the more humane and spiritual views of the later prophets. They, in their turn, while preparing the way for his coming, bowed their heads and faded into the background when the culmi- <note>The text likely continues with "culmination" or "culminating point," referring to the arrival of Christ.</note>

# INTRODUCTION.

The culminating point in the religious history of humanity was reached when Jesus, the son of Joseph, appeared on earth. Our great Exemplar and Teacher, however, did not leave his doctrine to the world in a comprehensive and absolutely authentic form, dictated by himself and bearing the stamp of his authority. Or, if he did, that record has been lost over the centuries <note>original: "perished in the lapse of ages"</note>. His views and his precepts must be gathered from imperfect narratives put together long after the events they describe <note>original: "recite"</note> had occurred. These were written by men who often clearly gave their own interpretation <note>original: "colouring"</note> to the matters recorded, and who at times seem not to have understood their Teacher well.

Christ, in fact, shared <note>original: "scattered"</note> his sayings among curious or careless crowds. His precepts often fell upon ears that did not understand their meaning. This led to early disagreements <note>original: "dissidence"</note> regarding the world's estimate of the entire scope of Christian doctrine, and to the differences in specific ideas that began to take hold <note>original: "obtain"</note> soon after Christ’s death. This assures us that his simple moral doctrine quickly faded <note>original: "waned"</note> from its original <note>original: "pristine"</note> brightness and became mixed and corrupted by the rituals and notions of the pagan systems with which it inevitably came into such close contact. 

Many of these ideas and rituals actually belonged to the Jews, just as they did to all the civilized <note>original: "policied"</note> nations of antiquity; they were therefore familiar to the early Christians as the children of Hebrew parents. One of the most widely spread of all the religious ideas of antiquity was that of winning God's favor <note>original: "propitiation"</note> through sacrifice. An animal—or, tragically, sometimes even a human being—was slaughtered upon the altar of the deity being addressed. In its death, the victim was believed to appease <note>original: "propitiate"</note> the God <note>original: "Deity"</note> and to atone for <note>original: "expiate"</note> the sins of the people. 

Christianity should have escaped this barbarous idea, and it was undoubtedly free from it at first, though this certainly did not last for long. The savior <note>original: "deliverer"</note> whom the Jews had anticipated during their misfortunes was, beyond all question, a political <note>original: "temporal"</note> leader or ruler. Jerusalem was to become the center of a world empire, and all the nations of the earth were to bow down there before Jehovah and serve the chosen people, led by—

# INTRODUCTION.

...his anointed. But when this new lawgiver and victorious leader failed to appear at the expected time, the Jewish-Christian sect eventually concluded that the deliverer promised by the prophets could not have been a physical ruler <note>original: "a deliverer with an arm of flesh"</note>. 

They developed the more refined <note>original: "nobler"</note> idea that it was a spiritual savior—one who would set them completely free from the burden <note>original: "bondage"</note> of ceremonial laws, which had become almost unbearable. A certain number of his countrymen soon <note>original: "anon"</note> convinced themselves that they recognized this great deliverer in Jesus, who had forcefully declared that his kingdom was not of this world. 

Like all religious reformers, Christ was inevitably offensive to the priesthood of his time. As the New Testament writers tell us, he was put to death as a blasphemer and a rebel against <note>original: "subverter of"</note> the law of Moses. Long afterward—once several generations had passed and this sad, though natural, end to the religious reformer’s career was fading into the distant past—ancient Hebrew and Pagan influences began to take root <note>original: "bear fruit"</note>. 

The pure heart that Christ had preached and the holy life he had taught <note>original: "inculcated"</note> were no longer considered enough to make a person acceptable to God. The Deity, it was felt, must be appeased <note>original: "propitiated"</note> in a more physical and dramatic way. In ancient times, sacrificial victims were chosen for being without spot or blemish. Since Christ—the pure and holy—had died while standing up for his noble principles, what sacrifice could be more fitting than the noblest human form ever seen on earth: Christ himself?

...around us that we have the privilege to observe, reconfirm the Absolute Religion taught by Christ. This religion does not differ from what reason and nature together declare to be the only true faith. Another of those great religious waves that sweep across the world from time to time seems to have been building in Europe for a long while. Religious philosophers with what are called heterodox <note>original: "heterodox"; opinions that differ from official or orthodox church doctrine</note> views—and the educated world is full of such people—are not enemies of religion itself, nor of the institutions established to teach humanity their religious and moral duties. On the contrary, they view these institutions as a means to an end designed by God and as essential parts of the social structure. They are only hostile to what they see as unreasonable and objectionable in the teachings; they want to amend and improve, not tear down or destroy. 

In the system of the Church of England, especially when used correctly, they see perhaps the most admirable tool ever devised for the general improvement of humanity. With their pastors leading them, the various local parish <note>original: "parochial"</note> communities of worshippers in England make up the Church. In the parish, everyone has a voice in managing local affairs. Similarly, in the governing bodies of the kingdom <note>original: "estates of the realm"</note> assembled in Parliament, the most capable people have a voice through their representatives in deciding the articles of their faith and the rituals of their worship. The parish system, of which the Church is such a primary part, is the true birthplace of our English liberties. 

The pastor himself, as we find him today, is both a gentleman and a scholar—a man of good upbringing and broad education. He is the social equal of the highest classes, yet also the friend, advisor, and comforter to the lowest. Perhaps most importantly, through his humanizing influence as the head of a family—as a husband and father—he serves as both the center and the model <note>original: "ensample"</note> of civic and domestic virtues, duties, and affections. It is time that another test of human worth was appealed to besides religious profession. In particular, men of letters and good breeding should stop insulting those who differ from them in their theoretical theology with such labels as "infidel" and "atheist."

The path entered upon at the glorious Reformation, in short, cannot now be abandoned, nor may we linger on the way. "Forward, ever forward, without haste, but without rest" <note>original: *Ohne Hast, aber ohne Rast*</note>† is the motto written in letters of light on the modern banner. Infallibility and rigid dogma <note>original: "dogmatism"</note> are no more; scientific truth associated with reason, justice, and charity must henceforth show the way. It would be a deliberate lack of trust in the Almighty to question the healthiness of the conclusions to which they will lead, however much these may clash with preconceived opinions and personal interests. Our science is not that of the Jews from the days of Moses and Joshua; it is not the science of our ancestors, nor even the science of yesterday, but ever progressive, ever extending, ever becoming...

The Hebrew Scriptures—which are themselves merely evidence of the existence of certain basic mental faculties in the human mind—are neither the only nor even the oldest records of a religious system still in existence. The Hindus <term>Hindoos</term> preceded the Hebrews in civilization by hundreds, perhaps even thousands, of years. In their Vedas <term>Vedas</term>, which existed in writing centuries before the Jews became enslaved to Egyptian taskmasters, they have not only given us a clear insight into their religious world but have also preserved this record in the language that is the root of all the dialects spoken in Europe today.

Since the Persians were closer neighbors to the Jews than the Hindus were, we find that they influenced Jewish ideas much more significantly. We now clearly see the Zoroastrian <term>Zoroastrian</term> concepts that form the foundation of the Book of Job <term>Book of Job</term>. But we must not be tempted to follow this line of thought any further; the field opening up before us is almost limitless.*

# INTRODUCTION.

Spinoza, whose work it is our present business to introduce to the reader, was, like all the great thinkers of the world, far ahead of his time. Almost as a matter of course, he was persecuted by those contemporaries who only wanted things to stay as they were. He made himself especially hated by the narrow-minded members of the religious community to which he belonged by birth—the Jews—but which he left upon reaching manhood. Because intolerance and fanaticism still held the upper hand in human affairs, there is perhaps no name to which "theological hatred" <term>original: *odium theologicum*</term> has stuck as persistently as that of Spinoza. 

Although he declared the concept of the Deity to be the foundation of all knowledge and all mental capacity to know—and although he saw God in everything and maintained that without God nothing could exist—he is nevertheless charged with the folly of atheism. He held the love of God and the deep contemplation of the Infinite to be the chief joy and privilege of existence, yet he is commonly spoken of as a man without piety! And though he led a life of saint-like purity, rejecting the wealth and honors that were within his easy reach, he is denounced as a heartless and greedy <note>original: "avaricious"</note> impostor! Time has already, however, largely restored the reputation of *Benedict de Spinoza*. To many of the greatest intellectuals, especially in Germany, Spinoza has been better known for some time, and is at length—

***

M.A., Anquetil de Perron, and others, have made the world their debtors forever. Spinoza expresses his wish for some authentic proof that the Book of Job was written by a non-Jew <note>original: "Gentile"</note>, as we would then be certain, he says, that non-Jewish nations had their religious books as well as the Jews.

The reader who is anxious for information on the history and progress of religious ideas among mankind is referred with confidence to the noble work of Creuzer and Guigniaut, "*History of Ancient Religions*" <note>original: *Histoire des Religions d'Antiquité*</note>, (4 volumes, octavo, Paris). Except for a single area which is not covered, this work explores the subject completely. It is a grand monument to both learning and industry. The omission mentioned—the Hebrew system—has lately been most ably supplied by an English scholar of the highest achievements, Mr. R. W. Mackay. His masterful work on the *Progress of the Intellect*, regarding the religious ideas of the Greeks and Hebrews, will be read with pleasure by every lover of learning and good taste, and by anyone with an ear for excellent <note>original: "sterling"</note> English.

# INTRODUCTION.

He is regarded with feelings of entire respect, even where his specific views do not command agreement. God, as conceived by Spinoza, has indeed been the concept of Divinity for many of the most distinguished figures in literature and science in central and northern Europe since his day. Lessing, the great scholar, critic, and poet of his age, once held up the works of Spinoza in his hands and exclaimed to his distinguished contemporary Jacobi: "The One and the All! <note>original Greek: Εν και παν (Hen kai Pan)</note>—behold the sum and substance of philosophy." Goethe, to the end of his long life, was in the habit of seeking refuge and refreshment from other studies in the *Ethics*. Herder used to wish he could, for once, find Goethe engaged with a book other than the *Ethics*. Goethe himself, in one of the most pleasant of his works—*Poetry and Truth from My Own Life* <note>original German: Aus meinem Leben: Dichtung und Wahrheit</note>—describes with delight the remembrance of the new world that was awakened in his mind by the study of this work. Novalis, another of Germany’s great writers, spoke with rapture of the "Divine Nature" as portrayed by the slandered <note>original: "traduced"</note> Spinoza; and Schleiermacher, the eloquent preacher, in his enthusiasm, once exclaimed from the pulpit to his astonished audience:

> “Sacrifice a lock of hair with me to the memory <note>original: "manes," referring to the souls of the departed</note> of the pure and misunderstood Spinoza. The sublime spirit of the Universe filled his soul; the Infinite was his beginning and his end; the Universal was his sole and eternal love. Living in saintly innocence and in deep humility, he viewed his being in the mirror of everlasting nature, and knew that he too reflected something that was not unworthy to be loved. Full of religion, full of the Holy Spirit, he appears to us as dwelling apart from the world, raised above the common people and a master in his art, but without disciples or a school.”

Spinoza has therefore had his passionate admirers among the learned and eloquent men of Europe; but he has not been fortunate in finding sympathetic or admiring biographers. The greatest critic and master of logic <note>original: "dialectician"</note> of the 17th century, Bayle, has not only shown himself to be entirely hostile to the philosophy of Spinoza, but cold and hardly just to the philosopher himself.

# INTRODUCTION.

...devout philosopher himself. To Bayle, indeed, the frequent—though by no means universal—disfavor among the learned in which the name of Spinoza was so long held can be traced.* Pastor Colerus, whose biography of our author is the most well-known, was personally acquainted with him. Although there are undoubtedly some points that a devoted admirer would have seen through a different lens, the blameless life and the gentle, truly attractive character of the man are made sufficiently clear. 

It is not difficult for us to excuse a hint of irritable <note>original: "splenetic"</note> feeling in the Lutheran minister against such a bold thinker as Spinoza. As a theologian, he could not tolerate <note>original: "could not away with"</note> the uncompromising critic of the Hebrew Scriptures, but he evidently had no dislike for the man himself. It is with much regret that we discover a different spirit in a quarter where we should not have expected such a display: in the work of the latest and certainly one of the most capable translators and editors of Spinoza, M. Émile Saisset. 

In a learned and instructive article on the *Philosophy of the Jews and Arabs*, published recently (see *Review of the Two Worlds, January 15th, 1862* <note>original French: Revue des deux Mondes</note>), M. Saisset has been strangely led astray by his dislike of Pantheism and other points in Spinoza’s philosophy. This led him to attempt to diminish the position Spinoza assuredly holds in the world of both intellect and morals. For our own part, we have no more affection for Pantheism than M. Saisset does; nor do we care to set sail in the intellectual ship <note>original: "brain-built bark"</note> that carries Spinoza’s metaphysical cargo. However, looking simply at the truth and regardless of the consequences, we are bound to state that in everything we can discern of Spinoza—in his works, in his letters, in the reputation he held while alive, and the social standing of those who were his friends—we find nothing that is not intellectually great, and morally good, gentle, and lovable. And yet, strange as it seems to us, this is the man of whom M. Saisset speaks disparagingly as a heartless recluse and a merely selfish dreamer. Spinoza was very certainly neither. He was much more one of nature’s own nobility: intellectually great, and as self-reliant and independent as he was courteous, considerate, and generous.

# INTRODUCTION.

Spinoza’s writings are extremely rare in England. His name does not even appear in the catalogs of some of our greatest libraries. His works have, nevertheless, been reprinted several times in the original Latin in Germany, and there are translations by skilled hands into both French and German. The German translation by Mr. Berthold Auerbach\* is extremely faithful and is preceded by a good biography <note>original: "Life"</note> of the author. M. Émile Saisset’s French version, which has now reached a second edition,† has the great merit of being both accurate and readable. It further contains Colerus’s *Life of the Philosopher* and an excellent explanation <note>original: "exposition"</note> of his doctrines written by M. Saisset himself.

During his lifetime, Spinoza published the following works:

1.  ***The Principles of René Descartes’ Philosophy; to which are added Metaphysical Thoughts.*** <note>original Latin: "Renati Descartes principia philosophiæ; cujus accesserunt cogitata metaphysica."</note> Amsterdam, 1663.
2.  ***A Theological-Political Treatise containing several dissertations, in which it is shown that the freedom to philosophize can not only be granted without harm to piety and the peace of the commonwealth, but that it cannot be suppressed without destroying the peace of the commonwealth and piety itself***, <note>original Latin: "Tractatus Theologico-politicus continens dissertationes aliquot, quibus ostenditur libertatem philosophandi non tantum salva pietate et reipublicæ pace posse concedi, sed eandem nisi cum pace reipublicæ ipsaque pietate tolli non posse."</note> 4to. Hamburg, 1670.
3.  After his death, the following were published under the supervision of his friends Louis Meyer and Jarig Jellis, under the general title of ***B. de Spinoza’s Posthumous Works*** <note>original Latin: "B. de Spinoza Opera Posthuma"</note>: the ***Ethics*** <note>original Latin: "Ethica"</note>, Spinoza’s great philosophical work; a short political treatise entitled ***Political Treatise*** <note>original Latin: "Tractatus Politicus"</note>; another short essay, ***On the Improvement of the Understanding*** <note>original Latin: "De Emendatione Intellectus"</note>; a ***Compendium of Hebrew Grammar*** <note>original Latin: "Compendium Grammatices Linguae Hebraicae"</note>; and a selection of letters to and from friends and correspondents, folio. Amsterdam, 1677.

Besides these works, it is known that Spinoza at one time occupied himself with a translation of the Hebrew Scriptures into Latin. If the versions that follow the Hebrew texts quoted in the *Theological-Political Treatise* are from his pen, it is much to be regretted that he himself, shortly before his death, committed this work to the flames.

# INTRODUCTION.

For the translation now presented to the English reader, the writer offers beforehand every apology that can be accepted. Many years had passed since he first read the work in the original Latin, but his attention was recently drawn back to it—first by Christian Charles Josias von Bunsen’s *Biblical Criticisms*, and then by the volume *Essays and Reviews*. In these, he seemed to encounter many ideas that were already familiar to him from the *Tractatus* <note>original Latin: *Tractatus Theologico-Politicus*</note>. To occupy himself during a period of forced solitude, and to understand the subject more deeply, he began a translation of the chapter on Miracles. This subject seemed to be of particular interest to the public at the time, and once he began the work, he found it so attractive that he continued regularly until it was completed. For his own part, the writer is ready to declare that his task has been both interesting and spiritually rewarding <note>original: "edifying"</note>. Since all the better thinkers of the world now believe that a "moral bed of Procrustes" <note>In Greek mythology, Procrustes was a bandit who forced travelers to fit into his bed by either stretching them or cutting off their legs; the author uses this to describe the cruel enforcement of arbitrary intellectual conformity.</note> is as miserable an idea as the original device was cruel, he trusts that readers will generally support his high opinion of Spinoza’s short but masterly work.

Spinoza himself informs us in his preface that he wrote only for the liberal-minded and the educated. He did indeed have a great contempt for the "vulgar" <note>The "vulgar" refers to the uneducated common people of the 17th century.</note> and did not care for anyone unable to read the learned languages to be able to read his work. But in the course of two centuries, the world has progressed in its understanding of what constitutes true commonness and true learning. It has decided that neither depends on knowing or not knowing Greek and Latin. Only the tyrant and the bigot—those who advocate for keeping the public ignorant and superstitious—begrudge humanity the freedom of thought or action. But freedom of thought and the vernacular <note>The "vernacular" refers to the common, everyday language spoken by people (in this case, English) rather than scholarly Latin.</note> are inseparable; they are as necessary to human progress as sunlight is to the life of the world. In the present day, we have no doubts about the invaluable benefits of free discussion in language accessible to all. Light only dispels the dark; it is feared by no one except those who have selfish motives to serve, or those who harbor unworthy fears of their fellow human beings.

<meta>This page introduces the psychological origins of superstition, focusing on the instability of human emotion when faced with uncertainty.</meta>

## SCOPE AND PURPOSE OF THIS WORK.

---

If men always acted with understanding and discretion, or if fortune were always favorable, they would never be the slaves of superstition. But because they frequently fall into straits and difficulties where they find no wisdom within themselves, and because they mostly strive without moderation for the uncertain favors of fortune, they are often tossed miserably between hope and fear in their vain aspirations. Consequently, their spirits are commonly inclined toward credulity <note>original: "credulity"; the tendency to believe things too quickly or without proof</note>. Indeed, a mind involved in doubt is easily swayed by every impulse, especially when wavering between hope and fear; in other moods, the mind is all too apt to be self-sufficient and presumptuous.

No one, I imagine, is ignorant of these facts, though I believe that few truly know themselves. Whoever has lived in the world must surely have seen that in times of prosperity, the mass of mankind—however poorly informed—seem to themselves so full of wisdom that they deem it an insult if anyone presumes to offer them advice. In contrast, during times of adversity, they appear not to know where to turn, but seek counsel and support from everyone. In such a state, nothing can be suggested that is so vain, so unreasonable, or so absurd that they will not incline to follow it. Furthermore, the most inadequate causes usually suffice to make men now hope for better things, and now fear the worst. If anything occurs while they are depressed by fear which brings to mind some former good or ill that has befallen them, they forth—

# SCOPE AND PURPOSE

People will imagine that an event betokens a happy or a disastrous outcome to their plight. Even though the same thing may have occurred a hundred times before without any consequence, they still persist in calling it a lucky or an unlucky omen. If anything unusual happens and their wonder is aroused, they believe it to be a prodigy or a portent <note>original: "prodigy, a portent"; these terms refer to extraordinary events interpreted as signs of divine will</note> implying the displeasure or the anger of God. The superstitious then think it impious and irreligious not to seek to propitiate <note>to appease or regain the favor of a deity</note> Him by vows and supplications. In this way, thousands of strange fancies take their rise; as if all nature were delirious like themselves, men interpret its processes in the most unreasonable manner.

Such being the state of things, we see that those who are most under the influence of superstitious feelings—and who covet uncertainties without stint or measure, especially when they fall into difficulty or danger and cannot help themselves—are the very persons who implore Divine assistance with vows, prayers, and womanly tears. They call reason blind and human wisdom vain, all because they cannot find an assured way to the vanities they desire! These are the men who credit the whisperings of fancy and their own puerile <note>childish or silly</note> conceits, calling them divine promptings and responses. Indeed, they think that God turns His face from the wise and has written His decrees, not in the mind of man, but in the entrails of beasts. They believe He has given the idiotic and insane among them, or the birds of the air, the power of foretelling events by instinct or divine inspiration! Such power has fear in making men irrational!

The mainspring of superstition, then, is fear; by fear, too, is superstition sustained and nourished. If proof of this beyond what has just been said were required, or if particular illustrations of our position were demanded, we have but to turn to history—to *Quintus Curtius’ Life of Alexander* <note>A Roman historian's biography of Alexander the Great</note>, for instance. We can observe that the great commander first began to consult soothsayers <note>people who predict the future</note> only when he had learned to mistrust fortune due to reverses in the Cilician passes <note>A strategic mountain pass in southern Turkey where Alexander faced military challenges</note>. After his triumph over Darius <note>Darius III, the King of Persia defeated by Alexander</note>, however, he no longer troubled himself about seers and—

# SCOPE AND PURPOSE

Superstition is, in fact, the cause why at one time nations have been led to worship their kings as gods, and at another to curse <note>original: "execrate"</note> them as the primary pests of humanity. This is also why vast efforts have always been taken to surround the religions—whether true or false—that have prevailed in the world with such pomp and ceremony. The goal is to ensure that religious observance is esteemed as more important than anything else, and as a matter to be regarded by all with the highest reverence. This purpose, though it has had enough success closer to home, seems to have been most thoroughly accomplished among the Turks <note>A common 17th-century reference to the Ottoman Empire, often used as a rhetorical example of absolute authoritarianism.</note>, who even hold it unlawful to question or discuss anything. Their minds are filled with so many prejudices that there is no room left for reason to find an entrance or for curiosity to raise a doubt.

If, however, the grand object in despotisms is to keep mankind deceived and to have means of terror always at hand by which they may be coerced; if religion is made the pretext there for inducing citizens to fight for slavery as though it were salvation, and it is not held base but highly honorable to risk limb and life for the vainglory of one man, I can think of nothing more disastrous for a free State than the imposition of such a system upon it. I hold that it is in every way contrary <note>original: "repugnant"</note> to the general welfare <note>original: "weal"</note> to fill the minds of the community with prejudices, or to seek to coerce them by any means except the laws. 

As for those seditious movements that take place under the pretext of religion, they only become possible because laws are passed concerning speculative matters <note>Theological or philosophical opinions that cannot be proven by observation.</note>, and because opinions are made subjects of punishment just like crimes. The creators and defenders of such laws, indeed, are moved by no regard for the public safety, but only by the desire of reaching their opponents and sacrificing them to their vengeance. Were it otherwise—were the law of the land to declare nothing criminal but an overt act—seditious movements could not be undertaken under the cloak of religion. If words were free and could be spoken with impunity where they involved no threat, controversy could never be turned into rebellion. As we, however, have the rare good fortune <note>original: "felicity"</note> of living in a State where—

Entire <note>The text begins mid-word, continuing "entire" from the previous page.</note> freedom of opinion prevails, where all may worship God in their own way, and where nothing is held sweeter or more precious than such liberty. I have thought that I would undertake a task that is neither unwelcome nor useless by showing that such noble privileges can always be granted, not only without danger to the State and to true religion, but further, that they could not be denied without harming the interests of true devotion <note>original: "piety"</note> and good government.

### SCOPE AND PURPOSE

Here, I decided to immediately re-examine the Bible <note>original: "Scriptures"</note> with a completely free and unbiased mind. I committed myself to asserting nothing about its meaning and accepting no doctrine that I did not find very clearly stated in its pages. 

Strengthened by these resolutions, I developed my own "method of studying and interpreting the sacred volume." Guided by this, I began with some preliminary questions: What is prophecy? How might God have revealed himself to the prophets? Why were these men chosen by God? Was it because they had profound ideas about God and nature, or was it because of their exceptional <note>original: "signal"</note> devotion? 

Once I was satisfied with the answers to these points, I found it easy to conclude that the authority of the prophets only matters in things regarding lifestyle and moral behavior. In other areas, their opinions are not particularly relevant to us. Having reached these conclusions, I next asked why the Jews were called God’s "chosen people." When I discovered that this was only because God had selected a specific region where they could live safely and comfortably <note>original: "commodiously"</note>, it led to a further realization: the laws God revealed to Moses were merely a legal code suited specifically to the Hebrew state or empire. Consequently, no other nation needs to follow this code—and even the Jews themselves were only bound to its rules as long as their kingdom lasted. 

Furthermore, to learn from the Bible whether the human heart and mind are naturally corrupt, I asked whether the universal religion <note>original: "Roman Catholic system of religion" — here the author likely uses "catholic" in its original sense of "universal," referring to a faith for all mankind rather than specifically the Church of Rome.</note>, or the divine law taught by the prophets and apostles to all of humanity, was different from the religion taught by the "light of nature" <note>"Light of nature" refers to truths about God and morality that can be discovered through human reason alone, without the help of supernatural revelation.</note>. Next, I asked whether miracles happen in violation of the laws of nature. I also asked whether God’s existence and providence are more clearly shown through miracles or through the things we understand clearly and logically by their primary causes. However, when I found that nothing in the Bible...

I then discuss the prejudices that have arisen because the masses <note>original: "the vulgar"</note> have worshipped the physical Book of Scripture rather than the Word of God—masses who have abandoned themselves to superstition and love the relics of time more than eternity itself! 

After this, I show that the Word of God was not revealed in a specific set or number of books. Rather, it is the simple concept of the Divine mind shared with the prophets. This Word is proclaimed to consist mainly of love and obedience to God with one's whole heart and mind, and the practice of justice and charity toward one's neighbor. I then demonstrate that the teachings of Scripture are consistent with the abilities and opinions of those to whom the prophets and apostles were accustomed <note>original: "wont"</note> to preach this, the true Word of God. They spoke in a way that would not cause offense in the minds of their listeners, using a style that would lead to a ready acceptance of their doctrines. 

Once the foundations of faith are established, I conclude that the end and object of revealed knowledge is nothing but obedience. This is entirely distinct from natural knowledge <note>meaning: knowledge gained through logic and science</note> in its goals, its grounds, and its methods. They have nothing in common, and each may occupy its own province without ever clashing.

# SCOPE AND PURPOSE

And neither need be subordinate to the other. Further, as one man differs notably from another in capacity and disposition—as one agrees and another disagrees with this or that opinion, and as one is moved to devotion by that which moves another to laughter—I conclude that freedom of opinion belongs by right to all. I also conclude that the privilege of interpreting articles of faith is to be left to every man according to his own capacity, with no one being judged pious or impious except by his works. On this footing, all will be able to obey God with an unconstrained mind, and justice and charity will be held in universal estimation.

After thus proclaiming what the Divine Law, as revealed, allows to all, I proceed to another part of my subject. I argue that this liberty may be granted safely without threatening the peace of the State or the rights of the sovereign <note>original: "summi potestates," referring to the supreme ruling powers</note> or ruling powers. I argue that it ought always to be enjoyed, and that it cannot be denied without great peril to the peace and much damage to the well-being of the whole commonwealth. 

In the demonstration of this principle, I begin with a summary of the natural rights of man. I show that these extend as far as the desires and power of the individual extend, and that no one is bound by natural law to live according to the pleasure of another; rather, everyone is by natural title the rightful protector of his own independence. I show, besides, that no one can truly surrender this right unless he transfers the power of defending himself to another. Furthermore, I show that the person to whom this right is transferred—the right of each individual to live in his own way and to defend himself—necessarily acquires this right absolutely. 

Hence, I prove that whoever holds the sovereign or supreme authority in the State has a title to all he can command, and is the sole arbiter of right and liberty, with the other members of the body politic <term>the collective body of people under a single government</term> being bound to act exclusively according to his decrees. But as no one can so divest himself of the right of self-defense as to cease to be a human being, I conclude that no individual can be absolutely deprived of the whole of his natural rights. However, if anything I have said is judged to violate the laws of the State or to oppose the common good, I wish it to be challenged <note>original: "impugned"</note> and corrected. I know that I am human and prone to error, but I have taken great pains to avoid it. I have been especially careful to express myself so that everything I have written is in harmony with the laws of my country, with piety, and with good conduct <note>original: "manners"</note>.

# CHAPTER I.

## OF PROPHECY.

Prophecy, or revelation, is certain knowledge communicated by God to humanity. *A prophet is someone who interprets things revealed by God for those who cannot gain certain knowledge of these things on their own, and who therefore can only accept the imparted revelations as matters of faith.* The Hebrew word *Nabi* <note>original: *נָבִיא* (Nabi)</note>, commonly translated as "prophet," signifies an orator or interpreter, but it is always used to signify an interpreter of the Divine will. This is evident in Exodus 7:1, where God says to Moses, "See, I have made you as a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet." This is the same as saying, "Since Aaron, by interpreting what you say to Pharaoh, acts as a prophet, you shall therefore be like a god, or stand in the place of a god, to Pharaoh."

It will be our task to discuss the *prophet* in the next chapter; here, we shall speak only of *prophecy*. From the definition provided above, it follows that all *natural knowledge* may be called *prophecy*; for what we know by the *light of nature* <note>original: "light of nature"; this refers to human reason and the innate ability to understand the world and its laws without supernatural help</note> depends entirely on a knowledge of God and His eternal decrees. However, because this *natural knowledge* is accessible to all people—resting as it does on foundations common to all humanity—it is not highly valued by the *common people* <note>original: "the vulgar"; in the 17th century, this term referred to the uneducated masses or the general public rather than being a personal insult</note>. Their tendency is to be attracted by rare and strange occurrences while looking down on natural events. This is why the *common people*, when

# OF PROPHECY.

Whenever we discuss prophecy, we must assume that natural knowledge is set aside. Natural knowledge has just as much right as any other form of knowledge to be called "divine," since it is imparted to us by the nature of God and His decrees. Indeed, it differs from what is commonly called "divine knowledge" only because divine knowledge exceeds the limits of natural knowledge, and the laws of human nature, considered on their own, cannot be its cause. 

However, in terms of the certainty that natural knowledge always involves and its source—which is God—it is in no way inferior to prophetic knowledge. One would have to imagine, or rather dream, that the prophets possessed human bodies but had minds that were not human, which would make their sensations and consciousness entirely different from our own. Even though natural knowledge is truly divine, those who teach it cannot be called prophets;* for the things they teach can be perceived and understood by all people through our shared natural abilities, with the same certainty as those who teach them, and without needing the assistance of faith.

Since our mind contains the nature of God within itself <note>original: "objectively within itself"; in 17th-century philosophy, "objective" reality referred to the reality of an idea as it exists in the mind</note> and thereby participates in His nature, it has the power to form clear and certain ideas that explain the nature of things and teach the purposes of life. Because of this excellence, the mind may be assumed to be the primary cause of Divine revelation. For all that we clearly and adequately understand is dictated to us by the idea of God and—

***

\* Prophets—that is, God’s interpreters. In fact, only those who reveal Divine commandments (communicated to them by God) to people who have not received such a revelation are truly God’s interpreters. The belief of the audience rests solely on the authority of the prophet and the trust he inspires. If the listeners became prophets themselves—just as those who listen to a philosopher become philosophers—then the prophet would no longer be the only interpreter of the Divine will. In that case, the listeners would know the truth not through faith in the prophet, but through a direct Divine communication and internal testimony. It is similar to how a ruler in an absolute monarchy is the only interpreter of the law, because his authority alone creates and enforces it. <note>Note: The notes without the signature *Ed.* are the author’s own.—*Editor*</note>

# OF PROPHECY.

...nature, as has been said already—not through words, certainly, but in a much more excellent way. This way aligns perfectly with the nature of the mind and has undoubtedly been experienced by anyone who has tasted the joys of intellectual certainty. 

But since my goal is to speak specifically about things related to the Scriptures, I will be content here to say no more about the light of nature <note>original: "light of nature"; this refers to natural human reason or understanding</note>. Therefore, I will proceed to discuss in detail the other causes and methods by which God has revealed things to humanity—both things that are beyond the reach of natural knowledge and those that fall within its scope. There is no logical reason why God should not also use other ways to share things with us that we already understand through the light of nature.

Everything said on this subject must be drawn from Scripture alone. After all, what can we say about things that exceed our understanding, except what we have received from the mouths of the prophets and the pages of Holy Writ <note>the Bible</note>? Since there are no prophets among us today (as far as I am aware), we have no choice but to rely on the sacred writings left to us by the ancient prophets. We must be careful not to attribute anything to them, or claim anything as their teaching, that they have not clearly and explicitly stated.

However, we must specifically note that the Jewish writers never mention secondary or specific causes <note>original: "mediate or particular causes"; these are the natural, intermediate steps in a process</note>. They do not even seem to consider them. Instead, out of religious piety or devotion, they always attribute everything directly to God. For example, if they make a profit in trade, they say God gave them the advantage. If they desire something, they say God inclined their hearts toward it. If a thought enters their minds, they say God put it there. Therefore, we should not assume that everything the Scripture says God "imparted" to someone is actually a prophecy or a supernatural communication. We should only accept as such what the Scripture specifically declares...

If we turn to the sacred volume <note>the Bible</note>, therefore, we shall find that everything God reveals to the prophets is imparted to them either by words or by visions, or in both ways at once. The words and the visions were, however, either *real*—meaning actual and independent of the prophet’s imagination—or they were *imaginary*. In the latter case, the imagination of the prophet (even while awake) was affected in such a way that it led him to believe he clearly heard certain words or distinctly saw certain visions.

Now, it appears from Exodus (25:22) that God revealed the laws he wanted given to the Jews through a real voice. We find these words: 

> “And there I will meet with you, and I will speak with you from above the mercy-seat, from between the two cherubim <note>original: "cherubims"; the celestial beings atop the Ark of the Covenant</note>.”

These words show that God made use of an *actual voice* to give them utterance; for there, in the place specified, Moses found God ready to communicate with him whenever he desired. I shall show later that it was by a true voice that the law was made known. 

I also suspect that the voice with which God called Samuel was a real voice, for we find the incident stated this way in 1 Samuel (3:21):

This suggests that God manifested himself to Samuel by *vocal sounds*, or that Samuel heard God speaking. That the words of the Decalogue <note>the Ten Commandments</note> were not actually pronounced by God is the opinion of some among the Jews. They believe that the Israelites only heard a noise, and no distinct words, during which they became mentally aware of the laws of the Decalogue. I have sometimes leaned toward this view myself, because I see that the words of the Decalogue as delivered in Exodus differ considerably from those of the Decalogue as it occurs in Deuteronomy. This circumstance suggests (since God spoke only once) that the Decalogue does not give the very words of God, but is intended to convey his instructions <note>original: "precepts"</note> only. 

Nevertheless, unless violence be done to the plain sense of Scripture, we must admit that the Israelites heard a real voice on the occasion when the Decalogue was communicated. In Deuteronomy (5:4) it is said expressly, “The Lord talked with you face to face,”—that is <note>original: "i. e."</note>, he spoke as two persons hold verbal communication with one another by means of their physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> organs. Therefore, it seems more in accordance with Scripture to conclude that God created a certain real voice by which he revealed the Decalogue; and in our eighth chapter we shall take the opportunity to explain how it happens that the words and instructions of one of these Decalogues differ from those of the other.

Yet, I do not see how those who previously knew nothing of God but his name, and who desired to hear him speak so they could be certain of his existence—I do not see, I say, how their desire would be satisfied by a created being (which has no closer connection to God than any other created thing) saying to them, "I am God." I ask: if God had arranged the lips of Moses—or why only Moses? any created thing—to speak these words, "I am God," would the existence of God have been understood because of that?

It only teaches that he is God; that he alone is to be believed in and worshipped, and that no image of him is to be made, lest his true worship be compromised. 

Since an image or likeness of God had never been seen, none could be fashioned in his resemblance. Instead, an image would have to be modeled after some created thing that *had* been seen; thus, if homage were paid to it, people would think of the thing represented rather than Jehovah, giving the honor and worship due to him alone to a mere object. Nevertheless, Scripture clearly declares in several places that God has a form. When Moses petitioned God to see his glory while conversing with him, he was informed that no man shall see God and live. # OF PROPHECY.

...much nobler than that which belongs to humanity at large. Therefore, I do not believe that anyone except Christ alone ever attained such superiority over others as to have had the precepts of God which lead to everlasting life revealed to him immediately <note>directly; without any middle step</note>, and without the intervention of words or a vision. In my opinion, God manifested himself to the apostles through the mind of Jesus Christ immediately, just as He formerly revealed himself to Moses by the medium of a voice. Consequently, the voice of Christ—even as the voice which Moses heard—may be called the voice of God. In this sense, we may also say that the wisdom of God—that is, the wisdom which is more than human—took on humanity in Christ, and that Christ, consequently, is the way of salvation.

But it is necessary for me here to warn my reader that I do not speak to either affirm or deny those things which some churches declare concerning Christ, for I freely confess that I do not understand them. What I affirm, I derive from the Scriptures alone; and there I nowhere read of God having ever appeared to or spoken with Christ, but of God revealed through Christ to the apostles as the way of life. Finally, I read of the old law having been delivered through an angel or a voice, but not immediately revealed by God to man. Therefore, if Moses spoke face to face with God, as one man speaks with another (that is, by means of their individual physical organs), then it must be maintained that Christ communicated with God in the way of mind with mind.*

Our position, therefore, is that with the exception of Christ, no one has received the revelations of God except by the aid or medium of imagination—namely, by means of words, signs, or visions. # OF PROPHECY.

...imagination, as I shall clearly show in the next chapter. Meanwhile, it seems proper here to ask what is to be understood by the expression, "The spirit of God infused into the prophets," or, "The prophets spoke from or were inspired by the spirit of God." This is an inquiry in which it is important, first, to learn the true significance of the Hebrew word *ruagh* <note>original Hebrew: רוח</note>, commonly translated as "spirit."

Now, in its most simple sense, the word *ruagh* signifies wind or vapor, but it is also used in a great variety of other senses:

1st. In Psalm 135:17, for example, we find the word employed to signify the breath of the mouth: "Neither is there any breath in their mouths." 

2nd. In 1 Samuel 30:12, *ruagh* means strength in the sense of bodily power: "And when he had eaten, his spirit came again to him." 

3rd. The word means courage or moral strength, as in Joshua 2:11: "Neither did there remain any more courage (*ruagh*) in any man." In Ezekiel, the word occurs with the same meaning (2:2): "And the spirit entered into me and set me on my feet." 

4th. The word is further used to signify virtue or aptitude, as in Job, where we find these words (32:8): "There is a spirit in man, and the inspiration of the Almighty gives them understanding." These words are in reply to Elihu <note>In the Book of Job, Elihu is the younger fourth friend who speaks after the three older friends have finished.</note>, who has just expressed himself hesitantly on account of his youth in the presence of Job and his friends, "because they were very old." "Great men," continues the speaker <note>In the biblical text of Job 32, Elihu is the one speaking here, though the author attributes the sentiment to the discussion surrounding Job.</note>, "are not [necessarily] wise, neither do the aged understand judgment," which is as much as if he had said that knowledge and understanding depend on the capacity of each individual man. In nearly the same sense, we find the word employed in Numbers 27:18: "Take Joshua, a man in whom is the spirit." 

5th. The word *ruagh* is still further used to signify conduct or disposition, as in Numbers 14:24: "But Caleb, my servant, because he had another spirit with him, him will I bring into the land," etc. In Proverbs 1:23, we find these words: "I will pour out my spirit (that is, make known my purpose) unto you." 5th, The word signifies will, desire, or mental impulse, as in Ezekiel (1:12), where it is written, “Wherever the spirit was to go, they went,” and in Isaiah (30:1), “Woe to the rebellious children who carry out a plan, but not of my spirit;” and again (29:10), “The Lord has poured out on you the spirit (that is, the desire) of deep sleep.” In Judges (8:3\*) we find this phrase, “Then their spirit was softened,” and here the word implies temper; and in Proverbs (16:32) we are told that “He who is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit (that is, his passions) than he who takes a city,” and yet again in the same book (25:28), “He who has no rule over his own spirit (that is, temper) is like a city without walls.” In Isaiah again (33:11) the word breath (*ruagh* <note>original Hebrew: רוח</note>) evidently signifies an evil disposition, in these words, “Your breath as fire shall devour you.”

The word *ruagh*, moreover, as it signifies a disposition of mind, is used to express all the passions and even states of the soul. We have, therefore, the phrase "lofty spirit" for a proud spirit or pride, "lowly spirit" for humility, "good spirit" for benevolence, "spirit of jealousy" for jealousy, "spirit of lust" for fornication, "spirit of wisdom, of counsel, of fortitude," etc., for these qualities respectively, though, in Hebrew, words are more frequently used as nouns than as adjectives. 

6th, *Ruagh* signifies the mind or soul itself, as in Ecclesiastes (3:19), “All have one breath, and all go into one place.”

# OF PROPHECY.

The heavens are called the "heavens of God" because they are His chariot and His dwelling place. Assyria is titled the "Scourge of God," and Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: Nebuchodonosor</note> is called the "Servant of God," and so on. 

Third, because the thing spoken of is dedicated to God, such as the "temple of God," the "bread of God," or a "Nazarene of God." 

Fourth, because things are made known by the prophets and not revealed by natural understanding; for this reason, the law imparted by Moses is titled the "Law of God." 

Fifth, when things are spoken of in the superlative degree <note>the highest or most extreme form</note>, they are said to be "of God." Thus, very high mountains are called "mountains of God," and a very deep sleep is a "sleep of God." It is in this sense that the prophet Amos (4:11) is to be understood when he portrays Jehovah Himself speaking this way:

> "I have destroyed you as the destruction of God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah,"

That is to say, he destroyed them completely, like that memorable instance of destruction. Since God Himself is speaking, it is impossible to explain the passage appropriately in any other way. The natural wisdom of Solomon is titled the "wisdom of God"; in other words, Solomon was very wise and possessed wisdom far above the ordinary. In the Psalms, great cedar trees are designated "cedars of God" to indicate their unusual size. In 1 Samuel (14:7), we find the expression,

> "And the fear of God fell upon the people,"

This is used to signify that it was a great fear which seized them. In this same way, everything was habitually spoken of that surpassed the understanding of the Jews, and for which the natural causes were unknown to them:

> "Thunder is the muttering or angry voice of God; lightnings are His arrows, etc."

The Jews indeed believed that God kept the winds confined in certain caverns, which they called the "treasures of God." They differed in their views from the Pagans in this only: they thought Jehovah, not Aeolus <note>original: Æolus; the Greek god of the winds</note>, was the ruler of the storm. On the same grounds, miraculous works are called "works of God" or "mighty works." And, indeed, all natural events are the work of God and happen by the Divine will and authority alone. It is in this view that the Psalmist calls the miracles of Egypt the "powers of God," because...

In the Scriptures, we observe that unusual natural events are called "works of God," and trees of massive dimensions are spoken of as "trees of God." It is not surprising, then, that we find men of great stature and strength—even if they were plunderers and oppressors—designated as "sons of God," as we see in the Book of Genesis. Indeed, ancient people in general, both pagans <note>original: heathen</note> and Jews, were accustomed to attributing everything of exceptional excellence to God. When Pharaoh heard Joseph’s interpretation of his dream, he declared that the understanding of the gods lived within him; similarly, Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: Nebuchodonosor</note> told Daniel that he possessed the understanding of the holy gods. Among the Romans <note>original: Latins</note>, it is very common to find exceptional works of art attributed to a "divine hand"—what the Jews would have called the "hand of God."

Consequently, the passages in Scripture that mention the "spirit of God" are easily interpreted and understood. In many places, the words *spirit of God* and *spirit of the LORD* <note>original Hebrew: ruagh Elohim and ruagh Jehovah</note> signify nothing more than a violent and extremely dry or blighting wind. For example, in Isaiah 40:7 we read: "*The grass withers, the flower fades: because the spirit of the Lord blows upon it*." This means the grass was blown upon by a very parching and strong wind. In Genesis 1:2, it is said that the "spirit of God"—meaning a strong wind—moved over the face of the waters. 

In other places, the word *spirit* <note>original Hebrew: ruagh</note> is used to describe a powerful soul. Gideon and Samson, for instance, are spoken of as having "spirits of God"; in reality, they were daring men prepared for any emergency. Likewise, any virtue or power that is beyond the common level is called a "virtue" or "power of God." This appears in Exodus 31:3, where we find these words: "And I will fill him with the spirit of God." As the text itself immediately proceeds to explain, this means he was filled with genius and artistic skill far beyond the common run of men. In Isaiah

The depression <note>original: melancholy</note> of Saul, moreover, is described as an "evil spirit of God," which actually means nothing more than a very intense or deep melancholy. For the servants of Saul, who called the depression with which he was possessed a "melancholy of God," were the ones who suggested that he should summon a musician to his presence. They believed that by playing on the harp, the musician might calm Saul's mind and soothe his ailment <note>original: distemper</note>. This course of action plainly shows that the people around Saul understood the phrase "melancholy of God" to mean a common but very severe depression. 

The expression "spirit of God," again, is used to signify the soul, life, and mind of man, as in Job (27:3): "And the spirit of God is in my nostrils." This is evidently an allusion to what is said in Genesis regarding God breathing the breath of life into the nostrils of man. 

In the same way, Ezekiel, prophesying to the dead (37:14), says: "And I shall give my spirit to you and you shall live," meaning that by breathing on them, he would restore them to life. It is in this same sense that we are to understand the words in Job (34:14-15 <note>The text cites 34:13, but the quote corresponds to 14-15</note>): "If he (God) set his heart upon man, if he gather unto himself his spirit (that is, the mind he has given) and his breath, etc." 

We must also read the passage in Genesis (6:3) this way, where it is said: "My spirit shall not always strive with man, because he also is flesh." The interpretation here is that, from then on, man would act according to the impulses of the flesh and not of the understanding <note>intellect or reason</note>, which he originally had for his guidance. 

In Psalm 51 (10–11), we find this prayerful plea: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me; cast me not away from your presence, and take not your holy spirit from me." The meaning of this becomes obvious when we know that all sins were believed to proceed from the flesh, and that the spirit, mind, or understanding prompted only what is good. * Although some men are gifted with certain advantages that nature has denied to others, it is not said that these men are raised above human nature. # OF PROPHECY.

...prophecy is not common; it does not remain for long with those who possess it, nor does it come to them frequently. On the contrary, prophetic power is rare—very few people possess it, and in those few, it is only manifested at distant and unpredictable intervals. 

Since this is the case, we are led to ask: how did the prophets gain certainty about the things they perceived through the power of their imagination, rather than through the established principles of the understanding? Any answer to this question must be drawn from Scripture itself. Because we have no true or practical science regarding these matters, we cannot explain them using first principles or natural causes. However, we can determine what Scripture teaches about the certainty of prophetic messages, and we will proceed to do so in the following chapter.

<note>
**Imaginary, Imagination.** These words are used by Spinoza to refer to internal, sensory conceptions that occur independently of any outside influence. The parts of the brain where impressions from the sense organs are processed—and where they become mental concepts—can sometimes become active on their own. This causes impressions or concepts that the person mistakenly attributes to the outside world. This is how people "see" ghosts or hear "spirit" sounds while awake, or experience vivid music and banquets in their sleep, or are visited by familiar faces in dreams. 

In this same way, we can account for the idea of "spirit" and the spiritual world in general, which is entirely a creation of our own minds. It has no existence outside of ourselves; it is within us, not without. While some philosophers argue that it is the act of the mind that brings the material world into being, this must be understood carefully. While it is true that the world does not "exist" for us until we exist to perceive it, we have an intuitive certainty that the world existed before we were born and will continue to exist after we are gone. —*Editor's Note*</note>

# CHAPTER II.

## OF THE PROPHET.

From what has been said in the preceding chapter, it appears that prophets were not gifted with any special superiority of intellect, but only with a more vivid power of imagination than the rest of humanity. Indeed, this is clearly shown by the biblical narratives themselves. Solomon, for instance, surpassed all his contemporaries in wisdom, but he did not, for that reason, possess the gift of prophecy. Those highly wise individuals, Heman, Darda, and Kalchol <note>These three men are cited in 1 Kings 4:31 as examples of great wisdom, though they were still surpassed by Solomon.</note>, were not prophets; meanwhile, others—simple uneducated people, and even women such as Hagar, the servant of Abraham—possessed prophetic powers. 

This is consistent with both reason and experience. Those who excel greatly in the strength of their imagination are often less capable of seeing things truly by the pure light of the intellect. On the other hand, those distinguished for the vigor of their understanding usually have a more tempered power of imagination, which is kept under control and remains distinct from pure intelligence. 

Therefore, those who seek wisdom and a knowledge of natural and spiritual things within the writings of the prophets are completely mistaken. I will now proceed to demonstrate this at length. I care little for what superstitious people may say, since the present time, the nature of philosophy, and the subject itself all demand plain speaking.

To proceed systematically, however, I will now show that prophecies have varied in their meaning, not only because of each prophet’s imagination and physical temperament, but also because of the opinions they already held. From this, we can infer that the gift of prophecy never made a prophet wiser or more learned than they already were, as I will explain in more detail shortly. First, we must examine the nature of the prophets' certainty; this is important both for the argument of this chapter and for the overall demonstration I intend to make.

Since imagination does not naturally carry certainty—unlike a clear and distinct idea <note>original: "clear and distinct idea" — A technical term in 17th-century philosophy, particularly Cartesianism, referring to thoughts so self-evident they cannot be doubted.</note>—we must use reasoning to be sure of what we imagine. It follows that prophecy, being a product of the imagination, can never provide certainty on its own. This is why prophets were never certain of God's revelation through the revelation itself, but always required some additional sign or condition. This is clear from Genesis 15:8, where Abraham, after hearing the promise made to him by God, asks for a sign. He did this not because he lacked faith, but so that he might know for certain that it was indeed God making the promise. The same point is even clearer with Gideon, who says to God, "Show me a sign that [I may know] it is you talking with me" (Judges 6:17). God also says to Moses, "And this [shall be] a sign to you, that I have sent you" (Exodus 3:12). Hezekiah, who had long known that Isaiah was a prophet, still asks for a sign by way of...
