These examples are enough to show that prophets always looked for a sign to confirm the things they prophesied through their imagination. This is why Moses warns the people always to demand a sign from a prophet—such as the prediction of a future event—as a guarantee that he was not speaking falsely. In this respect, prophecy is surpassed by <note>original: "yields the palm to" — an idiom meaning to admit defeat or give way to something superior</note> natural knowledge, which requires no external sign because it contains its own certainty by its very nature.

Prophetic certainty, however, was not mathematical, but only **moral** certainty, as is shown in Scripture. For example, Moses (Deuteronomy 14 <note>The instructions regarding false prophets are actually found in Deuteronomy 13 in modern Bibles.</note>) instructs the Jews to put any prophet to death who proposes following new gods, even if he supports his teachings with signs and miracles. Moses explains that "God sometimes sends signs and miracles to test and try the people." Even Christ spoke in very similar terms to his disciples, as seen in Matthew 24:24: "For false messiahs <note>original: "false Christs"</note> and false prophets will appear and perform great signs and wonders to deceive, if possible, even the elect."

Furthermore, Ezekiel clearly teaches (14:9) that God sometimes deceives people through prophets using false revelations: "And if the prophet is deceived when he has spoken a thing, I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet," etc. Micah (1 Kings 22:22) says the same thing regarding the prophets of Ahab, whose false predictions led the king into battle at Ramoth-Gilead, where he was killed.

Now, although all this seems to imply that prophecy and revelation were very uncertain matters, there was still much certainty within them, as previously mentioned. God never deceives those who are truly pious and chosen. According to the old proverb quoted by Samuel (1 Samuel 24:13), and as we gather from the story of Abigail and the language used, we should conclude that God uses the pious as instruments of His mercy, and the wicked as the tools and agents of His wrath. This is clearly seen in the case of Micah mentioned above; although God had decided to deceive...

->THE PROPHET.<-

...Ahab by means of prophets, he only made use of false prophets for this end, revealing things as they would actually happen to the true prophet, who was not forbidden from speaking the truth. Still, as I have said, the certainty of prophecy was only **moral certainty**; <note>In this context, "moral certainty" refers to a high degree of probability or conviction based on character and experience, rather than "mathematical certainty," which is derived from logical or scientific proof.</note> for no man can justify himself before God, nor boast that he is the instrument of God’s mercy <note>original: "clemency"</note>, as Scripture and reality itself declare. For example, the displeasure of God led David to take a census of the people, although Scripture elsewhere provides abundant testimony to his piety. <note>Refers to 2 Samuel 24, where David is moved to take a census, an act later punished as a sin, illustrating that even the most pious individuals can be led into error.</note>

The whole of prophetic certainty was founded upon these three considerations: 

1. That the revealed things were imagined by the prophets in a most vivid manner, just as people are usually affected or impressed by objects while they are awake. 
2. That they were confirmed by signs. 
3. Lastly and especially, that they were the thoughts of prophets who had minds devoted to justice and goodness alone. 

And although Scripture does not regularly mention a sign, it is still to be believed that the prophets always received one; for Scripture does not constantly list all the conditions and circumstances of an event, but often proceeds on the assumption that these are already known. Besides, we may concede that the prophets who foretold or spoke of nothing new—that is, nothing that was not already contained in the Law of Moses—did not require a sign, because what they said was confirmed by the Law. 

The prophet Jeremiah, for example, speaking of the destruction <note>original: "desolation"</note> of Jerusalem, was confirmed by all the other prophets and by the warnings <note>original: "denunciations"</note> of the Law, and therefore he did not require a sign. But Hananiah—who, in opposition to Jeremiah and the rest of the prophets, foretold the speedy restoration of the city—necessarily required a sign. His prediction had to be doubted until the event had declared its truth or falsehood (see <note>original: "vide"</note> Jeremiah 28:9); and as the prediction was not supported by the event in this case, Hananiah was put to death as the punishment for his false prophesying.

Since the assurance which the prophets received from their signs was not mathematical—or such as arises from the...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of prophetic certainty, explaining that because this certainty was "moral" rather than mathematical, the signs and revelations were adapted to the individual prophet's personal characteristics.</meta>

->THE PROPHET.<-

...necessity of the thing perceived or seen, but was only moral, and signs were merely granted to the prophets as additional testimonies. It follows that the signs exhibited must have been in accordance with the opinions and capacity of the prophets. Thus, the sign that would have been enough to make one prophet certain of his prediction would have been completely inadequate to convince another who held different views and opinions. 

The consequence of this was that the signs shown varied with each individual prophet; just as we have shown that the revelation itself varied with every prophet, in harmony with his natural temperament, his imagination, and the kind of opinions he had already embraced. 

Regarding temperament, for example: if the prophet were of a hopeful and lively spirit, his prophecies spoke of victory, peace, abundance, and everything that moves mankind to gladness. If, on the contrary, he were of a sad and gloomy disposition, then disaster, defeat, and every evil became the burden <note>original: "burthen"</note> of his revelation. Hence, as the prophet was mild and merciful, or quick-tempered <note>original: "irascible"</note> and cruel, and so on, he was inclined to receive revelations of either an agreeable or a harrowing nature. 

Again, if the prophet was a man of taste and culture, he received and shared God’s communications in an elegant and ornate style; but if he was unrefined <note>original: "rude"</note> and uncultivated, his revelations were confused and inelegant. 

The same principle holds true regarding the revelations created by the imagination. If the prophet was a farmer <note>original: "rustic"</note>, then oxen, cows, and similar figures were the images that appeared to him. If he was a soldier, he saw armies and their leaders. If he was a courtier, then the royal throne and attending ministers were the images that served the purpose of communication. 

Finally, the prophecy varied according to the specific opinions held by the prophet. The Magi, for instance (see <note>original: "vide"</note> Matthew 2), who believed in the follies of astrology, had the birth <note>original: "nativity"</note> of Christ revealed to them through the imagination of a star appearing in the east. To the fortune-tellers <note>original: "augurs"</note> of Nebuchadnezzar (Ezekiel 21:26), the destruction of Jerusalem was revealed in the entrails <note>The internal organs of a sacrificed animal, used in ancient divination to predict the future.</note> of sacrificial victims, and the king himself...

<summary>This page argues that prophetic revelations were not objective truths but were filtered through the prophet’s individual temperament, social status, and personal beliefs. Consequently, the imagery and tone of a prophecy (whether hopeful, violent, or cultured) reflected the prophet's own mind rather than a singular divine style.</summary>

->THE PROPHET.<-

...had information of the same event from the oracles he consulted, and from the direction of the arrows which he shot into the air over his head. <note>This likely refers to the King of Babylon’s use of divination as described in Ezekiel 21:21.</note> And to conclude, God was revealed as indifferent to and unaware of <note>original: "unwitting"</note> the actions of men to those prophets who believed that men acted of their own free will and personal power. I proceed to demonstrate these several positions one by one <note>original: "seriatim"</note> from the text of Scripture.

The first position is proved by the case of Elisha (2 Kings 3:15), who, so that he might prophesy to Jehoram, requested a musician <note>original: "minstrel"</note> or a musical instrument to be brought to him. It was only after he had been calmed by sweet sounds that he was enabled to speak joyful news to Jehoram and his associates—something he had not been in a condition to do before because of his anger toward the king. For those who are angry with anyone, though they are likely enough to imagine evil, are little inclined to imagine good of them. 

Some, indeed, have said regarding this matter that God does not reveal himself to the angry and the sorrowful, but these persons are plainly dreaming. For Moses, while in anger against Pharaoh and without having recourse to music, foretold that wretched slaughter of the firstborn of Egypt (Exodus 11:5, 8). God was also revealed to Cain in a paroxysm of rage. To Ezekiel, restless with anger, the misery and the stubbornness <note>original: "contumacy"</note> of the Jews were revealed (Ezekiel 3:14). 

Furthermore, Jeremiah—plunged in sorrow and weary of his life—prophesied the calamities that were to befall his countrymen in such dark colors that King Josiah <note>original: "Josias"</note> would not consent to consult him. Instead, he preferred a contemporary female prophetess <note>Huldah, see 2 Kings 22:14</note>; the task of declaring God’s mercy and loving-kindness, which he wished to hear about, seemed more especially adapted to the feminine disposition <note>original: "female genius"</note> (see Chronicles <note>original: "Paralipomena"</note>, Book 2, chapter 35). Micah, also, never prophesied any good to Ahab (which other true prophets did, nevertheless, as appears from 1 Kings 20), but all his life long prophesied evil (1 Kings 22:7 and still more clearly 2 Chronicles 18:7). Prophets, therefore, according to their various temperaments, were more inclined toward revelations of one kind than another.

->THE PROPHET.<-

Furthermore, the style of the various prophets varies greatly in terms of their elegance of language <note>original: "diction"</note>. The prophecies of Ezekiel and Amos are not like those of Isaiah and Nahum, but are written in a much rougher style. Anyone somewhat familiar with the Hebrew tongue who would examine this matter more carefully <note>original: "curiously"</note>, by comparing the different prophets chapter by chapter where the subject matter happens to be the same, would discover a vast difference in their individual styles. 

To cite one or two examples: compare the courtier Isaiah (Isaiah 1:11–20) with the rustic farmer Amos (Amos 5:21–24) in the passages mentioned. Let the structure and reasoning <note>original: "ratiocination"</note> of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 49) writing to Edom be compared with the order and logic of Obadiah; and compare the 40th (verses 19, 20) and 44th (verse 8) chapters of Isaiah with the 8th (verse 8) and 13th (verse 2) chapters of Hosea. These and other instances, when rightly considered, clearly seem to show that God used no particular style in making his communications. Instead, depending on the degree of learning and ability the prophet possessed, the communications were either brief and clear or, on the contrary, they were rough, wordy <note>original: "prolix"</note>, and unclear.

Prophetic representations and symbolic visions <note>original: "hieroglyphics"</note>, although intended to express the same thing, nevertheless varied. For instance, the glory of God leaving the temple was represented differently to Isaiah and to Ezekiel. The Rabbis <note>original: "Rabbins"</note>, in fact, insist that the two representations are nearly identical, arguing that Ezekiel, being an unrefined <note>original: "rustic"</note> person who was overwhelmed by what he saw, simply gave a more particular and detailed account. But unless the Rabbis have a traditional and certain historical record of the matter—which I do not believe for a moment—they are clearly making things up. 

In reality, Isaiah saw seraphim with six wings, while Ezekiel saw living creatures <note>original: "beasts"</note> with four wings. Isaiah saw God in white clothing and sitting on a royal throne, while Ezekiel saw Him as fire. Each undoubtedly believed he saw God in the way or likeness in which he was accustomed to imagining Him.

The visions of the prophets differ greatly in their clarity <note>original: "perspicuity"</note>. The representations given to Zechariah, as we learn from the biblical accounts themselves, were so obscure that he could not understand them without an explanation. Similarly, those of Daniel were so dark that even when they were explained, they remained unintelligible—not only to others but even to the prophet himself. 

This obscurity was not due to any inherent difficulty in the subjects being revealed—for the topics were purely human and did not exceed human understanding, except for the fact that they were predictions of the future. Rather, it was because Daniel's imagination was not as active, nor did he possess the same prophetic power, when he was awake as when he slept. This is evident from the fact that, at the start of his prophecies, he was so terrified that he almost despaired of having the strength to bear their burden <note>original: "burthen"</note>. 

It was likely because of this weakness in his imagination and physical constitution that his visions appeared so dimly; as a result, he could not fully grasp them even with the aid of an explanation. We should also note that the words Daniel heard were only imaginary (as has been demonstrated previously). Therefore, it is not surprising that, in his state of agitation <note>original: "perturbation"</note>, he heard things so indistinctly and imperfectly that he later found them impossible to understand. 

Those who claim that God did not intend to reveal Himself clearly to Daniel seem to have overlooked the words of the angel. The angel expressly states (Daniel 10:14) that he had come to help Daniel understand what would happen to his people in the future <note>original: "latter days"</note>. What was intended has remained a mystery <note>original: "enigma"</note> because there was no one alive at that time whose imagination was strong enough to make a clearer revelation possible. 

Finally, consider the prophets who received the revelation that God was about to take away Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note>. When they tried to convince Elisha that Elijah had merely been moved to another location where they might find him, it became clear that they did not correctly understand the revelation they had received. (I speak only of speculative <note>original: "speculative matters"; here meaning theoretical, scientific, or philosophical ideas as opposed to moral laws</note> matters in this way; for regarding those which bear on morals and conduct, a totally different view is to be taken.) 

I shall proceed with this inquiry at some length, for I consider this subject to be of great importance. I believe I shall be able to show from it that prophecy never made a prophet more learned than he was before, but instead left him in possession of his preconceived opinions. By recognizing this, we shall escape the bondage of feeling ourselves tied down in purely theoretical matters by anything that the prophets have said.

It is indeed wonderful with what eagerness men have constantly tried to persuade themselves that the prophets knew everything that the human understanding could embrace. Although several parts of Scripture clearly inform us that the prophets were ignorant of certain things, the world has preferred to maintain that people simply did not understand those passages of Scripture, rather than admit that the prophets were ignorant of anything. Alternatively, they have striven to twist the words of Scripture so as to make it say what there plainly was no intention of saying. 

But if either of these courses is permitted, the authority of Scripture is finished; for we would then seek in vain to prove anything from Scripture if those things that are most clearly set forth are placed among the obscure or impenetrable matters, or if the plainest text is to be arbitrarily interpreted. 

Nothing in Scripture, for example, is clearer than that Joshua—and the writer of his history as well—was of the opinion that the sun moved around the earth: that the earth was at rest and the sun in motion, and that the sun stood still in the heavens for a certain time upon a certain occasion <note>This refers to Joshua 10, where Joshua commands the sun to stand still. Let us then admit this without hesitation: a sign might appear and Isaiah might prophesy to the king, even if the prophet understood nothing about the actual cause of the miracles he saw.

Moses himself does not fully grasp that God is all-knowing <note>original: "omniscient"</note> and governs all human actions solely by his decrees. Thus in the Song of Moses (Exodus 15:11), he says, "Who among the gods is like to you, O Jehovah?" and further (18:11) Jethro exclaims, "Now I know that the Lord <note>Hebrew: *Jehovah*</note> is greater than all gods"; as if he had said, "Now I am compelled by Moses to admit that Jehovah is greatest among the gods and possesses unique power." Whether Moses believed that those beings who administered in the place of God were created by Jehovah may be doubted, because he said nothing, as far as I know, of their creation or beginning. However, he taught that God <note>Hebrew: *Elohim*</note> brought this visible world from chaos into order, scattered over it the seeds of natural things, and so held the highest power and highest authority over all. 

Furthermore (see <note>original: "vide"</note> Deuteronomy 10:14, 15), by virtue of this supreme right and authority, he had chosen the Hebrew people for himself and given them a certain territory or land to live in, leaving other nations and regions of the earth to the care of other gods, who were his substitutes (Deuteronomy 4:19, 32:8, 9). For this reason, he was called the GOD of the Israelites, or the God of Jerusalem in the singular, while the rest of the gods—those belonging to other nations—were called GODS, in the plural. For this reason, the Jews believed that the country which Jehovah had chosen for himself required a specific <note>original: "peculiar"</note> form of worship, different from the worship adapted to other lands, and that the worship of the gods of other lands was on no account to be tolerated within their own boundaries. 

The Jews even thought that some of the people whom the King of Assyria had brought into the land of Judea were torn to pieces by lions "because they did not know the customs <note>original: "manner"</note> of the gods of that land" (see <note>original: "vide"</note> 2 Kings 17:25, and following <note>original: "et seq."</note>). The Israelites, in fact, knew almost nothing of God, even though he was uniquely revealed to them. He did this not as a philosopher, so that they might enjoy freedom of spirit, but as a <term>legislator</term> <note>a lawmaker who governs through authority and fear of punishment rather than rational persuasion</note>, compelling them to live a good life through commandments issued under the threat of legal penalties. Consequently, the rule of living rightly—the true life consisting of the love and adoration of God—was to them a form of slavery rather than real liberty and a gift of God's grace. Consider the revelation to Cain as an illustration. Cain informs us that God only warned <note>original: "admonished"</note> him to lead a good life—"If you do well," and so on—but taught him nothing about free will or other philosophical topics. Similarly, we see that the revelation of Micah was intended only to inform Ahab of the actual outcome of the battle against the Arameans <note>original: "Aram"</note>. We are only required to believe that much. All the other details set forth in that revelation—such as the true and false spirits of God, or the armies of heaven standing on either side of God, and so on—do not actually concern us. Everyone may believe whatever seems right to them or fits their own way of thinking. 

We should view the reasons given in God’s revelation to Job regarding His power over all things in the same light—assuming such a revelation actually occurred and the author intended to write a factual narrative, rather than an elaborate <note>original: "embroidered"</note> version of his own ideas, as some have suggested. Regardless of which is true, the claims made are entirely in line <note>original: "consonance"</note> with Job's own views and were meant to satisfy him alone; they were not intended to be universal truths or to convince all of humanity.

# CHAPTER III.

## ON THE ELECTION OF THE HEBREW NATION. WAS THE GIFT OF PROPHECY UNIQUE TO THE JEWS?

True happiness consists in the attainment <note>original: "Fruition"</note> of the Highest Good, not in any glory or advantage that one person enjoys while excluding others. Anyone who considers themselves blessed simply because they enjoy something alone, or because they enjoy more than others—or because they are more prosperous in any way than their neighbor—that person knows nothing of true happiness or the soul’s genuine joy. Whatever happiness they taste, if it is not childish or merely sensual, has its source only in envy and a malicious disposition. 

A human being's true happiness consists solely in wisdom and understanding—the study of truth—and in no way depends on being wiser than others or on the rest of the world lacking true understanding. Such a comparison would not add to one's own wisdom or real happiness. Anyone who rejoices for such reasons would, in fact, be rejoicing in the misfortunes of others; they would show themselves to be envious and ill-tempered, and as someone who knows nothing of true wisdom and peace of mind. 

Therefore, when Scripture declares that God had elected <note>Theological term meaning "chosen" for a specific divine purpose or status.</note> the Jews for himself in preference to other nations (Deuteronomy 10:15), that he was near to them and not to others in the same degree (Ibid. 4:4–7), that he had ordained just laws for them alone (Ibid. verse 8), and finally, that he had made himself known to them alone while setting others aside (Ibid. verse 32, etc.), we can only conclude that such reasoning was adapted <note>original: "accommodated"</note>...

<summary>Spinoza argues that true happiness lies in universal wisdom rather than exclusive privilege, suggesting that biblical claims about the Jews being God's "chosen people" were tailored to the specific audience's understanding rather than being absolute truths.</summary>

...language was used that was adapted to the mental state and capacity of the Jews. As has been shown in the preceding chapter, and as Moses himself bears witness (Deuteronomy 9:6–7), the Jews at that time knew nothing of true happiness. For it is obvious that they, as a people, would have been no less happy and prosperous had God called all other nations to salvation as well as them. 

God would have been no less favorable <note>original: "propitious"</note> to the Jews had he chosen to be equally near to other nations. Neither would the laws he gave them have been less just, nor they themselves less understanding, had he given similar laws to all. Furthermore, the signs and wonders he showed them would not have proclaimed his power any less if they had been manifested over a wider range. Nor would the Jews themselves have been less bound to worship him had he chosen to pour out his bounties upon all mankind alike. 

If God, therefore, says to Solomon (1 Kings 3:12) that he had given him more wisdom than any man who had ever lived, or who should ever come after him, this is probably to be understood as meaning no more than that God had given him an exceptionally large measure of understanding. At all events, it seems impossible to believe that God—merely for Solomon’s greater delight <note>original: "delectation"</note>—had promised from then on to bestow no such ample measure of understanding on any other human being. Such a promise could have added nothing to Solomon's own wisdom; nor would a wise king have been less thankful for the Divine generosity <note>original: "beneficence"</note>, had he been informed that God intended to be equally bountiful to everyone.

However, even while admitting that Moses spoke to the Jews in the passages just quoted according to their limited powers of understanding, we do not wish to be seen as denying that God had delivered those laws of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Hebrew Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note> to them alone, or that he had spoken with them only, or, finally, as saying that the Jews had not seen such wonders as no other people had ever witnessed. What we meant to say amounts only to this: Moses, for the reasons already assigned, proceeded as he did so that he might more easily lead the Jews to the worship of the true God. <meta>This page continues the argument that the biblical "election" of the Hebrews was not based on their intellectual or moral superiority, but on their social and political success as a nation, which Spinoza identifies with the natural order of the world.</meta>

<page-num>73</page-num>

the Jews excelled other nations neither in natural knowledge nor in piety, but in very different things. In other words—and here, following Scripture, I use language adapted to their understanding <note>original: "on a level with their capacities"</note>—I say that the Jews were clearly chosen by God ahead of all other nations for reasons other than the virtue of the lives they led or the profound philosophical thoughts <note>original: "sublime speculations"</note> they entertained. It will now be my task to show, point by point <note>original: "seriatim"</note>, on what grounds this preference was based.

Before I begin, however, I would like to explain briefly what I mean by the "government of God," by the "outward and inward help of God," by the "election of God," and finally, by what is called "fate," "fortune," or "destiny." By the "government" or "guidance" of God, I mean the fixed and unchangeable order of nature, or the linked chain <note>original: "concatenation"</note> of natural events. For I have already stated, and will have further opportunity to show, that the universal laws of nature—according to which everything happens—are nothing other than the eternal decrees of God, which always involve eternal truth and eternal necessity. Therefore, whether we say that everything happens according to the laws of nature, or is ordered by the decree and direction of God, we are saying the same thing. 

Furthermore, since the power of all natural things is nothing but the power of God himself—who alone determines and brings everything to pass—it follows that whatever a person (who is himself a part of nature) does to help himself and sustain his existence, or whatever nature provides for this purpose without his effort, is all accomplished through divine power. This is true whether that power acts through human nature or through means that are external to the nature of man. Therefore, whatever human nature can achieve on its own toward preserving its existence may rightly be called the **inner help** of God, and whatever happens for our benefit through the force of things outside of us may be called the **outer help** of God. 

From this basis, we can easily understand what is meant by the "election" of God; for, since no one does anything except by the predetermined order of nature—in other words, by the eternal decree and direction of God—it

<meta>This page continues Spinoza’s argument that "divine election" is not a supernatural favoritism based on intellect or morality, but a natural result of how a society is organized and governed. It follows that no one chooses a specific way of life for themselves, or does anything except by the special calling <note>original: "vocation"</note> of God, who chooses them over others for this way of life or for this particular work. Finally, by "fortune" or "destiny," I mean nothing more than God’s guidance, in the sense that he governs human affairs through external and unexpected causes. With these points established, let us return to our subject: discovering why the Hebrew nation was said to be chosen by God as his people above all other nations.

Everything we rightfully desire can be grouped into these three categories: 
1. To understand things through their primary causes <note>The fundamental principles or origins of how things work.</note>.
2. To master our passions or develop virtuous habits.
3. To live our lives in safety and health. 

The means that directly support the first and second categories—which can be seen as the immediate and effective causes <note>original: "proximate and efficient causes"</note>—are built into human nature itself. Therefore, gaining knowledge and virtuous habits is entirely within our own power, or depends solely on the laws of human nature. For this reason, we can confidently say that these gifts do not belong to any specific nation but are—and always have been—common to the entire human race. To think otherwise would be to daydream and imagine that nature once created different species of humans. 

On the other hand, the means that ensure a safe life and good health consist mainly of external factors. These are called "gifts of fortune" because they mostly depend on the flow of outside events whose causes we often do not understand; in this area, the foolish can be just as happy or unhappy as the wise. Even so, human planning and alertness are extremely helpful in achieving a secure life and avoiding harm from other people, wild animals, or negative influences. To achieve this, both reason and experience show that there is no better or more certain way than establishing a society or state. This society should be governed by clear laws, occupy a specific territory, and unite the strength of all its members into a single body—specifically, the body of—

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the three categories of human desire—knowledge, virtue, and physical security. Spinoza has just argued that while knowledge and virtue are universal to all humans, physical security depends on the specific way a society is organized.</meta>

...a society, commonwealth, or state. However, establishing and maintaining such a society requires significant intelligence <note>original: "genius"</note> and vigilance. Therefore, the most secure and long-lasting society—the one least vulnerable to chance accidents—is one founded and governed by wise, prudent, and alert people. Conversely, a state established and ruled by those of a less sophisticated <note>original: "ruder mould"</note> nature will depend more on luck and will not last as long. 

If a state founded and governed in this latter way does endure for a significant length of time, it will be due to external guidance rather than its own internal strength. If it survives great dangers and even prospers, the people will inevitably admire and worship the "guiding hand of God." By this, I mean that God acts through hidden external causes rather than through the inherent mind or nature of man. In such cases, events happen unexpectedly and against all odds, occurring in ways that are naturally regarded as miraculous.

Nations are primarily distinguished from one another by the institutions and laws they live under and are governed by. It was on these grounds—not because of superior intelligence or a more noble soul—that the Jews were "chosen" by God in preference to other nations. Their political structure <note>original: "polity"</note> was designed to ensure prosperity, to expand their power <note>original: "empire"</note>, and to last for a very long time. 

This is clearly stated in the Bible itself. Anyone who reads the Hebrew Scriptures, even briefly, will see that the Jews excelled other nations in only one way: they successfully managed the affairs that lead to a secure life and survived many great dangers, primarily through external divine help. In other respects, the Jews seem to have been no different from other nations, to whom God was just as favorable. Regarding their intellectual understanding (as shown in the previous chapter), the Jews were not unique; they held very limited <note>original: "poor"</note> ideas about...

<meta>This page continues the author's argument against the idea that the Jewish people were chosen by God for all eternity. It shifts from discussing the Apostle Paul's views to examining Old Testament passages that demonstrate the conditional nature of the "election."</meta>

<page-num>85</page-num>

There are other passages besides these that are often referenced, especially by the Pharisees <term>A prominent Jewish sect during the Second Temple period known for strict adherence to traditional and written law.</term>; but once I have replied to the two most frequently quoted, I believe I will have answered them all. My task will be neither long nor difficult, as I will show from the Scriptures themselves that God did not choose <term>original: "elect"; the theological concept of being "chosen" by God.</term> the Jews for all eternity. Instead, he chose them only on the same conditions as he had previously chosen the Canaanites. As we have seen earlier, the Canaanites also had their own priests to religiously conduct the worship of their god, yet God eventually rejected them because of their luxury, apathy, and immoral behavior. 

Moses warns the Israelites (Leviticus 18:27–28) that they must not defile themselves with sexual immorality <note>original: "incests"</note> as the Canaanites had done, lest the earth should spit them out just as it had cast out the nations that lived in those lands before them. In the book of Deuteronomy (8:19–20), we see the Jews threatened, in very plain words, with total ruin and rejection if they are disobedient:

> “And if you ever forget the Lord your God and follow other gods, and serve and worship them, I warn you today that you will surely perish. Just like the nations which the Lord is destroying before your face, so shall you perish, because you would not obey the voice of the Lord your God.”

There are indeed many similar passages in the Old Testament where we read plainly that God had not chosen the Hebrew nation for himself absolutely, unconditionally, and forever. Therefore, if the prophets are found preaching to the Jews about a "new and eternal covenant of grace and love," this must be understood as referring only to the good and righteous among them. By maintaining customs and ceremonies that are always opposed to those of other peoples—and especially by the rite of circumcision, which they observe most religiously—they have drawn the hatred of everyone else upon themselves.

# CHAPTER IV.

## OF THE DIVINE LAW.

The word Law, taken in an absolute sense, signifies that by which individuals of the same species act in a certain, fixed, and determined manner. This occurs either through natural necessity or because it depends on the will and pleasure of an agent. A law depending on natural necessity is one that follows inevitably from the very nature of things. On the other hand, a law that depends on the will and pleasure of an agent—specifically man—and which might be more appropriately called *Jurisprudence* <note>original: "Jus"</note>, is prescribed by men for themselves and others to ensure the safety and convenience <note>original: "commodity"</note> of life, or for any other reason. 

For example, it is a universal law of all physical matter <note>original: "ponderable matter"</note> and a natural necessity that bodies in motion, when striking <note>original: "impinging"</note> other bodies, lose as much of their own motion as they communicate to the others. Similarly, it is a law that follows necessarily from the constitution of human nature that when we remember one particular thing, we immediately bring to mind another similar thing, or something that we experienced <note>original: "were cognizant of"</note> at the same time as the first. 

However, when men surrender—or are forced to surrender—any of the rights they possess by nature and restrict themselves to a specific way of living, this depends on human will and choice. And although I admit without reservation that all things are determined in their existence and their actions in certain definite ways by virtue of the universal laws of nature, I still maintain that the specific kind of law we are discussing depends on the human will.

<summary>This chapter defines the concept of law, distinguishing between laws of natural necessity (like physics and psychology) and human-made laws (jurisprudence) created for social stability.</summary>
<keywords>Divine Law, natural necessity, jurisprudence, human nature, physics, social contract, universal laws</keywords>

The will and consent of man. 1. Because man, in so far as he is a part of nature, is also a part of the power of nature. Consequently, whatever happens from nature—in so far as we conceive this to be determined by human nature—still follows, and necessarily follows, from human agency. Therefore, we say with perfect propriety that laws for the regulation of society depend on the will, pleasure, and consent of man. They are clearly so immediately connected with the faculties of the human mind that, although the mind itself (in its power of perceiving things in their relations to the true and the false) can be perfectly well conceived without these social laws, it cannot be conceived without the idea of divine or necessary law, as we have just defined it.

2. I have also said that jurisprudence <note>original: "jurisprudence," referring here to the theory or philosophy of human law</note> or human social law depends on the will of man, because we ought always to define and explain things by their immediate causes. General considerations of the order of nature and the linking <note>original: "concatenation"</note> of causes cannot assist us in the least when considering particular things. Furthermore, as we are clearly ignorant of the actual coordination and linking of things—in other words, the way and manner in which all things in the universe are connected and chained together—we see that, regarding the practical customs of life, it is better to consider things in their immediate connections as contingencies or possibilities, rather than as absolute necessities. So much for the definition of law considered in an absolute sense.

However, as the word "Law" has been applied to common things by an extension of its meaning, and as the term usually implies nothing more than a precept or command which men may choose to observe or neglect—something which human capacity may violate, and not something beyond human power—it seems necessary to define law in a more specific manner: as a rule of conduct which man imposes on himself and others for a definite end. # DIVINE LAW

The true ends and objects of law are understood by very few. However, because the great majority of mankind is incapable of grasping these, the course which legislators have taken to enforce obedience upon everyone alike is this: they have proposed an object entirely different from that which necessarily follows from the nature of laws. They occasionally promise rewards most prized by the common people for their observance, but much more constantly attach pains and penalties—those most dreaded—for their neglect or violation. Legislators may be said to have undertaken to control mankind in the same way as a horse is controlled by his food <note>original: "provender"</note>, the bit, and the spur. 

From this, it has come to pass that it is usual to designate as "law" those rules of conduct imposed by a certain man or by certain men on all the rest of their tribe or nation. It is also common to speak of those who obey these laws as living under them, and in a sort of slavery. And the truth is, that he who only gives others their due through fear of the prison or the gallows <note>original: "gibbet"</note> obeys an alien authority and acts under the constraint of an evil which he fears; the title of *just* does not belong to him. 

He, on the contrary, who renders to everyone his due because he knows the true reason for laws and their necessity, acts with a resolved soul—not from any foreign authority, but of his own proper will—and truly deserves the title of *just*. This, without doubt, is what the Apostle Paul intended to say when he tells us that they who lived under the law could not be justified by the law (Romans 3:20). Justice, indeed, according to the definition usually given of it, consists in a strong and settled will to render to everyone his due. This is why Solomon says that "it is joy to the just to do judgment, but destruction to the wicked" (Proverbs 21:15).

Since, then, law—as commonly understood—is nothing more than the rule of life which men prescribe to themselves and others for certain ends, it is therefore to be distinguished into Human and Divine. By human law, I understand that which applies to the security of life and estate, and the advantage of the commonwealth. By divine...

# DIVINE LAW

By law, I mean that which solely regards the highest good or true happiness: namely, the knowledge and love of God. The reason why I call this law "divine" is because of the nature of the supreme good, which I shall explain here as briefly and as clearly as I can.

Since our better part consists in our understanding, it seems certain that if we wish to seek what is truly good for us, we should strive above all things to make our understanding as perfect as possible; for our chief good ought to consist in the perfection of this understanding. All our knowledge and certainty—everything that removes doubt from the mind—depends entirely on the knowledge of God. Because nothing exists or can even be conceived without God, and because we doubt everything as long as we lack a clear and distinct idea of God, it follows that our supreme good and highest perfection depend on the knowledge of God alone. 

Furthermore, since nothing exists or can be conceived without God, it is certain that everything in nature involves the concept of God. The more intimately we know natural things, the larger and more adequate a conception of God we acquire. To know an effect through its cause is nothing more than knowing a specific property of that cause; therefore, the more we know of natural things, the more we enter into the essence of God, who is the cause of all things. Thus, the whole of knowledge resolves itself into a knowledge of God, in which it may be said to entirely consist. 

The same conclusion follows from this: a person is more perfect according to the nature and perfection of that which they love and strive to know above all things. Therefore, the person who is necessarily the most perfect, and who participates most fully in the supreme good, is the one who delights most in the intellectual cognition <note>original: "cognition"; here meaning the process of knowing or understanding through reason</note> of God, the most perfect of beings. Our supreme happiness and our highest joy, therefore, resolve themselves into a knowledge and love of God. The means calculated to attain this end of all human thought and striving—namely, the knowledge and love of God, insofar as we have an idea of him—may well...

They may be called his commandments, for they are prescribed to us by God himself, insofar as God dwells in our souls; and so the rule of life which regards this end is most properly entitled the Divine Law. Assuming, then, that the love of God is the supreme good, the chief end of man, and the purpose of all human action, it follows that he only observes the divine law who is diligent to love God—not from affection for any other thing, such as sensual pleasure, fame, riches, etc., and not from fear of punishment or any other motive, but from this only: that he knows God, or rather that he knows the knowledge and love of God to be the highest bliss. The first precept of the divine law, therefore—indeed its sum and substance—is to love God unconditionally as the supreme good. I say unconditionally, and not from any love or fear of anything else; for the idea of God informs us that he is the supreme good, and that the knowledge and love of HIM are the final goal toward which all our thoughts and actions are to be directed. 

The carnal or animal man <note>original: "animalis homo"; referring to one driven by physical instincts rather than reason</note>, however, cannot understand this; to him such a proposition even seems absurd. This is because he has too poor a conception of God, and because in our idea of the supreme felicity <note>supreme happiness or bliss</note> he finds nothing which he can handle, nothing which he can eat or drink—nothing, in short, which affects his sensual nature wherein he finds his chief delight—nothing, in a word, but lofty speculation and purity of mind. But those who are aware that there is nothing more excellent than understanding and integrity of mind conclude differently and more justly.

If, then, we turn to the nature of divine law, as it has just been defined, we shall find that it is:

1st, Universal or common to all men; for we have inferred it from the whole nature of man.

2nd, It does not require faith in historical narratives or historians. Faith in history, however, although of itself inadequate to impart to us a knowledge of God or to fill us with the love of him, may nevertheless be useful. The perusal of historical records, as they bear upon the social state and condition, may be extremely edifying. # DIVINE LAW

If we perceive eternal truths as depending solely on the necessity of the divine nature and intelligence, rather than on the nature of a triangle itself, then we use the terms "will" or "decree" of God to describe what we also call His "intelligence." Therefore, in respect to God, we are affirming the exact same thing whether we say that He has understood from eternity, or that He has decreed and willed from eternity, that the three angles of a triangle shall be equal to two right angles. 

From this, it follows that affirmations and negations made in connection with God always involve eternal necessities and truths. If, for example, God said to Adam that He willed that Adam should not eat of the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, it would imply a contradiction for Adam to have the power to eat of that fruit. It would have been impossible for Adam to eat of it, because a divine decree must involve an eternal necessity and an eternal truth. 

However, since Scripture tells us that God gave such a command to Adam, and yet Adam ate of the fruit, we must conclude that God only revealed to Adam the evil that would befall him if he ate of the fruit, but did not decree that the occurrence of this evil was a matter of absolute necessity. <note>original: "Deum Adamo malum tantum revelavisse quod eum necessario sequeretur si de illa arbore comederet, at non necessitatem consecutionis illius mali." Translation: God only revealed to Adam the evil that would necessarily follow if he ate from that tree, but not the necessity of the occurrence of that evil.</note> 

Consequently, Adam understood the commandment given to him not as an eternal and necessary law, but as an ordinance <term>a decree or authoritative order</term> accompanied by reward or punishment—not as a natural consequence of the act itself, but as if by the arbitrary will and pleasure of a sovereign prince. Therefore, the commandment in question should be regarded as having been made specifically for Adam. It was a "law" only because of his lack of understanding <note>original: "defect of apprehension"</note>, and God stood in relation to him as a legislator or a prince stands to his people. 

For the same reason—namely, the lack of knowledge <note>original: "cognitionis"</note>—the Decalogue <term>The Ten Commandments</term> was a law only in respect to the Jews. Because they did not know the existence of God as an eternal truth, when it was revealed to them in the Decalogue that God existed and alone was to be worshipped, they must have perceived this as a law in the social sense...

# DIVINE LAW

<page-num>97</page-num>

This is because, had God spoken to them immediately—without making use of physical means for his communication—they would have understood the revelation not as a law in the human sense, but as an eternal truth. The same thing may be said of all the laws spoken by the prophets in the name of God; they were never fully understood as decrees of God that involve eternal truths and necessities. 

Regarding Moses himself, for example, it may be argued that although he saw from the revelations given to him how the people of Israel might be united in a specific country and a separate community or empire established—and further, how the people might be inclined toward obedience—he did not perceive, nor was it revealed to him, that the methods he used were the absolute and best means for achieving his goal. Moses had no perfect assurance that even if the children of Israel were united in common obedience within the promised land, the intended purpose would follow. 

In short, Moses understood the revelations made to him not as eternal truths and necessities, but as precepts <note>original: "precepts and institutes"; rules or established laws</note> and regulations. He therefore prescribed them as laws of God in the strictly human sense. In doing so, he caused the Israelites to imagine God as a king, ruler, or legislator—as merciful, just, jealous, and so on—even though all these attributes belong to human nature alone and ought not to be associated with the Divine nature. 

In this way, and from this perspective, we should view those prophets who have delivered laws in the name of God. But Christ is an exception to this rule. Regarding him, I hold that we must conclude he perceived things immediately, adequately, and truly. For although Christ also appears to have delivered laws in the name of God, he was not so much a prophet as he was the "mouth of God." God revealed certain things to mankind through the mind of Christ immediately, just as He had formerly made revelations mediately <note>indirectly, through an intervening medium</note> through angels (see chapter 1), by using spoken words, visions, dreams, and the like. Therefore, it would be as irrational to maintain that God adapted his revelations to the personal opinions of Christ as it would be to say He had formerly adapted them to the opinions of the angels.

->7<-

<summary>The author argues that while Moses and the prophets perceived God's revelations as human-like laws and decrees, Christ understood them as immediate, eternal truths. This distinction explains why God is often described with human emotions in the Old Testament, whereas Christ acted as the direct "mouth of God."</summary>

# DIVINE LAW

<margin>The nature of Christ's revelation</margin>
His revelations were adapted to the opinions of "angels" (that is, to voices, visions, dreams, and so on) in order to impart to the prophets the things that were to be made known. An idea more absurd than this can hardly be conceived, especially when we know that Christ was sent as a teacher not to the Jews only, but to the whole of humankind. It was not enough, therefore, that his ideas should be adapted to Jewish views and opinions; they required to be in harmony with the opinions common to the whole of mankind—in other words, with absolutely true and universal ideas. 

Indeed, when we say that God revealed himself immediately to Christ (that is, to the mind of Christ) and not mediately <note>original: "mediately"; meaning through an intermediary or middle-man</note> as he did to the prophets by words and signs, nothing more is to be understood than that Christ perceived revealed things truly, adequately, and in themselves—or that he comprehended them. For a thing is only really comprehended when it is perceived by the mind itself without the interference of words or signs. 

Christ, therefore, perceived revealed things in themselves and adequately. If he ever prescribed them as rules or laws, it was only because of the ignorance and obstinacy of the people he addressed. Standing as the representative of God, he adapted himself to the capacity of the common people <note>original: "the vulgar"</note> and spoke more clearly than the prophets generally had done, though still somewhat obscurely, often teaching by parables—especially when he was addressing those to whom it was not yet given to understand heavenly things (Matthew 18:10, and following). 

To those to whom it was given to know the mysteries of heaven, Christ undoubtedly taught eternal truths rather than prescribing them as rules or commandments. In this sense, he declared that he freed his disciples from the slavery of the law, even while he confirmed and established the law by engraving it deeply on their hearts. Paul seems to point to this truth in several places (Romans 7:6 and 3:28); yet he nowhere declares himself altogether openly on the matter, but speaks instead, as he says (Romans 3:6, 19), in a purely human manner. This, indeed, he shows sufficiently when he speaks of God as "just," which is done only because of the weakness of the flesh and the limited human understanding.

<summary>The author argues that while prophets received revelation through signs and visions adapted to their culture, Christ possessed a direct, intellectual grasp of universal truth. He suggests that Christ only framed these truths as "laws" to accommodate the ignorance of the masses, while teaching eternal truths to those capable of understanding.</summary>

# DIVINE LAW

To meet the views of the people, who always connect with the idea of God such qualities as mercy, grace, anger, jealousy, and so on. In 1 Corinthians (3:1–2), the language of Paul is at first plainly adapted to the ideas of carnal <note>original: "carnal men"; referring to those focused on worldly or physical desires rather than spiritual understanding</note> men; for further on, he teaches absolutely that the mercy and anger of God do not depend on the actions of men, but on the sole nature—in other words, the will—of God. Previously, indeed, Paul has said that no man is justified by the works of the law, but by faith alone; by which we are to understand the entire assent of the soul. And finally he says (Ibid. 8:9) that no man is blessed unless he has in him the mind of Christ, whereby he comes to know the laws of God as everlasting truths. Let us conclude, therefore, that it is only to meet the common <note>original: "vulgar apprehension"</note> understanding, or from a lack of right understanding, that God is spoken of as just, merciful, jealous, and so on, as though he were a king and lawgiver. God in reality acts and governs all things by the necessity of his nature and his all-perfection alone: his decrees and his volitions always involve eternal truths and eternal necessities. So far the first point which I proposed to illustrate.

2. We now pass to our second head, and turning to the Sacred Volume <note>The Bible</note>, we seek to know what is taught therein regarding natural light <note>The innate human capacity for reason and understanding</note> or understanding, and of divine law. At the very outset, we encounter the history of the first man, and the narrative of God's command to Adam not to eat of the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil. This seems to signify that God commanded Adam to do good, and to proceed under the guidance of the good in itself, and not merely as it is the opposite of evil; or otherwise, that he should seek good from the love of good, not from the fear of evil. For he, as we have shown, who does good from true knowledge and love of good, acts freely and with constancy of soul; while he who acts from fear of evil acts under the constraint of evil as a slave, and as if he lived under the authority of another. The command which God gave to Adam (interpreted as above) may therefore be said to embrace the sum of the divine natural law. It accords absolutely with the dictates of the

That life or understanding is the only thing which gives laws to the wise is further and plainly taught by our Sage <note>original: "Sage"; referring to Solomon</note>, who says (Proverbs 13:14), "The law of the wise is a fountain of life." From the text quoted above, this law is seen to be understanding itself. Again, he teaches in the plainest terms (Proverbs 3:13) that understanding gives joy and true peace of mind to man: "Happy is the man that finds wisdom, and the man that gets understanding." The reason for this is (verses 16, 17) that "Wisdom gives length of days, and riches, and honor; her ways being ways of pleasantness and all her paths peace." 

Therefore, according to Solomon, the wise alone live in peace and equanimity <term>equanimity</term><note>mental calmness and composure, especially in a difficult situation</note>. They are not like the wicked, whose minds are disturbed by opposing emotions, so that, as Isaiah says (Isaiah 57:20, 21), "They are like the troubled sea, for them there is no peace."

But what we must particularly observe in these Proverbs of Solomon—inasmuch as our views are greatly confirmed by them—are the sentiments contained in the third verse of the second chapter. There we find these words: "If you cry after knowledge and lift up your voice for understanding... then shall you understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God; for the Lord gives wisdom; out of his mouth comes knowledge and understanding." 

By these words, Solomon clearly declares two things: first, that wisdom or understanding alone teaches us that God is to be reverenced with knowledge and worshipped in a truly pious spirit; and second, that wisdom and understanding flow from God, who is the only giver of these inestimable gifts. We have insisted on this truth ourselves when we showed that all our understanding and all our knowledge depend on the idea or knowledge of God alone, with whom they originate and by whom they are made perfect. 

Solomon proceeds immediately after (Proverbs 2:9) to teach that this wisdom involves true principles of ethics and politics. "When wisdom enters into your heart," he says, "and knowledge is pleasant to your soul, discretion shall preserve you, understanding shall keep you; then shall you understand righteousness and judgment and equity, yes, every good path." Now, all of this plainly agrees with natural knowledge.

# CHAPTER V.

## OF RELIGIOUS CEREMONIAL OBSERVANCE, AND FAITH IN HISTORICAL NARRATIVE. OF THE REASONS WHY RITES AND CEREMONIES ARE USEFUL, AND OF THOSE WHO FIND THEM NECESSARY.

In the preceding chapter, we have shown that the divine law—which renders mankind truly happy and teaches the perfect way of life—was of universal application and common to all. Indeed, we have deduced this law from the very nature of man and shown it to be innate, written, as it were, on his heart and mind. 

But when we come to speak of rites and ceremonies—at least those which in the Old Testament are declared to have been instituted specifically for the Jews, and so adapted to their condition that they might be observed by the people as a whole, though perhaps not by every individual member of the Hebrew community—we see for certain that they do not belong to the code of the divine law. In themselves, they contribute nothing of necessity either to mental happiness or to a virtuous life. 

They have reference, in fact, to the special "election" <note>The theological concept of being chosen by God for a specific purpose.</note> of the Jews; in other words, and as has been shown in our third chapter, they refer to the mere temporal well-being of the body and to the prosperity and peace of the Hebrew commonwealth. Therefore, except in connection with state policy, they are inapplicable and of no use. If ordinances of this description are consequently classified in the Old Testament with the laws of God, this is only because they—

This includes ceremony and observance of every kind; these being mere institutions, not good in themselves, and not written in the heart and understanding of man. Besides these, there are other passages in Scripture which have the same effect; but quoting the two above seems sufficient.

Furthermore, it appears from Scripture that ceremony and observance are no aids to true happiness, but rather that they relate to the temporal prosperity of the State. For ceremonial observance, Scripture promises nothing but personal benefits and sensual delights; while for the observance of the universal divine law, it assures us of true happiness. In the entirety of the five books commonly ascribed to Moses <note>The Pentateuch: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note>, nothing is promised but such temporal felicities as honor, renown, victory, riches, and health. 

And although many things concerning morals are scattered through these five books, they are never presented as universal moral precepts to be observed by all men. Instead, they are presented only as commands especially adapted to the capacity and character of the Hebrew people, having a specific bearing on the interests of their State alone. For example, Moses does not teach the Jews as a doctor or prophet that they are to commit no murder or that they are not to steal; rather, he speaks as a legislator and prince, or magistrate. He does not recommend these precepts by an appeal to reason, but adds pains and penalties to their infraction—penalties which may, and indeed ought to, vary according to the character of every nation, as experience proves. 

The command not to commit adultery, too, refers only to the advantages of the commonwealth and the rights of individuals. Had he intended to state a moral precept that would impact not only the conveniences or proprieties of public and private life, but the true happiness of all, then he would have condemned not only the outward act but the frame of mind that led or consented to it. This is what Christ did, who taught universal moral doctrines only (see Matthew 5:28*), and this is the reason why Christ—

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the historical development and purpose of Jewish religious ceremonies, specifically addressing their decline during the Babylonian captivity and their origins prior to the Mosaic Law.</meta>

They were great sticklers for their ceremonial, retaining the whole or the greater part of it, rather, as it seems, through hostility to the new Christian sect than with any purpose or thought of being therefore particularly acceptable to God. For after the first destruction of their city, when the Jews were led captive to Babylon, as they were not then divided into sects, they forthwith neglected their ceremonies. They may indeed be said to have abandoned the whole of the Law of Moses, suffering the code of their country to sink into oblivion and beginning themselves to mix with the nations among whom they were domiciled. All this appears plainly from the books of Ezra <note>original: "Esdras"</note> and Nehemiah.

It is not doubtful, therefore, that the Jews paid no more attention to the Law of Moses after the destruction of their empire than they had done before its establishment. For while they lived among other nations, and before their departure from Egypt, they had no peculiar laws, observing no code but that of natural right <note>The concept of universal moral principles discoverable by reason, rather than revealed religion.</note>, and doubtless conforming to the system of jurisprudence of the country in which they dwelt. As the patriarchs offered sacrifices to God, however, I presume that this was done to keep the flame of devotion alive in their souls, as they had been accustomed to sacrifices from the days of their youth. All, indeed, from the time of Enoch, were certainly habituated to sacrifices as the grand incentives to devotion [or means of making themselves acceptable to God]. 

The patriarchs, consequently, offered sacrifices to God, not in consequence of any divine command, or because taught to do so by the fundamental principles of divine or natural law, but in obedience to the uniform custom of their age. Or, if they sacrificed because of any special command, this was no other than that of the law of the land in which they dwelt, and in which the same rite was observed, as we have shown in our third chapter when speaking of Melchizedek <note>A mysterious king and priest mentioned in Genesis who predates the formal Jewish priesthood.</note>.

And now I think I have sufficiently established my view of the significance of rites and ceremonies as regards the people on the authority of Scripture. But I have still to...

# RELIGIOUS CEREMONIES

I will now show in what way, and for what reason, the ceremonial laws of the Hebrews contributed to the establishment and support of their empire; I shall proceed to do this as briefly as possible.

Society—or a State—is not only most useful because it enables us to live securely against the assaults of enemies, but it is also advantageous, and even necessary, on many other grounds. Unless men were disposed to cooperate and to lend each other mutual assistance, no individual would have the talent or the time necessary to maintain their own comfort. Not everyone is equally fit for every kind of work, and no single person is capable of providing everything indispensable even for themselves. Strength and time, I say, would fail anyone who, alone and single-handed, attempted to plow, sow, reap, grind, bake, brew, weave, stitch, and so on—too many tasks to mention, yet all of them absolutely necessary to support life. Furthermore, I have said nothing of the arts and sciences, which are all indispensable for the improvement of mankind and for their comfort and well-being. 

We see those who live in a state of barbarism, without a polity <note>original: "polity"; here meaning a structured system of civil government</note>, passing miserable lives, barely raised in condition above the beasts of the field. And even they, wretched and unorganized as they are, could not procure the few things they have without some kind of mutual assistance and cooperation. Were men constituted by nature so as to require nothing but that which right reason demands, society would require no laws; it would suffice then to teach men true moral doctrine, so that they would do of their own accord and free will that which is truly good and useful.

But human nature is constituted very differently. All people indeed strive after what they think will be advantageous to themselves; however, they do not do this in accordance with the dictates of right reason. Instead, they are mostly driven by mere desire and swayed by those appetites and passions of the mind which never consider the future or the reasonableness of things. Hence it follows that no State could exist without authority and power at its head, and consequently without laws, which moderate and restrain...

...or restrain human desires and passions, which would otherwise be prone to go uncontrolled. Human nature, however, will not long submit to any merely arbitrary or absolute control. As Seneca the tragedian says, "No one has ever exercised violent authority for long; only moderation endures" <note>original Latin: "Violenta nemo imperia continuit diu; moderata durant." from Seneca's *Troades*</note>. For as long as men act out of fear alone, they do that which they most dislike; they do not consider the reason, the utility, or the necessity of what they are doing. They have no concern except to escape the penalties with which they are threatened. 

Indeed, under such a system of arbitrary control, men cannot help but rejoice when misfortune befalls their ruler, even if they themselves should suffer along with him. Furthermore, they cannot help wishing him ill, and where they are able, they will not fail to inflict it. Again, there is nothing men can endure less than serving their equals or being governed by them. Finally, there is nothing more difficult than taking away liberties once they have been granted.

From these premises, it follows:

**First:** Either the whole community (if this were possible) should hold authority together, so that everyone might be seen as serving himself and no one as serving his fellow; or, if a few or only one person be entrusted with the supreme authority, he or they ought to be something above the common level of humanity—or should at least use every effort to persuade the common people <term>vulgar</term> <note>original: "vulgar"; here meaning the general populace or uneducated masses rather than a slur</note> that they are so.

**Secondly:** The laws of the State, however it is structured, should be such that men are restrained not so much by fear, but rather led by the hope of some advantage which they greatly desire; in this way, everyone will do his duty heartily and willingly.

**Lastly:** Since obedience consists in this—that commands are carried out solely on the authority of the person commanding—it follows that where authority belongs to everyone and the laws are made by common consent, no one can be said to rule and no one to obey. In a State so constituted, whether the laws are increased or diminished in severity, the people nevertheless remain equally free, seeing as they do not act under the authority of another, but by virtue of their own consent. It is very different where one person alone possesses...

Having introduced these general views, let us return to the Hebrew Republic <note>original: "Hebrew Republic"; referring to the ancient Israelite state as a political entity</note>. The Jews, upon their initial departure from Egypt, were no longer subject to the laws of any other nation. They felt themselves at liberty to institute their own system of jurisprudence <note>the theory or philosophy of law</note>, to make new laws, to establish their authority wherever they could, and to take possession of territory whenever they were strong enough. 

But they never showed themselves less capable than when attempting reasonable legislation and self-government. The people were mostly uncivilized in their manners, and every finer feeling had been blunted by long-continued and grievous slavery. The chief authority, therefore, had to be entrusted to one person whom all the rest would obey—one who would prescribe laws for the nation and, ultimately, be the interpreter of his own decrees. 

Now Moses, being more highly endowed than any of his contemporaries, naturally asserted and readily obtained this supremacy. He persuaded the people that he was divinely called and proved his title to their obedience by many signs and wonders (Exodus 14 and 19). On these grounds, he based his system and prescribed laws to the people. However, he always took special care that they should do his bidding of their own free will, rather than out of fear. He was led to adopt this course by two principal considerations: namely, the rebellious or contumacious <note>stubbornly disobedient or rebellious</note> temper of the people, who would not endure being driven by fear alone; and the constant state of warfare in which, by force of circumstances, the Jews were required to live. Now, for success in arms, it is much more necessary to encourage the soldier with the hope of honor and reward than to force him to do his duty through threats of punishment. In this way, everyone strives to distinguish themselves through daring and magnanimity <note>greatness of spirit and courage</note>, rather than merely seeking to escape notice or punishment while exposing himself as—

Moses, therefore, was led to institute the Hebrew Republic on the basis of virtue and a divine mission, in order that the people might be induced to do their duty from devotion rather than from fear. Besides, he was abundantly bountiful in providing immediate earthly benefits <note>original: "temporal favours"</note> and was lavish with promises for the future. Nor are his laws as severe as is often supposed; this is a fact of which anyone may satisfy himself who carefully studies them, especially if he pays attention to all the legal requirements that must be met before anyone charged with an offense can be found guilty. 

Finally, because the people—who had been accustomed to slavery for so long—could not be left to the freedom of their own will and needed to depend entirely upon their ruler, Moses left nothing to the personal judgment <note>original: "arbitrement"</note> of the Jews themselves. Everything was fixed by law; everything had to be done in a certain definite way, depending entirely upon the will of the ruler. A Jew was not at liberty to plow, to sow, or to reap in his own fashion; neither did he dare to eat, to dress, to shave his head or his beard, to grieve or to rejoice—in short, to do any single thing except in conformity with the orders and commands of the law. Nor was this all: he was ordered to wear certain signs on his hands, on his forehead, and on the doorposts of his house, which would constantly remind him of the duty of obedience.

This, then, is the whole scope and tendency of the Hebrew ceremonial law. The people were to do nothing of their own accord, but everything by the command of another. By all their actions and all their thoughts, they were to acknowledge that they were nothing by themselves, but were merely the instruments of the ruler's will. From all this, it clearly appears that ceremonial observances do not contribute in any way to true happiness. All those ceremonies of the Old Testament—indeed, the entire Law of Moses—had no other purpose than the political preservation of the Jews, and consequently refers to nothing but physical and personal advantages. 

As for Christian ceremonies—such as baptism, the Lord's Supper, festivals, public prayers, and the rest—if there are any others which are and always were common to the whole Christian community, assuming them to have been...

Even if these ceremonies were instituted by Christ or the apostles (and I am not quite certain that they were), they are still nothing more than outward signs of the universal Church. They do not in any way lead to true beatitude <note>original: "beatitudo"; a state of supreme blessedness or happiness</note>, nor do they have any inherent sanctity in their nature. Therefore, I say that these ceremonies—although not instituted for the sake of empire or state policy, but only for the Christian society—are not universally mandatory. A person living alone is in <margin>*</margin> no way bound by them. Likewise, someone living under a government <margin>*</margin> where the Christian religion is forbidden may ignore and abstain from them all, and yet still live the good life that ensures true happiness. 

We have an example of this in the Empire of Japan, where the Christian religion is prohibited; the Dutch who live there are ordered by the East India Company's express commands to abstain from all outward religious observance. I do not think it is necessary to illustrate this matter further, though I could prove its truth with many remarkable examples. Indeed, it would not be difficult to derive this principle from the pages of the New Testament itself, but I am inclined to pass those by, as my mind is focused on other matters. 

I therefore proceed to the second subject proposed for discussion in this chapter: the credibility of historical narrative and the trust to be placed in its authors. As this is one of the subjects to be investigated by natural light <note>The use of human reason and logic, independent of divine revelation</note>, I proceed as follows:

Whoever seeks to persuade or dissuade mankind of anything that is not self-evident is bound to state his proposition on acknowledged grounds. He must satisfy those he addresses by appeals to reason and experience—that is to say, by referring to things perceived by the senses, things that happen in nature, or things comprised of self-evident intellectual axioms <note>Fundamental truths that are accepted without proof</note>. However, unless experience is clearly and distinctly understood, it may convince people, but it cannot affect the understanding or clear away confusion to the same degree as when the things taught are deduced from mathematical axioms—that is, when they reach the mind through logical proof.
