The mind operates by the sole power of the understanding. This is especially the case when dealing with spiritual matters, which do not in any way fall under the <term>cognizance</term><note>original: "cognizance"; meaning the range of what can be known or perceived</note> of the senses. However, deducing truths from pure intellectual concepts usually requires a long <term>concatenation</term><note>original: "concatenation"; a series of interconnected things or events</note> of perceptions. Additionally, it requires the most stringent precautions, the highest intellectual <term>perspicacity</term><note>original: "perspicacity"; keenness of mental perception or understanding</note>, and the greatest reserve—all of which are rarely found in men. 

Therefore, people are more inclined to be taught by experience than to deduce and link their perceptions together from a small number of <term>axioms</term><note>original: "axioms"; self-evident truths that serve as a starting point for reasoning</note>. It follows that anyone desiring to have his doctrine presented to a nation—not to mention the whole of humankind—and who wishes to be understood by everyone in all things, must be prepared to refer to experience to confirm his teaching. He must be careful to adapt his reasonings and definitions of the things taught to the capacity of the common people, who constitute the great mass of mankind. He must be <term>chary</term><note>original: "chary"; cautious or wary</note> in the use of long chains of reasoning and of definitions intended to link his arguments together; otherwise, he will write for the learned only. In other words, he will be understood by only a very small number of people out of the great mass of humanity.

But seeing that the whole of the Scriptures were first revealed for the use of the Hebrew nation at large, and subsequently for the whole human family, it was imperative that the things contained within them should be adapted to the capacity of those to whom they were addressed, and that they should be referred to experience especially. Let us explain this point a little more fully. The things taught in Scripture that are of a purely <term>speculative</term><note>original: "speculative"; theoretical or philosophical rather than practical</note> nature are principally these: 

*   There is a God, or Being who made all things.
*   He rules and sustains the world with the highest wisdom.
*   He carefully watches over those among men who live <term>piously</term><note>original: "piously"; with religious devotion and morality</note> and honestly.
*   He threatens the wicked with punishment and distinguishes them from the good. 

Scripture confirms all its teaching to this effect by appeals to experience only, specifically through the histories of those whose laws and actions it records.

### CHAPTER VI.
#### CONCERNING MIRACLES.

Just as every field of study is called "divine" when it is beyond the reach of ordinary understanding, so are people inclined to see the hand of God in every event or phenomenon whose cause is generally unknown. The common people <note>original: "vulgar"</note>, in fact, are convinced that the power and providence of God never appear so clearly as when something happens that contradicts common experience <note>original: "use and wont"</note>, especially if it also happens to serve their own advantage or convenience. 

Nothing, for example, is thought to prove the existence of God so clearly as some presumed interruption of the regular course of nature. It is for this reason that those who seek to explain unusual events and phenomena through natural causes are very commonly regarded as guilty of questioning the existence—or at the very least, the providence—of God. 

So long as nature proceeds in its smooth and accustomed order, the common people think that God is doing nothing; conversely, they imagine that the powers of nature are suspended when God interferes. In this way, two distinct powers are imagined: the Power of God and the Power of Nature. This Power of Nature is presumed to be influenced and ordered in a certain way by God, or, as is generally believed at the present time, is something created by God. However, what is precisely meant by these two powers—God and Nature—is not explained.

<summary>This chapter introduction explores the popular misconception that God's power is only visible through miracles that interrupt the natural order, rather than through nature itself. The author argues that people mistakenly separate the "Power of God" from the "Power of Nature."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion regarding the nature of miracles and the human tendency to separate the power of God from the laws of nature.</meta>

### MIRACLES.

<note>original: "plained"</note> This is explained; unless it be that God is conceived as a king and sovereign ruler, while Nature is imagined as a special subordinate force. The common people, therefore, give the title of a miracle or "work of God" to every extraordinary natural event. Partly from devotional feeling, and partly from a spirit of opposition to those who study natural science, they do not care to inquire into the causes of phenomena. They will listen to nothing but that of which they are actually most ignorant, and for which they therefore feel the highest admiration. Now, this mainly proceeds from the fact that men in general have no other reasons for adoring God—and referring all that happens to his will and pleasure—than by supposing natural causes are abolished <note>original: "abrogated"</note> and the order of nature is arbitrarily suspended. In short, they only bow to the power of God when they believe the power of nature has been, as it were, subjugated by Him.

When we inquire into the origin of such prejudices, we have to look as far back as the times of the ancient <note>original: "primitive"</note> Jews. In order to convince the surrounding heathen nations—who were worshippers of visible deities such as the sun, moon, stars, earth, air, and water—that such gods were weak, inconstant, and under the dominion of the invisible God whom they adored, they narrated many wonderful miracles He had performed <note>original: "wrought"</note>. Furthermore, they endeavored to show that the whole of nature was ruled by Him for their own particular advantage. 

The system thus established <note>original: "inaugurated"</note> took such a hold on the minds of men that, even to the present day, every tribe or nation has not ceased from imagining miracles that support the conclusion that they are more acceptable to God than all the rest of mankind. They believe they are, in fact, the ultimate purpose <note>term: "final cause"; the philosophical idea that something exists for a specific end or goal</note> for which God at first created and still continues to uphold the world. Such common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> folly arises from the fact that men in general have no sound conception of either God or nature; they confound the desires and imaginations of man with the desires of the Almighty, and they imagine nature on such a small scale that they believe man is its principal part. But it is enough merely—

I have already hinted at the opinions and prejudices of the common people <note>original: "vulgar"</note> concerning nature and miracles. I therefore proceed to the consideration of the four principles which I propose to demonstrate here, in the following order:

1st, I shall begin by showing that nothing happens contrary to the order of nature, and that this order subsists without pause or interruption, eternal and unchangeable. I shall at the same time take the opportunity to explain what is to be understood by a "miracle."

2nd, I shall prove that miracles cannot make known to us the essence and existence of God, nor consequently his providence; these great truths are much better illustrated and proclaimed by the regular and invariable order of nature.

3rd, I shall prove by various examples taken from Holy Scripture <note>original: "Holy Writ"</note> that the Bible, when speaking of the decrees and the will of God—and consequently of his providence—means nothing more than the order of nature itself, which necessarily results from his eternal laws.

Fourthly and lastly, I shall discuss the proper manner of interpreting the miracles of Scripture, and insist on the main points which seem to require consideration in the narratives we have of these miracles. 

Such are the principal headings that form the argument of the present chapter; they have an especial bearing upon the whole scope and purpose of this work.

1. With regard to my first position, it would be almost enough to refer to my fourth chapter on Divine Law. In that chapter, I demonstrated that everything God wills or resolves involves the conception of eternal truth and eternal necessity. Since the intelligence of God cannot be conceived as distinct from his will (as I have shown above), to say that God thinks a thing or that God wills a thing is to affirm one and the same thing. Consequently, the same necessity by which it follows from the nature and perfection of God that he thinks a certain thing exactly as it is, this same necessity, I say, implies that God wills the thing exactly as it is. But as nothing is absolutely true except by divine decree alone, it is evident that the universal laws of nature are the very decrees of God, which result necessarily from the perfection of the...

Divine nature. If, therefore, anything happened in nature at large that was repugnant <note>original: "repugnant"; meaning contradictory or inconsistent</note> to its universal laws, this would be equally and necessarily repugnant to the decrees and intelligence of God. So, anyone who maintained that God acted in opposition to the laws of nature would at the same time be forced to maintain that God acted in opposition to His own nature—an idea more absurd than anything that can be imagined. I might show the same thing, or strengthen what I have just said, by referring to the truth that the power of nature is, in fact, the Divine Power; Divine Power is the very essence of God Himself. But this I pass by for the present. 

Nothing, then, happens in nature <margin>*By nature here I do not understand the material universe only and its properties, but besides matter, an infinity of other things.</margin> which is in contradiction with its universal laws. Not only this, but nothing happens which is not in accordance with these laws, or does not follow from them. For whatever is, and whatever happens, is and happens by the will and eternal decree of God; that is, as has been already shown, whatever happens does so according to rules and laws which involve eternal truth and necessity. 

Nature, consequently, always observes laws—although all of these are not known to us—which involve eternal truth and necessity, and thus it preserves a fixed and unchangeable <note>original: "immutable"</note> course. Nor will sound reason ever persuade us to ascribe a limited power and effectiveness <note>original: "efficacy"</note> to nature, or to conceive of its laws as operative in a certain restricted sense only, and not universally. Since the power and effectiveness of nature are the power and effectiveness of God, and the laws of nature are the ordinances of God Himself, we must believe that the power of nature is infinite, and its laws of such extent that they reach and pervade all that is understood by the divine intelligence. Were they not so, what else could be inferred than that God had made nature so powerless <note>original: "impotent"</note> and given it laws and statutes so barren that He is forced frequently to intervene anew if He would have these laws continued and the framework of things upheld in conformity with His wishes? This is a doctrine as far removed from reason as can well be conceived.

# MIRACLES

From these premises—namely, that nothing happens in nature which does not follow from its laws; that these laws extend to everything conceived by the divine mind; and, lastly, that nature proceeds in a fixed and changeless course—it follows most obviously that the word "miracle" can only be understood in relation to human opinion. It signifies nothing more than an event or phenomenon whose cause cannot be explained by a familiar example, or, at least, one which the narrator is unable to explain. I might say, indeed, that a miracle is something whose cause cannot be explained by our natural understanding through the known principles of natural things. 

However, as miracles were intended for the common understanding <note>original: "vulgar apprehension"</note>—which lacks knowledge of the principles of natural things—it is certain that the ancients regarded as a miracle anything they could not explain in their usual way. Their method of accounting for natural things was simply to recall a similar event that they were accustomed to seeing without wonder; for the common people always think they understand a thing once they have ceased to marvel at it. 

The ancients, therefore, and almost all people even up to the present time, have had no other standard for a miracle but this. There can be no question that many things are related in Scripture as miracles which are easily explained by the known principles of natural things. This was already suggested in Chapter II when we spoke of the sun standing still in the time of Joshua and moving backward in the days of Ahaz. I shall have more to say on this when I discuss the explanation of miracles, a subject I promised to address in this chapter. 

But it is time I passed on to my second proposition: to show that from miracles we can neither obtain a knowledge of the existence nor of the providence of God. On the contrary, these truths are much better understood from the eternal and changeless order of nature.

It must necessarily be inferred from ideas, the truth of which is so unquestionable that no power can be assigned or even imagined adequate to shake them. From the moment we conclude from these ideas that God exists, they ought to present themselves to the mind as beyond the sphere of doubt. For if we could imagine that these notions could be changed by any power whatsoever, then we would doubt their truth, and consequently doubt our conclusion regarding the existence of God as well. The effect of this would be that we should no longer feel certain of anything. 

Furthermore, we really know of nothing that agrees with nature or differs from it, except for that which we have shown to agree with or differ from these principles. Therefore, if we could conceive that anything could happen in nature by any power (whatever this might be) which was repugnant to nature, this would also be repugnant to these primary notions. Thus, it would have to be rejected as absurd; otherwise, we would be forced to doubt our first notions (as previously stated), and consequently doubt God and all conceptions whatsoever. 

Miracles, therefore—conceiving these as events contravening <note>original: "contravening," meaning to go against or violate</note> the established order of nature—are so far from proving the existence of God to us that they would actually lead us to call it into question. Without miracles, we can be absolutely certain of the existence of God, as we truly are when we know that all things in nature observe a definite and unchanging course.

But suppose it is said that a miracle is that which cannot be explained by natural causes...

<gloss>We have only a confused, instead of a clear and distinct, idea of God. Just as he who does not know the nature of a triangle does not know that the sum of its angles is equal to two right angles <note>original: "two rectangles," a geometric term for 180 degrees</note>; in the same way, he who only conceives the Divine nature in a confused manner does not see that *to exist* belongs to the nature of God. Now, to conceive the Divine nature in a clear and distinct manner, it is necessary to attend to a certain number of extremely simple notions, which are called common notions, and with their assistance to connect the conceptions which we form of the attributes of the Supreme. Then only for the first time does it become evident to us that God exists necessarily; that he is omnipresent; that all we conceive envelopes the nature of God and is conceived by its means; and lastly, that all our adequate ideas are true. On this point the reader is referred to the introduction of my treatise, entitled, "*Principles of Cartesian Philosophy demonstrated in a Geometric manner*" <note>original: "Principia philosophiæ Cartesianæ more Geometrica demonstrata"</note>.</gloss>

But of anything in general—and of the particular thing in question, namely the miracle—which surpasses our powers of comprehension, nothing whatever can be known. Therefore, from a miracle, as an incident surpassing our powers of comprehension, we cannot understand anything regarding the essence, existence, or any other quality of God or nature. 

On the contrary, when we know that all things are determined and sanctioned by God, that the operations of nature follow from the essence of God, and that the laws of nature are eternal decrees and volitions <note>original: "volitions"; meaning acts of willing or choosing</note> of God, we conclude unconditionally that we know God and his holy will better as we gain a better knowledge and a clearer comprehension of natural things—how they depend on God as their first cause, and how they exist and act according to eternal, changeless laws ordained by him. 

Therefore, as far as our understanding is concerned, those events which we clearly and distinctly comprehend are with much better right entitled "works of God" and referred to his will than those which are wholly unintelligible to us, even though they strongly seize upon our imagination and wrap us in amazement. This is because only those works of nature which we clearly and distinctly apprehend render our knowledge of God truly sublime and point to his will and decrees with the greatest clearness. They, therefore, plainly trifle who, when they do not know a thing, fall back upon the will of God—a most ridiculous way of proceeding...

For, inasmuch as a miracle is a limited act and never expresses more than a certain limited power, it is certain that we can never from such an effect infer the existence of a cause whose power is infinite. We could at the most conceive a cause whose power was relatively greater. I say at the most, for a certain event might happen from many causes concurring to produce it, of which the immediate cause should be of less potency than the mass of concurring causes, though greater than that of each of them severally.

But the laws of nature (as already shown) reach to infinity and are conceived by us as a kind of eternity. Since nature, by virtue of these laws, proceeds in a certain and immutable <note>original: "immutable" — unchangeable</note> order, they declare to us in an assured manner the Infinity, the Eternity, and the Unchangeable nature of God. Let us conclude, therefore, that we can know nothing by miracles regarding the existence and providence of God; on the contrary, these attributes are far better inferred from the regular and unchanging order of nature. 

In this conclusion, I of course speak of miracles as understanding by them nothing more than events which surpass, or are believed to surpass, the common comprehension of mankind. For if miracles be understood as interruptions or abrogations <note>original: "abrogations" — the repeal or doing away with a law</note> of the order of nature, or as subversive of its laws, not only could they not give us any knowledge of God, but, on the contrary, they would destroy that which we naturally have, and would induce doubt both of the existence of God and of everything else. Nor do I here recognize any difference between a phenomenon or event "contrary to nature" and one "beyond nature"—a phrase by which some understand a phenomenon not repugnant to, but not producible by, nature. Because a miracle takes place not beyond but *in* nature, if it be held to be above nature, it must necessarily interrupt the order of nature, which we otherwise conceive to be, by the decrees of God, fixed, immutable, and eternal. If anything were to take place in nature which did not follow from its everlasting laws, it would necessarily contravene the order which God has established in nature by the universal laws he has decreed for its government. It would thus subvert nature and its laws, and consequently lead to general skepticism and atheism.

From these views and reasonings, I think I have sufficiently established my second proposition. I believe we may safely conclude once more that a miracle—whether it is claimed to be contrary to nature or above nature—is a sheer absurdity. Therefore, by a "miracle" in Holy Writ <note>original: "Holy Writ"; refers to the Bible</note>, we are to understand nothing more than a natural phenomenon which surpasses, or is believed to surpass, human powers of comprehension.

Before proceeding to my third position—namely, that we cannot know God from miracles—I gladly take this occasion to confirm the above conclusions by the authority of Scripture. Although the Bible nowhere openly teaches this doctrine in so many words, it nevertheless gives it clearly enough to be understood in many passages. Thus Moses teaches (Deuteronomy 13) that a false prophet, although he works miracles, is yet to be put to death:

> "If there arise among you a prophet... and gives you a sign or wonder, and the sign or wonder comes to pass, saying, 'Let us go after other gods,'... you shall not listen to the words of that prophet; for the Lord your God is testing you... and that prophet shall be put to death."

From this it plainly appears that wonders or signs could be worked by false prophets. It shows that men, unless they are duly imbued with a true knowledge and love of God, could be led with equal ease by the guidance of miracles to worship false gods as to adore the true and only God. For in the same passage these words are added: "For Jehovah, your God, tempts you, that he may know whether you love him with all your heart and all your mind." 

Furthermore, of what use did miracles prove in giving the children of Israel reasonable ideas of God? When they had persuaded themselves that they were forsaken by Moses, they demanded visible gods from Aaron, and—to their shame!—a calf was their idea of God. The wonders they had seen did not prevent doubt. Asaph the psalmist, too, although he had heard of so many miracles, nevertheless doubted the providence of God. He had almost strayed from the right path, until he finally acquired better ideas of what true happiness consists of (see Psalm 73 <note>original: "Psalm xxxvii." The author likely intended Psalm 73, which deals with Asaph's doubt regarding the prosperity of the wicked, whereas Psalm 37 is attributed to David.</note>). Solomon also, during the times when the Jewish nation was at the height of its prosperity, suspected that all things happen by chance (see Ecclesiastes 3:19, 20, 21, and 9:2, 3, and following <note>original: "et seq."</note>). Lastly, almost all the prophets exhibit a very confused idea of God's providence; they were evidently at a loss to make the order of nature and the events that happen in the world agree with the ideas they held. 

Nevertheless, the matter has always been clear enough to the philosopher who strives to comprehend it—not by means of miracles, but by forming clear conceptions of God and nature. This is the philosopher who understands that true happiness consists in virtue and peace of mind alone, and who studies to obey nature rather than trying to make nature bend to his will. He knows for certain that God governs nature according to the requirements of His universal laws, not in the manner that the specific laws of man would require; thus, God has regard not for humankind alone, but for the structure of the entire world. It is therefore certainly proved from Scripture itself that miracles give no true knowledge either of God or of His eternal providence.

There is one thing, however, constantly repeated in the Scriptures: namely, that God showed signs and wonders, or performed miracles, so that He might become known to the Jewish people. Thus in Exodus 10:2, we read that God mocked <note>original: "deceived." The Hebrew 'hith'allel' in Exodus 10:2 is often translated as "wrought my signs" or "mocked/made a fool of."</note> the Egyptians and gave signs of Himself to the children of Israel, so that they might know He was the Lord. But it does not follow from this that miracles were the means by which God taught this truth. It only shows that the Jews held opinions which led them to be easily persuaded by signs and portents. In our second chapter, we have satisfactorily shown that prophetic reasons—or reasons formed from revelation—are not derived from universal and common ideas, but from the specific prejudices and opinions of those to whom the revelation is made.

God did not send Saul to Samuel in the way that men are accustomed to send someone expressly to another. Instead, Saul’s visit to Samuel arose out of concurrent circumstances: Saul was in search of the donkeys he had lost, as narrated in the preceding chapter of the book. Failing to find them, and even thinking of returning home without them, he sought out Samuel the seer <note>original: "seer"; a term for a prophet or someone with divine insight</note> at the suggestion of his servant, so that he might inquire of him where he should discover his strayed cattle. From no part of the whole narrative does it appear that Saul received any special command from God to visit Samuel. 

In Psalm 105:25, it is said that God changed the hearts of the Egyptians so that they hated the children of Israel; but this was obviously a natural incident, as appears from Exodus 1. There, we find very sufficient reasons why the Egyptians oppressed the Jews and reduced them to slavery. <margin>And the children of Israel multiplied, and grew exceedingly mighty; and there arose a new king over Egypt, and he said, "The children of Israel are more and mightier than we: let us deal wisely with them, lest they join with our enemies and fight against us," etc.—*Editor.*</margin> 

In Genesis 9:13, God informs Noah that he would show himself in the clouds and set his bow <note>the rainbow</note> there. This is but another way of expressing the natural law by which the rays of the sun undergo refraction when they fall upon drops of water. In Psalm 147:18, the natural action of wind and heat by which hoar-frost and snow are melted is spoken of as the "word of God," and in verse 15, the wind and the cold are entitled the "commandment" and "word" of the Lord. In Psalm 104:4, again, wind and fire are called the angels (or messengers) and ministers of God. 

Indeed, very many expressions of the same kind are met with in Scripture, all of which proclaim most distinctly that the words "commandment," "decree," and "word of God" are often nothing more than expressions for the agency and order of nature itself. Therefore, there is no reason to doubt that everything related in Scripture happened naturally, though it is always referred immediately to God. This is because it is not the business of Holy Writ <note>The Bible</note> to teach by reference to natural causes, but rather to describe events in a way that moves the heart to devotion.

If, therefore, some things are found in Scripture for which we can assign no reason, and which moreover seem to have happened contrary to the usual course of nature, this ought really to be no hindrance to us. These accounts ought not to affect us any more than when we read that because of the sins of men, God is angry or sorrowful, or repents the good he had promised and done, or is reminded of a promise he had made by a sign in the heavens, and many other things of the same sort. These are either mere poetical expressions or narratives written in conformity with the opinions and prejudices of the writer. Let us unhesitatingly conclude, then, that whatever truth we find in the Scriptural narratives of events, these uniformly came to pass in accordance with the laws of nature which necessarily govern all things. When we meet with any incident there which may be demonstrated as opposed to the laws of nature, or which can in no way be reconciled with them, we may feel assured that it has been added to the sacred Scriptures by some sacrilegious hand. For whatever is against nature is against reason [and against God], and what is against reason is absurd, and therefore to be rejected <note>original: "scouted"</note>.

4. I have now only to make a few remarks on the interpretation of miracles; or, rather, to summarize the main points of what I have just said and illustrate them by one or two examples. What makes it the more necessary to do so is to prevent anyone, by interpreting a certain miracle incorrectly, from rashly suspecting that he has found something in Scripture which is contradictory <note>original: "repugnant"</note> to natural reason.

It is very seldom that men relate an event simply as it happened, without mingling any of their own fancies or opinions with the narrative. When they see or hear anything new, indeed, unless they are especially on their guard against preconceived opinions, they mostly perceive things quite differently than they are in fact. This is especially true if the matter in question is beyond the capacity of the listener or narrator, and even more so if it interferes in any way with his interests or affections. From this it follows that in their chronicles and histories, men are much more apt to give their own views and opinions than to narrate events as they actually happened. Thus, it turns out that the same incident related by two persons of dissimilar views often appears as if two different events were being described.

In the time of Joshua, the Jews believed—as the common people <note>original: "vulgar"</note> do at the present time—that the sun was in motion and the earth at rest. They did not fail, accordingly, to accommodate the account of the miracle which happened in the great battle against the five kings to this opinion. For they have not said simply that the day on which the battle took place seemed longer than usual, but that the sun and moon stood still in their course and ceased from their motions. Now, this manner of stating the event was obviously well calculated to impress the minds of the heathen of those times who worshipped the sun; it gave them the conviction that this luminary was under the control of another more powerful divinity, at whose command <note>original: "nod"</note> it could be made to pause in its course against all former experience. Partly on religious grounds, therefore, and partly from preconceived opinions, the Jews perceived and related the event of the long day during the battle with the five kings very differently from the way in which it occurred in fact.

To interpret the miracles of Scripture consequently, and to understand them from the narratives, it is absolutely necessary to be informed of the opinions of those who first witnessed or narrated them, and also of those who have left us an account of them in writing. We must make a fundamental <note>original: "cardinal"</note> distinction between the event in itself and the impression it may have produced on the minds of those who witnessed it. Without this precaution, we should certainly confound the opinions and prejudices of witnesses and historians with events in themselves. Nor would this be all; we should still be liable to confound things that actually happened <note>original: "transpired"</note> with things

In describing an approaching war, the prophet expresses himself thus: "It shall be one day which shall be known to the Lord, not day nor night; but at evening time it shall be light." <note>Zechariah 14:7</note> These words seem to involve a great miracle or mystery; and yet they signify nothing more than this—that the battle would be doubtful through the whole of the day, its issue being known only to God, but that in the evening the victory would be won. It is in such enigmatical <note>original: "enigmatical"; meaning mysterious or metaphorical</note> language indeed that the prophets were accustomed to speak and to write of the victories and disasters of nations. 

Isaiah, for instance, depicting the desolation of Babylon (chapter 13), makes use of these words: "The stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light; the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine." Now, I do not suppose anyone imagines that all this happened literally when the Babylonian empire fell, any more than that which the prophet immediately adds: "For I will make the heavens to tremble, and remove the earth out of her place." 

In like manner, the same prophet (chapter 48), desiring to make it known to the Jews that they should assuredly return to Jerusalem from Babylon and not suffer from thirst on their journey, says: "And they thirsted not when he led them through the deserts; he caused the waters to flow out of the rocks for them; he split the rock and the waters gushed out." The meaning of this is simply that the Jews found springs in the desert to slake <note>original: "slake"; to satisfy or quench</note> their thirst—and springs do well up in the desert at intervals—for when the Jews returned to Jerusalem with the consent of Cyrus, it is certain that no such miracle occurred literally as that which the prophet describes. 

Very many things of the same kind are met with in the sacred writings—mere modes of expression in use among the Jews, which I do not think it necessary to specify more in detail. I remark generally that the Hebrews were accustomed not only to embroider their statements with flowery or poetical language, but, further, that they almost always used devotional expressions. This is the reason why in Scripture we sometimes find the expression *bless God* used for the contrary <note>original: "bless God for the contrary"; a euphemism for "curse God," as seen in the Book of Job</note>, as in...

"Regarding the Persian Empire? Concerning these matters (miracles), therefore, everyone should be left free to think as he pleases." Such are the words of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian</note>, and his opinion on whether it is necessary to believe in miracles.

If the reader will proceed to read Mr. Hume’s <note>David Hume (1711–1776), a Scottish philosopher famous for his skeptical arguments against miracles</note> masterly essay on the subject discussed here, he will—however inclined toward belief he may be—feel himself forced to forever abandon all belief in miracles. The different lines of argument pursued by Spinoza <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), who argued that miracles are impossible because they violate the immutable laws of nature</note> and by Hume complement each other and seem to leave nothing more to be said on the subject. 

Miracles, indeed, have long disappeared from the world of science; they only linger now among the uneducated—who, unfortunately, in the truest sense of the term, still make up a very large portion of the world! The uselessness of miracles as a means to any good end is an idea as old as the Book of Genesis: "If a prophet arises among you and performs *signs and wonders*, and if he says, 'Let us follow other gods,' that prophet shall be put to death." <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 13:1-5, though the author attributes the sentiment to the era of Genesis</note> 

To come closer to the present age, we ask: what does it matter to us whether Christ walked on the Lake of Galilee or not? Our lives and our conduct are not influenced by our belief or unbelief in the report of such an unnatural incident. However, it is of the utmost importance to us, and to all mankind in the future, that we have the example of our Lord’s blessed life, the prayer he taught his disciples, and the sermon he delivered on the mount. —*Editor*.

## CHAPTER VII.

### ON THE INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE.

That the Scriptures are the word of God is a phrase in everybody’s mouth; it is also commonly said that they teach true happiness and point out the way of everlasting life to humanity. However, the reality of how people treat the text is clearly very different. Most people seem to care for nothing less than living according to the teachings of Holy Writ. While some are seen eagerly parading their own personal opinions <note>original: "conceits"</note> as the word of God, others, under the pretext of religious zeal, seem only interested in forcing the rest of the world to think exactly as they do.

Theologians, I must say, have until now shown themselves to be especially ingenious at twisting their own inventions and fabrications <note>original: "figments"</note> out of the literal text of Scripture, and in supporting their various conclusions with divine authority. They never act more recklessly or with fewer moral scruples than when they set about interpreting the Bible. If they show anxiety about anything, it is not for fear that they might attribute errors to the Holy Spirit; rather, they fear that they themselves might be proven wrong, and consequently have their own personal authority despised <note>original: "contemned"</note>. 

But if mankind truly felt that hearty conviction regarding the excellence of the Scriptures which they are so ready to profess with their mouths, they would follow a very different way of living. Their souls would not be disturbed by so many clashing passions, nor distracted by such burning hatreds; neither—

<summary>The author critiques the hypocrisy of his contemporaries, arguing that while people claim the Bible is the word of God, they actually use it to justify their own prejudices and personal authority rather than following its moral teachings.</summary>
<keywords>Interpretation of Scripture, Theology, Religious Hypocrisy, Divine Authority, Biblical Criticism</keywords>

# INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE

If they did not, would they make so many and such rash attempts to interpret Scripture and to produce novelties in religion? They would not venture to embrace as Scripture doctrine anything which was not most plainly set forth as such in Scripture itself. Then, too, would those sacrilegious men—who have not feared to tamper with Scripture in many places—have withheld their hands from such wickedness. 

But vanity and audacity have gone so far that religion is made at length to consist less in obeying the decrees of the Holy Spirit than in adopting and defending the commentaries and conclusions of men. The effect of this is that instead of teaching charity and good-will, religion becomes the vehicle of hatred and discord in the world, and all under the name and pretext of zeal for sacred things. 

With such ills superstition, moreover, has been associated—superstition which teaches men to despise reason and nature, and only to admire and respect that which these alike ignore. It is not to be wondered at, therefore, if some, while striving to excite a greater reverence and respect for Scripture, have actually explained it in such a way as to make its precepts seem repugnant <note>original: "repugnant"; meaning contradictory or offensive to</note> both to common sense and nature. This is the reason why such profound mysteries have been supposed to lurk in Holy Writ <note>A traditional term for the Bible</note>, and why, in searching after these to the entire neglect of useful truths, many have plainly lost their way. They have ascribed their own delirious dreams to the Holy Spirit and expended their strength and ingenuity in defending absurdities. 

For even thus does it fare with man: that which he conceives by pure intelligence, he defends by reason and understanding; and that which he imagines by the affections <note>original: "affections"; here meaning emotions or passions</note> of his mind, he justifies by temper and passion.

That we may not get entangled in this maze, that we may keep our minds free from theological prejudices and not adopt the imaginations of man as divine truths, we shall now proceed to treat of the true method of interpreting Scripture and of commenting upon it; for without this, we can know nothing certainly of what Scripture or the Holy Spirit would teach. Now on this point, in few words, I say that the proper method—

<page-num>144</page-num>
# INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE

The method of interpreting Scripture does not differ from the proper method of interpreting nature, but agrees with it almost in every particular. For, just as the way of interpreting nature consists especially in bringing together, arranging, and contrasting the facts of natural science—from which, as from assured data, we arrive at general conclusions and definitions—so also in interpreting Scripture it is necessary to coordinate its simple statements and histories. From them, as from fixed data and principles, we must come to legitimate conclusions regarding the meaning and purpose of the authors of the narrative. Whoever proceeds in this way, taking particular care to assume no other principles or data in his interpretations than those which are contained in Scripture itself, may advance without fear of mistake. He may even discuss matters which are beyond our comprehension, as well as those which we appreciate by our common faculties.

But so that this may be clearly seen, not merely as the safe way, but as the only way—and as agreeing entirely with the method of interpreting nature—it is to be observed that Scripture most commonly treats of matters which cannot be deduced from the principles supplied by natural intelligence. For by far the larger portion of the Bible is made up of histories and revelations. The histories are principally of miracles—that is, they are narratives of extraordinary and unusual events in nature, adapted to the opinions and prejudices of the writers. Meanwhile, the revelations (as we have shown in Chapter II) are in conformity with the opinions and insights of the prophets who propound them; indeed, they very frequently transcend human capacity altogether.

From this it follows that the interpretation of all these things—that is, of almost everything contained in Scripture—is to be sought from Scripture alone, just as the interpretation of nature is to be derived from nature. As to the moral doctrines which are also comprised in the Bible, although these may be demonstrated from common or natural notions <note>original: "natural notions"; referring to universal truths accessible to human reason without divine revelation</note>, still, the demonstration that Scripture teaches them in a particular way must not be sought for by natural light <note>original: "natural light"; the innate human capacity for reason and logic</note>, but must be derived from Scripture itself.

<summary>The author argues that the Bible should be interpreted using the same empirical methods used in natural science, relying solely on the internal data of the text rather than external philosophical assumptions.</summary>
<keywords>hermeneutics, biblical interpretation, natural science, miracles, revelation, reason vs. revelation, methodology</keywords>

# INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE.

From the words of Scripture itself. If, indeed, and without prejudice, we would test the divineness of Scripture, we ought to be assured from the text itself that its teaching consists of sound moral doctrine. For in this way only can its divinity be demonstrated. Just as we have already shown that certainty regarding a true prophet was especially derived from an assurance that he manifested a mind and temper solely disposed to goodness and truth—this being imperative before faith could be put in his words—so it is with the text. 

But it is impossible to have any assurance of the divinity of God from miracles, as has been already shown; for miracles were also performed by false prophets. Therefore, the sole sufficient test of the divinity of Scripture lies in the excellence of the precepts it declares, and in the fact that it teaches true virtue. Now, that it does so can only be shown from the text itself. Were it otherwise, we should indeed be much to blame in adopting Scripture as our guide and in speaking of it as being of divine origin. 

The knowledge of Scripture, therefore, is to be wholly and solely derived from its own pages. Scripture, however, never gives definitions of the things of which it speaks, any more than nature itself does. Therefore, whatever conclusions are formed regarding natural things, they are to be drawn from the different narratives that occur in Scripture regarding each individual thing. The universal rule in interpreting Scripture, then, is never to ascribe any doctrine to Scripture which we do not most plainly find set forth in its narratives. It will now be our business to inquire as to what we should expect Scripture history <note>In this context, "history" refers to a systematic account or study of the text's data, similar to "natural history."</note> to be, and of what things it should principally speak.

1. Scripture history necessarily includes the nature and properties of the language in which it is written, and in which its authors were accustomed to speak. From these, under the guidance of common usage, we should be enabled to investigate the various senses in which each word, phrase, or expression is employed. And as all the writers, both of the Old and New Testament, were Jews, it is certain that a knowledge of the Hebrew tongue is above all things necessary, not only for the understanding of the books of the Old Testament, but also for the New.

<summary>The author argues that the divinity of Scripture must be proven by its moral excellence as found within the text itself, rather than through miracles, and establishes that a linguistic study of Hebrew is essential for interpretation.</summary>

Testament, which are written in this language, but also of those of the New Testament; for although the New Testament was spread in other languages, it nevertheless bears the strong impress of Hebrew peculiarity <note>original: "peculiarity"; referring to the Hebraic idioms and thought patterns present in the Greek text</note> upon it.

2. Once the subject matter treated in each book is noted and organized under distinct heads, an immediate and connected view of every passage that treats of the same thing is obtained. Furthermore, the passages which are of doubtful or obscure meaning, or which seem to contradict one another, are to be identified. I categorize passages as clear or obscure based on whether they are understood easily or with difficulty from the words themselves or from the context. Our business here is solely with the *meaning* of the passages in question, and in no way with their *truth*. 

Therefore, it is of primary necessity that while investigating the sense of Scripture, we are not preoccupied with our own reasonings, even if those reasonings are based on an adequate knowledge of natural things. I say nothing here of our prejudices, lest we confound the true sense of the text with natural truths. The sense of Scripture must be determined from the words of the text itself, or by legitimate reasoning <note>original: "ratiocination"</note> based on those words alone; no basis for a conclusion <note>original: "induction"</note> should be admitted except that which Scripture itself contains. 

To ensure this position is more clearly understood, I shall illustrate it with an example. The views of Moses when he says that *God is fire*, and that *God is jealous*, are plain enough so long as we regard the meaning of the words only. I therefore place these expressions in my category of plain things, even though in regard to truth and reason they are most obscure. Still, although the literal sense of the words is contrary <note>original: "repugnant"</note> to natural reason, this literal sense must be retained unless it is also clearly opposed to the principles and fundamentals of Scripture. 

On the contrary, if the expressions, when interpreted literally, are seen to disagree with the principles derived from Scripture, they must be interpreted differently or taken metaphorically—even if the literal sense is entirely in accord with reason and the light of nature. Therefore, to truly know whether Moses believed God to be fire or not, we must not infer it from whether it is reasonable or not.

<summary>The author argues that the interpretation of Scripture must rely solely on linguistic and internal evidence rather than external "natural truth" or reason. He emphasizes that a passage's meaning is distinct from its philosophical truth and must be derived from the text's own principles.</summary>

# INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE

We determine the meaning not from whether an opinion agrees with or contradicts reason, but solely from the other expressed opinions and views of Moses. Now, as Moses in many places pointedly declares that God has no likeness to anything which is in heaven or earth, we must conclude that the words quoted are to be explained metaphorically. 

But as we are bound to depart as little as possible from the literal sense in any case, we must first inquire whether the words in the single phrase *God is fire* may have a sense other than the literal one. That is, we must ask whether the word *Fire* ever signifies anything else than fire—the effect of combustion. If it were found, from the usage of the Hebrew language <note>original: "Hebrew tongue"</note>, that the word equivalent to fire is never employed in any other sense, then the phrase *God is fire* could not be interpreted in any way that is not contrary <note>original: "repugnant"</note> to reason. In that case, even though it contradicts everything else in harmony with reason, the interpretation of literal fire would have to be adopted. 

Again, supposing that even this could not be done in conformity with the usages of the language, then the different interpretations would be found irreconcilable, and we would be forced to suspend our judgment regarding the true meaning of the phrase. But when we find the word *fire* also used to signify anger and wrath (see <note>original: "vide"</note> Job 31:12), then the views of Moses are readily reconciled. We can legitimately conclude that the two phrases, *God is fire* and *God is jealous*, embody one and the same meaning. 

Moreover, as Moses clearly teaches that God is a jealous God, and nowhere informs us that God is without passions or affections of the mind, we readily conclude that Moses himself believed—or at all events desired to teach—what he says, although the opinion expressed is, in our understanding, contrary to reason. For, as I have already shown, we are not at liberty to twist the sense of Scripture into conformity with the dictates of our reason and our preconceived opinions; rather, the interpretation of the whole Bible is to be derived from itself alone.

3. Finally, Scripture history ought to comprise an account of all the books of the prophets that have come down to us.

# INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE

We must have passed down to us the life, manners, and culture of the author of each particular book: who he was, on what occasion, at what time, for whom, and, lastly, in what language he wrote. Then, the history of the several books should be made known—namely, how and in what way each was first received, and into whose hands it fell. Next, we must know how many different versions of it exist, by whose advice it was received into the number of the sacred books, and, finally, how all the books now acknowledged as sacred were gathered together into one collection. 

All these things, I say, are to be expected in a history of the Hebrew Scriptures. In order for us to know which matters are presented as laws and which as moral precepts, it is proper that we should know something of the life, manners, and occupation of their authors. Besides, we can more easily explain the words of any person when we are better informed regarding their character <note>original: "genius"</note> and education. 

Then, it is well to know the occasion on which, and the age and nation to which, writings were addressed. This ensures that we are not led to confuse eternal and universal decrees with those that are only temporary or of limited application. It is important, further, to be informed of the other particulars just listed: so that, besides the books themselves and the authorities who accepted them, we should know whether they may have been tampered with by unscrupulous hands; or at all events, whether errors may have crept into them, and whether the text has been revised and corrected by men who were sufficiently skillful and perfectly worthy of trust. All of these things are most necessary to be known, lest, carried away by blind impulse, we embrace whatever is forced upon us instead of only that which is certain and of vital importance.

Even after we have secured and solidly established this history of the Scriptures—when we have certainly set down nothing as prophetic doctrine which does not follow from the narrative or may not be clearly inferred from it—then it will be time for us to prepare ourselves <note>original: "gird ourselves up"</note> for an inquiry into the purposes of the prophets and the Holy Spirit. But for this end...

# INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE

A method and order are required similar to that which we employ in interpreting nature from its history. For, just as in inquiring into natural things we endeavor above all to discover those which are most general and common to nature at large—namely, motion, attraction, gravitation, and so on—and the laws which nature always observes and by which she always acts, and from these proceed step by step to other less general laws; so also in Scripture history, that which is most general must first be ascertained. This is the basis and foundation of the whole superstructure, which finally leads to the special eternal law commanded by the prophet and most necessary to all mankind. 

Such a law or doctrine as this, for example: that there is one omnipotent and eternal God, who alone is to be worshipped, who rules over all, who cares for all, and especially regards those who worship him in truth and who love their neighbors as themselves. These and other similar precepts are so clearly taught in Scripture that there never was a man yet found who questioned the sense of the passages in which they are contained. 

But as to what God is, in what respect he sees all things, and how he provides for all things, and other like matters, Scripture does not professedly teach anything as eternal doctrine. On the contrary, it has been already shown that the prophets themselves were not agreed on such topics; so that nothing in regard to them is to be assumed as the doctrine of the Holy Spirit, although natural light <note>original: "natural light" refers to human reason or innate intellectual capability</note> would often of itself suffice for coming to satisfactory conclusions.

This most general or universal doctrine of Scripture being satisfactorily determined, we then proceed to search for other doctrines less general, which still bear reference to the common usages of life and which are derived as offshoots from the grand doctrine. These include the outward manifestation of the true virtues—such as charity, meekness, justice, and temperance—which are only called into action when the occasion arises. When any obscurity or doubt presents itself in connection with these less general precepts of Scripture, it is to...

Difficulties in the text should be cleared up or resolved by reference to universal doctrine. Furthermore, when any contradiction is encountered, the occasion, the time, and the writer must be reviewed before any conclusion is reached. 

For example, when Christ says, “Blessed are the mourners, for they shall be comforted,” the text itself tells us nothing about who these mourners were or why they grieved. However, when he later teaches that we should be concerned with nothing except the kingdom of God and his righteousness—which he declares to be the highest good (see Matthew 6:33)—it follows that he refers only to those who mourn for the kingdom of God and his righteousness because they are neglected by men. Only those who love nothing but divine rule and equity, and who openly despise all other things (the gifts of fortune), can grieve for such a cause. 

We must also interpret the passage where Christ tells the person who is struck on the right cheek to turn the left to the smiter in the same way. Had Christ given such a command as a legislator <note>original: "legislator"; here meaning a formal lawmaker like Moses</note>, he would have contradicted the law of Moses, which certainly gives very different advice. Therefore, we must inquire about the time when Christ spoke and the people to whom he spoke. We find that Christ was not speaking then as a legislator laying down laws, but as a doctor <note>original: "doctor"; used in the Latin sense of "teacher" or "learned instructor"</note> or teacher of precepts. His grand purpose was not to demand external observance, but to improve the mental state of mankind. 

Furthermore, he spoke those words to oppressed men who were members of a corrupt state where justice was ignored and whose ruin he saw was imminent. We find the prophet Jeremiah using very similar language under similar circumstances when prophesying the first destruction of Jerusalem (see Lamentations 3). Therefore, we see that Christ and the prophets only taught in such terms during seasons of oppression and public distress. Such precepts are nowhere in Scripture presented as laws. Moses, who did not write in times of disaster and oppression but labored to found a prosperous commonwealth, took a different approach. Although he condemns hatred and revenge against a neighbor, he nevertheless commanded equal punishment for equal damage done: an eye for an eye.

The method consists especially of this: next, we are to learn what a miracle is, and so in succession arrive at more common things. Then we come down to the opinions of each prophet, and from these, we reach at length the meaning of each particular prophecy, history, and miracle. Regarding the precautions to be taken—lest in this course the views of prophets and historians be confounded with the purpose of the Holy Spirit and the truth of the thing itself—we have already spoken in the proper place and illustrated our remarks with many examples. Therefore, I do not now hold it necessary to say more on the subject here. I will only add, in connection with the *sense of prophecy*, that our method only enables us to investigate that which the prophets saw or heard, but not what they desired to signify or represent by their hieroglyphics <note>original: "hieroglyphics"; here referring to symbolic visions or metaphorical language</note>. This indeed may be conjectured, but cannot be certainly deduced from the fundamentals of Scripture.

We have thus discussed the method of interpreting Scripture and have at the same time shown that it supplied the sole and certain way of ascertaining its true meaning. I confess, however, that those people would be still more certain of the meaning of Scripture—if any such persons existed—who had received a definite traditional explanation of its text from the prophets themselves (as the Pharisees think they have), or who had a pontiff <note>A high priest or Pope</note> who could not err in his interpretations (as the Roman Catholic Christians boast that they have). 

Still, as we could not really be certain either of this Pharisaic tradition or of the pontifical authority, we could found nothing decisive upon either of these. For the earliest Christians and the most ancient sects of the Jews denied the existence of any such traditional interpretation and recognized no such infallible authority. And then, when we look to the long series of years (to say nothing of other things) over which the traditions extend—which the Pharisees have received from their Rabbins <note>Rabbis</note>, who carry them back to the time of Moses—we find they can have no foundation in fact, as I shall show at length in another place.

Such tradition indeed would be suspicious under any circumstances; and although according to our method of proceeding we are obliged to suppose one of the traditions of the Jews to be uncorrupted—namely, the meaning of the words of the Hebrew language which we receive from them—still, while often feeling grave doubts about the events narrated, we feel none about the meaning of the words in which they are described. This is because usage never yet changed the meaning of a word, even though it has frequently altered the sense of a phrase. 

To change the meaning of a word, indeed, would be very difficult; for whoever should attempt to do so would have to explain the word in its new sense by referencing every writer who had used it in its old and usual meaning. Furthermore, the common people <note>original: "the vulgar"</note> in their everyday intercourse use and preserve language just as much as the scholars, while scholars are mostly interested in the meaning of formal speeches <note>original: "ornate discourses"</note> and books. So, while it is easy to imagine that scholars might have altered or corrupted the sense of some passage in a rare book, they could not have touched the meaning of a single word within it. Add to this that if anyone intended to change the meaning of a common word, he could scarcely hope to ensure that future generations <note>original: "posterity"</note> would observe the change, or cause it to be accepted in everyday conversation and writing. 

From these and similar considerations, we can readily understand that it could never enter anyone's mind to corrupt a language, though it might very well happen—and has very often happened—that an author's meaning has been altered by tampering with his expressions or by misinterpreting his language.

Since the method of investigation we have proposed, then, appears to be the true and only one—the entire method being founded on the principle of seeking a knowledge of Scripture from Scripture itself—it may be assumed that whatever Scripture will not supply to enable us to obtain a knowledge of its meaning is plainly to be despaired of. As for what more could be desired in order for us to arrive at a thorough and certain knowledge of the sacred writings by this means: the first great difficulty connected with our method arises from the consummate knowledge of the Hebrew tongue <note>original: "Hebrew tongue"</note> which its proper application implies. But from where is this knowledge now to be obtained? The ancient masters of the Hebrew language have left nothing to posterity regarding the elements and principles of the language; we, at all events, have little or nothing of theirs—no dictionary, no grammar, no syntax. The Hebrew nation has lost all that it ever had of the elegances and ornaments of life (which is not surprising after such long ages of depression, disaster, and persecution), and has preserved nothing but a few fragments of its language and its literature. Almost all the names of fruits, trees, birds, beasts, fishes, and so on, along with much else, have perished. 

Furthermore, the meaning of many nouns and verbs which are met with in the Bible is either wholly unknown or is a subject of dispute. Along with all this, when we apply ourselves to study the syntax of this language—a matter of so much importance—and seek to discover the idioms and modes of expression peculiar to the Hebrew people, we find that time, the consumer of all things, has blotted them almost entirely from the memory of man. We shall not, therefore, always be able as we would wish to determine the precise meaning of every passage that the common uses of the language would permit. We shall come upon many sentences which, although expressed in words that are extremely well known, are nevertheless of a most obscure meaning, and are sometimes even incomprehensible. 

To these difficulties, which spring from the impossibility of having a perfect history of the Hebrew language, must be added those that arise from the constitution and nature of the language itself. These occasion so many ambiguities that it is impossible to find a method that shall assuredly teach us how to investigate the true sense of all the expressions of Scripture. <margin>I should say, *impossible* for us who are not accustomed to the Hebrew language, and who have lost the secret of its syntax.</margin> Besides the causes of ambiguity common to all languages...

Inherent in all languages, there are certain other difficulties peculiar to Hebrew, from which many extraordinary problems arise. It is proper that I should say something regarding their nature.

1. In the first place, doubt and obscurity are often produced in the Bible because letters produced by the same vocal organ are used interchangeably for one another. The Jews divide the letters of their alphabet into five classes, corresponding to the five instruments or organs of the mouth that assist in articulation: namely, the lips, the teeth, the tongue, the palate, and the throat. For example, *Aleph*, *Chet*, *Ayin*, and *He* <note>original: "Alpha, Ghet, Ghain, He"</note> are called gutturals; they are used for one another without any distinction—at least, none that is known to us. Furthermore, *El*, which generally signifies *to* or *towards*, is often used for *al* <note>original: "hgal"</note>, which commonly means *above*, and vice versa <note>original: "vice versâ"; meaning "the other way around"</note>. Because of this, the meaning of an entire sentence is often rendered doubtful or made to look as if it has no meaning at all.

2. A second source of ambiguity exists in the numerous meanings attached to Hebrew conjunctions and adverbs. For example, the letter *vau* <note>The Hebrew letter 'Waw' or 'Vav'</note> serves indifferently as a conjunction ("and") or a disjunction ("or"), and can also signify *but*, *because*, *then*, and *however*. The word *Ki* has seven or eight significations: *wherefore*, *although*, *if*, *when*, *inasmuch as*, *because*, *combustion*, etc. This is true for almost all such particles.

3. The third source of doubt—and it is a very fertile one—consists in the fact that in the indicative mood <note>The grammatical mood used to state facts</note>, verbs lack the present tense, the preterite imperfect <note>past ongoing action</note>, the preterpluperfect <note>action completed before another past action</note>, the future perfect, and various other tenses commonly used in other languages. In the imperative <note>command</note> and infinitive moods, verbs have nothing but the present tense, and they are altogether without the subjunctive mood <note>used for hypothetical or desired actions</note>. Although all these defects in moods and tenses may be addressed and supplied—often with extreme elegance—by certain rules easily deduced from the structure of the language, the older writers neglect them entirely. They use the future tense indifferently for the present and the past, and conversely, the past for the future.

Besides the three causes of obscurity already noted in the Hebrew language, there remain two others to be mentioned, each of much more importance than all the rest. The first of these is that *Hebrew has no vowels*; the second is that *it lacks spaces between words and sentences, and has no accents to indicate the proper pronunciation*. Although these two deficiencies—namely, the vowels and signs of accentuation—are usually supplied by *points* <note>The Masoretic points (niqqud) added to the Hebrew text to indicate vowel sounds.</note>, it is impossible for us to accept these as sufficient, because they are the invention and resource of men from much later times, whose authority can have no weight with us. Modern scholars supplied vowel-points and accents according to how they thought the Bible should be interpreted; therefore, these points are to be regarded as mere recent interpolations. They deserve no more faith, and have no higher authority, than the scholarly labors <note>original: "lucubrations"</note> of ordinary commentators.

When the question involves speculative ideas, or when miracles and histories are narrated, we can come to no conclusion whatever by comparing different authors. # INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE

In order that I may proceed with my business of showing still further wherein the true method of interpreting Scripture is itself defective, and with what other difficulties it is beset: 

Another difficulty in following out our method arises from its requiring a particular account of all that has ever happened to the books of Scripture. Now, of this we for the most part know nothing. Of the authors—or, if you please, writers—of many of the books, we either know almost nothing, or we entertain grave doubts as to the correctness with which the several books are ascribed to the parties whose names they bear, as I shall immediately show. Then, we neither know upon what occasion nor at what time those books were composed <note>original: "indited"</note>, the writers of which are unknown to us. 

Further, we know nothing of the hands into which the books fell, nor of the manuscripts <note>original: "codices"</note> which have furnished such a variety of readings, nor whether perhaps there were not many other variations in other copies. But of the great importance of information on all these points I have already spoken briefly in the proper place, where, however, I have on purpose omitted certain considerations which must now come under review.

If we are reading <note>original: "have a book under perusal"</note> a book containing many incredible or incomprehensible statements, written, too, in language sufficiently obscure, of whose author we know nothing—neither anything of the time in which or the occasion on which he wrote—we shall certainly, for the most part, strive in vain to master the true meaning of the text. For with all these matters unknown, we can in no way know either what was or what might have been the purpose of the author. 

With all these preliminary facts known, on the contrary, we could then so guide our thoughts that, preoccupied by no prejudices, we should ascribe neither more nor less than of right belongs to the author, or to him on whose account he wrote; and we should think of nothing but that which the author may have had in his mind, or which the time and the occasion of writing seemed to require. So much, I think, will be admitted by all. It very often happens indeed that we read histories in different...

# INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE

Consider different books which in many respects resemble one another, but of which we form very dissimilar estimates according to the opinion we hold of the writers or of the purpose of their writing. I know that formerly I read in a certain book of a hero named Orlando <note>A reference to *Orlando Furioso* by Ludovico Ariosto, a popular 16th-century epic poem</note>, who was accustomed to fly through the air on the back of a winged monster over various regions of the earth, slaughtering vast numbers of men and giants, with other fantastical accounts of the same sort—all plainly absurd and inconceivable when tested by reason and understanding. In Ovid <note>The Roman poet Publius Ovidius Naso</note>, again, I have read a similar history of which Perseus is the hero. And in the Books of Judges and Kings, we have the history of Samson, who alone and unarmed (except with the jawbone of an ass) slew thousands of men; and of Elijah, who flew through the air and at length went up to heaven in a fiery chariot drawn by fiery horses.

These, I say, are all obviously tales of the same character; nevertheless, we form very different estimates of each of them. For of the first, we say the writer had no purpose but to compose vanities for our amusement; of the second, that he had a political aim in view; and of the third, that the matter is sacred. All this is for no other reason than because we entertain different opinions of the writers of the several narratives. It is certain, therefore, that some knowledge of the authors whose writings contain matter that is obscure or incomprehensible is essentially necessary to the right understanding of their works. For the same reason, moreover—and so that we may choose the proper reading from among a great variety of readings of extremely obscure productions—it is necessary that we know in what copies the several readings are found, and whether there are not others extant of still higher authority.

Another difficulty which we find in interpreting certain books of Scripture on this plan lies in this: that we do not have these books in the language in which they were originally composed. The Gospel according to Matthew and unquestionably also the Epistle to the Hebrews were written, as all agree, in Hebrew; but the Hebrew version is now nowhere to be found.

For things which are readily appreciated by their own nature can never be phrased so obscurely that they are not easily enough understood, according to the proverb which says, "A word is enough to the wise."

We find it necessary here to study the life and manners of the author, nor are we interested in knowing in what language he wrote, in what age he lived, to whom he addressed himself, and so on; neither do we see it necessary to inquire into the history of the books, nor their various readings, nor how or by whose advice they were accepted as genuine. What is said here of Euclid <note>Euclid of Alexandria (c. 300 BCE), the Greek mathematician whose works on geometry were considered the gold standard of logical clarity.</note> is also to be understood of all who have written of things that can be understood through their own internal logic. Therefore, let us conclude that the meaning of Scripture on all matters of moral doctrine is easily and certainly to be ascertained from the text itself.

For the principles of true piety are expressed in the most familiar words, because they are common to all people. There is nothing more simple or more easy to understand, as the conditions for salvation and true happiness consist in purity of life and peace of mind. Now, as we only entirely agree with those things which we clearly understand, it follows most obviously that we can be perfectly certain of the meaning of Scripture in all things beneficial and necessary for the conduct of life and peace of mind. Therefore, there is no reason why we should be very anxious about the rest; for as the remainder cannot, for the most part, be grasped by reason and understanding, it is really more a matter of curiosity than of importance.

And now I think I have revealed the true method of interpreting Scripture and sufficiently explained my views of its value. I do not doubt that everyone will see that this method requires nothing except natural light <note>original: "lumen naturale"; the innate human capacity for reason and logic, independent of supernatural revelation.</note> or understanding. For the nature and excellence of natural light consists especially in this: that it leads by legitimate deduction from things known (or assumed as known) to a knowledge of things obscure or unknown. There is no other requirement which our method of inquiry demands. And although we admit that it does not suffice for coming to definite conclusions on everything contained in the Bible, this does not arise from any deficiency in the method itself. Instead, it arises from the fact that the path which it points out as the right and safe one has never been regularly traveled by scholars; so that, with the passage of time, it has become overgrown and entangled, as it were.

If we pay attention to the explanations they offer, we find nothing supernatural about them; indeed, they are nothing but mere conjectures. The explanations of these "supernaturalists" are often found to be identical to those of the critics, who frankly admit that they have no guide but their natural understanding and arrive at their conclusions by entirely human means—namely, long, painful, and laborious research. 

Those who say that natural light does not suffice for this speak unwisely. As we have already shown, the difficulty of interpreting Scripture does not arise from any deficiency in human capacity. Instead, it arises entirely from the carelessness (I will not say malice) of mankind, who neglected the history of Scripture when they might have secured and verified it.

# INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE.

I therefore denounce the method which Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher who argued that Scripture should be interpreted to align with reason and Aristotelian philosophy.</note> proposes for the interpretation of Scripture as useless, harmful, and absurd.

With regard to the traditional interpretation of the Pharisees, we have already said that it is not consistent with itself. As for the Roman pontifical system, I say it requires clearer evidence for its authority than any I can discover. I therefore reject it for this and no other reason. For if the Scriptures now presented the same matters to us with the same certainty as they did formerly to the Jewish high priests, I would not be disturbed by the fact that among the Roman pontiffs there had been found more than one heretical and impious man. We know that among the ancient Jewish high priests, heretical and impious men were also encountered—men who obtained the office of high priest by corrupt <note>original: "sinister"</note> means. In spite of this, they were nevertheless invested by the command of Scripture itself with the supreme power of interpreting <note>original: "construing"</note> the law (see Exodus 17:11, 12, and 33:10, and Malachi 2:8). 

But as the Roman pontiff can show no such authority for the right he assumes, his power is questionable. Lest anyone, misled by the example of the Hebrew high priest, should think that the Christian religion also required a pontiff, it must be noted that the laws of Moses were the laws of the country—the foundation of public law—and necessarily required some public authority for their preservation. Had everyone been at liberty to interpret the laws of the State in his own arbitrary way, there would soon have been no true republic; its structure would have been dissolved, and public law converted into private law. 

But it is altogether different with regard to religion. Inasmuch as religion consists much less in outward acts than in simplicity and purity of soul, it has nothing whatever to do with public law and political power. Purity and integrity <note>original: "probity"</note> of soul are founded on no power of law and on no public authority. No one can be compelled by law or force to follow the path of true happiness. To pursue this, one requires pious advice, friendly and brotherly <note>original: "fraternal"</note> counsel, a good education, and, above all, a well-
