<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the individual's right to interpret sacred texts, contrasting personal reason with ecclesiastical authority.</meta>

<page-num>168</page-num>
# INTERPRETATION OF SCRIPTURE

A balanced and liberal mind is indispensable. Since, therefore, the <term>indefeasible right</term><note>original: "indefeasible right"; a right that cannot be lost, overturned, or taken away</note> of thinking independently on all subjects—even on religion—belongs to everyone, and as it is impossible to conceive of any reasonable man divesting himself of this right, the full and perfect title and authority to judge religion independently, and consequently to explain and interpret Scripture for himself, belongs by right to every man. 

The privilege of administering the laws and pronouncing final judgments on public affairs is lodged with the magistrate for no other reason than that it is a public right of which he is the guardian and expounder. In like manner, the right of judging and interpreting religion is lodged with each individual man because it is his own peculiar and private business. 

There is a great deal wanting, therefore, to satisfy us when—based on the authority of the Jewish high priest to interpret the laws of his country—it is inferred that the Roman <term>pontiff</term><note>The Pope</note> is also by right possessed of authority to interpret the Christian religion for the whole world. On the contrary, we much more readily arrive at the conclusion, from the nature of religion itself, that everyone can best do this for himself. 

And herein we believe that we see another proof of the excellence of the method we have proposed for arriving at a knowledge of the Scriptures. For, assuming as we do that the supreme right to interpret the Bible belongs to everyone individually, we conclude that the standard of interpretation should be nothing but the **natural light** or understanding which is common to all. It should not be any supernatural light, nor any <term>extrinsic authority</term><note>External authority, such as a church decree or a king's command</note>. The task ought not to be so difficult as to only be practicable by the most learned philosophers; rather, it should be found within the scope of the common genius and capacity of mankind, as it is by the plan which we have proposed. We have seen that the difficulties which still attach to it are owing to the carelessness of men, and do not in any way belong to the nature of the subject itself.

## CHAPTER VIII.

->### CONCERNING THE PENTATEUCH <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note>, AND THE BOOKS OF JOSHUA, JUDGES, RUTH, SAMUEL, AND KINGS. In the preceding chapter, we treated the grounds or principles on which a knowledge of the Scriptures should be based, and we have shown that a faithful history of their contents must underlie everything else. But this, although of primary necessity, the ancients almost entirely neglected; or if they wrote anything on the subject, it has perished in the lapse of time. The greater part of the grounds or first principles of historical Scripture knowledge is therefore wanting or lost to us. This is a misfortune that might have been endured had later writers confined themselves within proper bounds, transmitted the little they had received or discovered with good faith to their successors, and abstained from coining novelties out of their own brains. Because of these inventions, it has come to pass that the history of the Hebrew Scriptures is not only defective, but is so full of errors that it is now impossible to reconstruct it free from all imperfection. It is within the scope of my undertaking, however, to seek to amend the fundamentals of Scripture knowledge, and not to rest content with merely getting rid of a few of the more common prejudices of theologians. I only fear that I attempt this task at too late a date, for things have now gone so far that men will not readily suffer <note>original: "suffer," meaning to permit or tolerate.</note>

Moses is believed by almost everyone to be the author of the Pentateuch—that is, of the Books of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. So stubbornly did the Pharisees <note>A prominent ancient Jewish sect known for strict adherence to traditional and written law.</note> cling to this belief that they held everyone a heretic who ventured to think otherwise. This is the reason why Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a distinguished Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note>, a man of a liberal spirit and no mean erudition <note>learning or scholarship</note>, and who, so far as my reading extends, was the first to criticize <note>original: "animadvert upon"</note> this prejudice, has not thought fit to open his mind freely on the matter. Instead, he only hinted at it in words so obscure as to be generally unintelligible. These, however, I for my part shall not fear to render plain by placing the whole subject in the broadest light. The words of Aben Ezra, which occur in his commentary on Deuteronomy, are these:

> "Beyond Jordan... provided you understand the mystery of the Twelve;... also that Moses wrote the Law while the Canaanites were in the land;... it will be revealed on the mountain of God.... Then also behold his bed, his bed of iron;... then you will know the truth."

Now, in these few and disjointed words, Aben Ezra indicates his opinion that it was not Moses who wrote the Pentateuch, but some other person who lived long after him; and lastly, that the book which Moses wrote was not any one we now have under his name, but another. To shadow forth these particulars, Aben Ezra in the above passage shows:

First, that the preface to Deuteronomy could not have been written by Moses, as it refers to him in the third person and describes locations he never reached.

Fourth, our author in his third clause refers to Genesis 12:6, where the historian, relating how Abraham came into the land of Canaan, adds: “And the Canaanite was *then* in the land.” The word “then”—meaning at that time—plainly excludes the time when the narrative was written. Only under such a state of things could such language have been used. But it is not in this place only that we discover the writer of the Pentateuch interpolating <note>original: "interpolating," meaning inserting new words into an existing text</note> the words of Moses, for he says a little further on (Deuteronomy 3:14): "Jair the son of Manasseh took all the country of Argob unto the coasts of Geshuri and Maachathi, and called them after his own name, Bashan-havoth-jair, unto this day." The Jews, contemporaries of this writer, were aware without doubt which were the towns of Jair, of the tribe of Judah, but they did not know the name of the jurisdiction of Argob, nor of the land of giants. Therefore, he was forced to tell them what the places were which in former ages had been so entitled, and at the same time to give a reason why they were designated by the name of Jair, of the tribe of Judah, and not of Manasseh (see Chronicles 2:21, 22). Thus do we explain the enigmatical <note>mysterious or puzzling</note> passage of Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar and biblical commentator</note>, and quote the texts of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note> which support our interpretation of its meaning.

But Aben Ezra has neither noticed all nor even the principal passages of those books, which, as of still greater importance, require attention from us. For example and firstly: The writer of the books of the Pentateuch not only continually speaks of Moses in the third person, but moreover testifies to many things concerning him. Thus he uses such phrases as these: "God said to Moses"; "God spoke with Moses face to face"; "Moses was the meekest of men" (Numbers 12:3); "Moses was angry against the leaders of the host" (Ibid. 14:14); "Moses a divine man" (Deuteronomy 33:1); "And Moses, the servant of God, died; never was there a prophet in Israel like unto Moses." In Deuteronomy, on the contrary, where Moses himself explains the law to the people, he speaks and relates his deeds in the first person; thus he says, "God spoke to me" (Deuteronomy 2:1, 17, etc.); "I prayed to the Lord," and so forth. Finally, at the end of the first book, the historian, after having related the words of Moses, adds: "And Moses wrote this law and delivered it to the priests, the sons of Levi, and to all the elders of Israel" (Deuteronomy 31:9). This clearly shows that the historian was a different person from Moses.

It is also to be particularly observed that in this history, it is not only narrated how Moses died and was buried, and how the Jews mourned for him for thirty days, but over and above all this, we have a comparison established between him and all the prophets who lived after him. "Never was there a prophet in Israel," we are informed, "like unto Moses, whom God knew face to face." Now, testimony such as this could not be delivered by Moses about himself; nor yet by anyone who followed him closely. It must necessarily have been written by some person who lived long ages after him. This view is confirmed by the tense in which the historian speaks, which is always the past tense <note>original: "preter-past"</note>—"never was there," "never did there exist a prophet," etc. And then, when mention is made of the place of his burial <term>sepulture</term>, we are told in the present tense that "no one *knows* [where it is], not even unto this day."

3. It is further to be remarked that certain places are mentioned by names which they did not bear in the time of Moses, but by others which they acquired subsequently. For example, there is the passage where Abraham pursued the enemy even to *Dan* (Genesis 14:14), a name which the city did not obtain until long after the death of Joshua (Judges 18:29).

4. The historical narrative is sometimes carried on beyond the time of Moses. Thus, in Exodus we learn that the children of Israel were fed with manna for forty years, until they came to peopled territory, until they reached the borders of the land of Canaan. That is, until the time of which we read in the Book of Joshua (5:12). We also find this in the Book of Genesis (36:31), which contains these words: "These are the kings who ruled in Edom before a king reigned over the children of Israel."

Furthermore, when we search for the books which Moses himself actually wrote—as they are referred to within the Pentateuch—we can be certain from these references that they were different from any of the five books now generally attributed to him. 

First, it is known from Exodus (17:14) that Moses, by God’s command, wrote "the war against the Amalekites." However, we do not learn from that chapter where or in what book this was recorded. ## AND EZRA AS COMPILER.

What Moses wrote was not the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note>, but another book altogether, which the author of the Pentateuch introduced in what seemed to be its proper place in his own comprehensive work. This is a conclusion supported by everything that precedes it, as it will also be by all that follows. Thus, when it is related in the passage of Deuteronomy just cited that “Moses wrote a book,” the historian adds that Moses delivered it to the priests and commanded them that they should read it at certain stated times to the whole people. This circumstance is in itself sufficient to prove that the book in question was much less bulky than the Pentateuch, for it could be read through at a single meeting so as to be understood by everyone. 

Nor should it be overlooked that of all the books Moses wrote, he especially commanded this one regarding the second covenant and the song (which he wrote later for the whole people to learn by heart) to be religiously preserved and guarded. The first covenant was held to bind only those who were actually present; the second was to be considered mandatory for everyone, and even for future generations (see Deuteronomy 29:14, 15). Therefore, he ordered the book of this second covenant to be religiously preserved for future ages, for whom the song or canticle <note>original: "canticle"; a hymn or chant derived from biblical text.</note> is also especially designed. 

Since, therefore, it is not confirmed that Moses wrote any books other than those referred to above, and as he himself directed no other book but that on the law with the canticle to be religiously preserved for the sake of posterity <note>Future generations.</note>, and, lastly, as there are many things in the Pentateuch which could not possibly have been written by Moses, it follows that no one in their right mind can maintain that Moses is the author of the Pentateuch. Anyone who did so would have to go against every principle of sound reason.

But here someone might perhaps ask: Did Moses, besides these books, not commit the laws to writing when they were first revealed to him? That is to say, whether for the long period of forty years he wrote down none of the laws he carried in his memory, except those—

To the few points which I have said were contained in the original covenant, how do I reply to these questions? I reply that although I admit it is consistent with reason to believe that Moses wrote down the laws at the same time he received them, I deny, nevertheless, that we are therefore free to assert that he actually did so. As we have shown above, we must take nothing for granted on such subjects except only that which we find in *Scripture*, or which can be deduced from its teaching by logical inference—and nothing else, even if it seems to be in harmony with the soundest reason. 

Add to this that even reason does not force us to reach such a conclusion. Let us conclude, therefore, that all the books which we have just reviewed are apographs <note>original: "apographs"; copies or transcripts of original manuscripts, implying they are not the primary autographs written by the historical figures themselves</note>—works written ages after the events they relate had passed away. When we examine the subject matter and the connection between these books individually, we can readily see that they were all written by one and the same person. This author had the purpose of compiling a comprehensive system of Jewish antiquities, from the origin of the nation to the first destruction of the city of Jerusalem. 

The various books are so closely linked to one another that this alone reveals they comprise a continuous narrative by a single historian. For example, as soon as he ends the life of Moses, he passes immediately to the history of Joshua: "And it came to pass when Moses, the servant of the Lord, was dead, that God said to Joshua," etc. (Joshua 1:1). Once Joshua is dead, the historian begins the book of Judges using the same transition and conjunction: "And it came to pass, after Joshua was dead, that the children of Israel asked of God," etc. (Judges 1:1). 

The short book of Ruth is connected to the book of Judges as a kind of appendix in this way: "And it came to pass in those days, when the Judges ruled in Israel, that there was a famine in the land," etc. (Ruth 1:1). In the same manner, when the First Book of Samuel ends, the writer proceeds to the Second Book. Because the history of King David is not concluded there, he adds the First Book of Kings; and as the narrative requires even more space, he adds the Second Book. 

Finally, the context and the order of these histories indicate that they are all the work of one writer. He begins his task with a fixed and definite goal: starting with an account of the origin of the Hebrew nation, and then describing in regular sequence the times and occasions when Moses announced the law and prophesied to the Jews. Next, he tells how—guided by the predictions of Moses—they invaded the Promised Land (Deuteronomy 7); and how, once they had conquered it, they abandoned the laws of Jehovah (Deuteronomy <note>The text breaks off here, likely referring to the warnings in Deuteronomy regarding the consequences of apostasy.</note>

(Deuteronomy 31:16), from which many painful disasters followed (Deuteronomy 31:17); how they next desired to choose a king for themselves (Deuteronomy 17:14), who, depending on whether he observed or neglected the law, brought prosperity or disaster upon the people (Deuteronomy 28:36, *and following*), until the author reaches the conclusion—the destruction of the Jewish Empire, as it had been foretold by Moses. On other subjects which have nothing to do with the establishment of the law, the writer either keeps completely silent or refers the reader to other historians. The whole of these books, therefore, lead to one end: namely, to enforce the sayings and edicts of Moses and to demonstrate their sacredness through the course of historical events. 

From these three points taken together—the unity and simplicity of the argument across all the books, their connection or sequence, and their <term>apographic character</term> <note>original: "apographic character"; meaning they are copies or secondary accounts written long after the original events</note>, having been written many ages after the events they record—we conclude, as has just been said, that they were all written by one historiographer. Who this was, however, cannot be so readily shown, although from certain concurring and significant circumstances, I am led to suspect that Ezra was the man. 

I say I am led to Ezra as the writer. Thus, when the historian—whom we now know to have been the sole author of the work—has brought his narrative down to the time when Jehoiachin recovered his liberty, he adds that he himself had sat at the king’s table all his life. However, whether this was the table of Jehoiachin or of the son of Nebuchadnezzar is not certain, for the sense of the passage is doubtful. Whichever it was, it follows nevertheless that the books in question could have been written by no one before Ezra. 

Now, Scripture bears testimony to no one but Ezra who flourished at this time, whose studies were likely to have led him to investigate and illustrate the law of God, and who was a writer skilled—as we are informed Ezra was—in the law of Moses (see Ezra 7:6, 10, 11). I cannot, therefore, conceive of anyone but Ezra being the writer of these books. In the testimony to the accomplishments of Ezra just referred to, we see that he not only gave his mind...

The word "annotated" refers to the Hebrew *mephorash*, implying a clear explanation or translation.</note> Now, as the whole or the greater part of the law of Moses is comprised in the Book of Deuteronomy, and much additional matter is there interpolated <note>original: "interpolated"; meaning inserted or added later</note> with a view to its better comprehension, I conjecture that the Book of Deuteronomy is the identical book of the law of God, written fairly out, annotated, illustrated, and explained by Ezra, which was then read. 

But as there are many things interpolated in the Book of Deuteronomy by way of parentheses for the better understanding of the text, I shall give two instances of the sort, with the commentary of Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator</note> upon them. Thus, in chapter 2, verse 12, we find these words, "The Horites dwelt in Seir beforetime; but the children of Esau drove them out, and destroyed them out of sight, and dwelt in their stead, as Israel did in the land of his inheritance which God gave him." 

This passage is inserted as an explanation of the earlier verses of the same chapter, where Israel, after circling Mount Seir many days, is instructed to turn northward and to pass the territories of their brethren, the children of Esau, then dwelling in Seir—the district which had fallen to them by lot as a heritage, but of which the children of Esau had only obtained possession by invading it and expelling the Horites who dwelt in the land before them; exactly as the Israelites after the death of Moses had fallen upon and exterminated the Canaanites, and then taken possession of their lands. The words of Moses are also interpolated parenthetically in verses 6, 7, 8, and 9 of the 10th chapter. Every one must see that the 8th verse, which begins thus, "At that time the Lord separated..."

<margin>Deuteronomy 10:8</margin>
The passage stating that "at that time the Lord separated the tribe of Levi to bear the ark," etc., and ending with the words "unto this day," must necessarily refer to verse 5, and not to the death of Aaron. Aaron's death appears to be mentioned for no other reason than that Moses, in the history of the golden calf which the people worshipped, had said (see Deuteronomy 9:20) that he had prayed to God for Aaron. The author then proceeds to explain that God, at the time Moses speaks of, elected the tribe of Levi to himself, so that he might show the reason for that election and why the Levites were called to no share of the inheritance. Once this is done, he goes on with the thread of his narrative in the words of Moses. 

In addition to what precedes, consider the preface of the book and the places where Moses is mentioned in the third person. There are also numerous passages which we cannot detect now, but which were undoubtedly added so that the people of the writer’s own time might more readily understand the narrative. I say that had we the *Book of the Law* exactly as Moses wrote it, I do not doubt that we would find many discrepancies, both in the order of events and in the reasons given for the commandments. 

For when I compare the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> of the Book of Deuteronomy with that of Exodus (where the history of the Decalogue is expressly given), I find discrepancies between the two in these important particulars:
1. The fourth commandment is not only delivered differently, but is, furthermore, much more wordy in its details.
2. More important still, the reasons assigned for the commandment differ entirely <note>original: *toto cælo*, literally "by the whole heaven" or "as far as the poles apart"</note> from those in Exodus.
3. Lastly, the order in which the tenth commandment is explained here is also different from the order observed in Exodus. 

I am of the opinion, therefore, that all of this—as well as much more in other places—is the work of Ezra, because he set himself the task of explaining the law of God to the people of his own time. I am further of the opinion that the Book of Deuteronomy, as it has come down to us, is Moses’ *Book of the Law of God*, illustrated and explained by Ezra. I am, moreover, disposed to conclude that this was the first book written by Ezra of all those that came from his pen.

hand; and for this reason—that it contains the laws of the country, which are the most necessary for the people to know. Also, this book is not connected to the one preceding it by any conjunction <note>original: "conjunction"; referring to the Hebrew grammatical practice of starting books with "And," which Deuteronomy does not do</note>, as all the others are linked to their predecessors, as has been shown. Deuteronomy, on the contrary, begins abruptly: “These are the words which Moses spoke,” etc. 

Having achieved this first work, the purpose of which was to make a knowledge of the laws accessible to the people, I believe that Ezra then set about the task of narrating the entire history of the Hebrew nation, from the creation of the world to the destruction of Jerusalem. In this larger undertaking, he inserted this Book of Deuteronomy in its proper place. Perhaps he was led to call the first five books of his history by the name of Moses because they primarily comprise the incidents in the life of the great prophet; the leading personage gives his name to the narrative. 

For the same reason, the sixth book is entitled the Book of Joshua, as the deeds of this leader form its principal subject; the seventh is the Book of Judges, the eighth the Book of Ruth, the ninth and tenth are the Books of Samuel, and, lastly, the eleventh and twelfth are the Books of Kings. This is despite the fact that neither Joshua, the Judges of Israel, Ruth, Samuel, nor the Kings had any part in the composition of the books that bear their names. But whether Ezra put the finishing hand to his work and completed it as he may have wished is a matter of so much interest that we shall discuss the subject in the next chapter.

## CHAPTER IX.

->CONCERNING THE SAME BOOKS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT. DID EZRA PUT THE FINISHING HAND TO HIS WORK? ARE THE MARGINAL ANNOTATIONS OF THE HEBREW MANUSCRIPTS <note>original: "codices"</note> TO BE CONSIDERED AS VARIOUS READINGS <note>original: "variorum readings"</note> OF THE TEXT?<-

How much the preceding investigation <note>original: "disquisition"</note> on the actual writer of the first twelve books of the Hebrew Scriptures aids us in understanding them appears sufficiently from the passages quoted in support of the views advanced. Without some such guide as we have attempted to supply, indeed, these books must remain a mystery <note>original: "enigma"</note> to every one.

But, besides the writer, there remain many other things in the books themselves which demand critical observation <note>original: "animadversion"</note>, although superstition would persuade us to turn our eyes away from too curiously examining <note>original: "scrutinizing"</note> their contents. Among the number of interesting subjects of inquiry is the question of why Ezra—whom I shall continue to speak of as the writer or compiler of the earlier books of Scripture, until another is discovered with better claims <note>original: "pretensions"</note> to the authorship—did not, as he certainly did not, put the finishing hand to the work he undertook? Ezra did little, in fact, but gather materials from other earlier writers, and then, without much examination or any care for arrangement, set down the results of his labors in a simple style; and it is in this unpolished <note>original: "inartificial"</note> and unorganized <note>original: "undigested"</note> state that the narrative compiled by him has reached us.

<summary>The author argues that Ezra was the compiler of the first twelve books of the Old Testament but failed to finalize or organize the materials, leaving the text in an unpolished state.</summary>
<keywords>Ezra, Old Testament authorship, Hebrew Scriptures, biblical criticism, compilation process</keywords>

# THE OLD TESTAMENT.

These records have been transmitted to posterity. What cause prevented Ezra from revising his work I am at a loss to conjecture, unless perhaps it was a sudden or premature death. But that the matter is as I have stated it seems abundantly demonstrated by the few fragments of the earlier Hebrew historians that have come down to us. 

For the history of Hezekiah <note>original: "Hiskiah"</note>, from the 17th verse of chapter 18 of the Second Book of Kings onwards, is derived from the narrative of Isaiah. Everything said about Hezekiah in the Book of Isaiah is also contained in the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah; the same incidents are found narrated, with trifling exceptions, in the same words in both. From any diversity here, however, nothing more can be inferred than that there were different versions extant of Isaiah's narrative—unless, indeed, one imagines that there is some mystery lurking under the fact of this identity. 

Again, the last chapter of the Second Book of Chronicles is included in the last chapter of Jeremiah. Furthermore, the 7th chapter of the Second Book of Samuel is contained in the 17th chapter of the First Book of Chronicles; but the words in several places are found so singularly altered that it evidently appears these two chapters were derived from two different copies of the history written by Nathan <note>The prophet Nathan, to whom several lost historical books are attributed in the Bible</note>. 

Lastly, the genealogy of the Kings of Edom <note>original: "Idumea"</note> which we have in the 36th chapter of Genesis is found in the very same words in the 1st chapter of the First Book of Chronicles, although it is agreed that the author of Chronicles derived the particulars he narrates from other historical records, and not from any of the twelve books which we here ascribe to Ezra. 

There is no reason to doubt, therefore, that if we still possessed those original historical records, the facts would be immediately confirmed as I have represented them. But since these ancient documents have all perished, we have no resource but to critically study the histories that have come down to us. We must scrutinize their order and connection, the various repetitions in their course, and, finally, the discrepancies in the counting of years, so that we may form a judgment of what remains.

# THE OLD TESTAMENT.

We shall now, therefore, proceed to consider the chief of these matters, beginning with the account of Judah and Tamar, which the historian in the 38th chapter of the Book of Genesis enters upon in these terms:

> “Now it came to pass at that time, that Judah went down from his brothers.”

“At that time” necessarily here refers to some other time than that in which the historian is immediately speaking; but of the precise time referred to we have no means of judging. <margin>That this passage can only refer to the time when Joseph was sold by his brothers is made evident by the context, but the same thing may be concluded from the age of Judah, who was then 22 years old at the most, taking as a basis for the calculation the history of him which has just been given. From chapter 29 of Genesis, last verse, it appears that Judah was born in the 10th year of Jacob’s servitude to Laban, and Joseph in the 14th year. Now we know that Joseph was 17 years old when he was sold by his brothers, so that Judah was not more than 21. They, therefore, who pretend that the long absence of Judah from the house of his father occurred before the sale of Joseph try to deceive themselves, and their anxiety for the inspiration of Scripture only brings it into question.</margin> For from the time when Joseph was carried into Egypt to that when the Patriarch Jacob also proceeded there with the whole of his family, we can reckon no more than 22 years. Joseph, when he was sold by his brothers, was 17 years of age, and when released from prison by order of Pharaoh he was 30; if to the difference between these two numbers (13) we add the seven years of plenty and the two years of famine <note>original: "dearth"</note>, we have 22 years. 

But in this space of time no one can conceive that so many events could have happened as we find recorded; namely, that Judah fathered three children one after another by one wife, whom he had just then married; the eldest born of whom, when his age permitted, took Tamar as his wife; but he dying, a second brother married the widow; and he also dying, Judah himself had sexual relations with Tamar, and by her had twins, one of whom, within the interval mentioned, married and had children. Such a series of events is plainly impossible within the time specified in Genesis, and must therefore have occurred at some other time. Ezra <note>The author identifies Ezra as the likely compiler or "historian" of the Pentateuch, a common view in early biblical criticism.</note>, our historian, however, gave the story of Judah—

But this is not the only story derived from different records or traditions; the entire history of Jacob and Joseph appears to be compiled in a similar way, as the various parts of the narrative poorly agree with one another. 

For instance, in the 47th chapter of Genesis, it is recorded that Jacob was 130 years old when his son Joseph first presented him to Pharaoh. If we subtract the 22 years he spent grieving for the loss of Joseph, the 17 years of Joseph’s age when he was sold by his brothers, and finally the seven years he served for Rachel, we find that Jacob was at the very advanced age of 84 when he married Leah. On the contrary, this timeline would mean that Dinah could scarcely have been seven when she was raped by Shechem <note>original: "Sechem"</note>, and Simeon and Levi would have been only 12 and 11 years old when they destroyed a city and put all its inhabitants to the sword.

However, there is no need to review the entire Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note> here. Anyone who notices that in these five books, legal instructions <note>original: "precept"</note> and stories are jumbled together without order, that there is no respect for chronology, and that the same story is often repeated—occasionally with significant differences in the details—must conclude that the Pentateuch consists merely of notes and collections to be examined at leisure. These are the raw materials for history rather than a finished, organized history itself. 

Nor do these remarks apply only to the Pentateuch; the seven books that follow, down to the destruction of Jerusalem, have the same character and are compiled in the same way. Who can fail to see, for example, that from verse six of the 2nd chapter of Judges, the writer is drawing from another record that also describes the deeds of Joshua, and from which the very words used are likely derived? In a similar way, the 17th and 18th chapters of the First Book of Samuel are taken from a different record. After David engages and kills the Philistine giant Goliath in single combat, the fame of the deed reaches the king’s ears, and the young victor is brought before him.

I also suspect that in the 26th chapter of 1 Samuel, the writer uses another source to describe the same incident already recorded in the 24th chapter. But I will move on to consider the amount of time that must have passed between important events in the history of the Hebrew nation.

In the 6th chapter of the First Book of Kings, it is stated that Solomon built the Temple in the 480th year after the Exodus <note>The departure of the Israelites from Egypt.</note>. Furthermore, we must add the years of Saul’s reign, which I have not mentioned in the previous list because his history does not clearly state how many years he actually reigned. It is indeed stated in chapter 13, verse 1 of *1 Samuel* that Saul reigned for two years, but the text here is corrupted <note>original: "defective"; the author is pointing out a "lacuna" or gap in the surviving Hebrew manuscript.</note>; and from the history itself, we learn that he reigned for more than the number of years specified. Therefore, if Saul only reigned two years, all the other events of his reign must have occurred in an interval of no more than eight months, which I think no one will argue is probable.

Josephus, indeed, at the end of the sixth book of his *Antiquities of the Jews* <note>A famous history of the Jewish people written by the 1st-century historian Flavius Josephus.</note>, corrects the text in this way: “Saul therefore reigned during the lifetime of Samuel for eighteen years, and after the death of Samuel for two years more.” The entire history of chapter 13, however, does not agree at all with what has come before. Therefore, they avoided the dilemma of appearing to prefer one version over another by regularly writing one and constantly reading the other aloud. Thus, it became a universal rule that when the Bible was read aloud, the marginal words or phrases should be spoken.*

...did not fall under such a category. Therefore, I will proceed to show why the scribes were motivated to preserve both types of annotations. 

Many of the marginal notes <note>original: "marginalia"</note> explain obsolete words. At other times, they provide more polite substitutes for blunt or crude language that later standards of decency did not allow to be spoken in public. The ancient writers did not tend to use indirect, "courtly" language; they called things by their most common names. 

As society became more refined, however, expressions used naturally by previous generations began to be seen as offensive. To avoid these without changing the actual text of the sacred volume itself, a marginal note provided the words to be used during public readings. In this way, public concern for the text's integrity was respected: the written word remained unchanged, while the spoken version did not offend the listener's ear. 

Whatever the reason for using these marginal readings during the recitation of Scripture, it was certainly not because they were considered the "true" version, or because all interpretation had to follow them. Not only do the Rabbis in the Talmud <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, consisting of the Mishnah and the Gemara.</note> often differ from the Masoretic <note>Referring to the Masoretes, the Jewish scholars who, between the 6th and 10th centuries, standardized the text, pronunciation, and cantillation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> writers and approve other readings (as I will soon demonstrate), but many marginal notes also seem poorly suited to the natural character of the Hebrew language. 

In the Second Book of Samuel, for example (14:23), the text says, "In that the king has fulfilled the request of his servant." This construction is grammatically correct and matches verse 15 of the same chapter. However, the marginal variation suggests "of *your* servant," which does not match the grammatical person of the verb being used. Similarly, in the final verse of the 16th chapter of the same book, the text reads, "As if a man had inquired at the oracle of God." Opposite this, in the margin, are the words "who had inquired," adding the word "who" to serve as the subject <note>original: "nominative"</note> of the verb. This, however...

However, this is not done judiciously or properly, for the common custom in this language is to use impersonal verbs in the third person singular of the active verb, as is very well known to grammarians. Similarly, many other marginal notes are found that should by no means be preferred over the words in the main text.

In addition to doubtful readings, the scribes noted obsolete words. There is no doubt that in Hebrew, as in other languages, time and changing usage made many words outdated or antique. When more recent scribes—who, as previously mentioned, marked everything—found these words in the Bible, they annotated them so the text could be read aloud to the public in a way that aligned with current usage and custom. This is why the word *na'ar* <note>original: "nahgar"; a Hebrew word for "youth" or "servant." In the oldest parts of the Bible, this word was used for both boys and girls, but later Hebrew added a feminine suffix for girls.</note> is noted wherever it appears, because in more ancient times it was of a common gender, used for both masculine and feminine. 

Likewise, the capital city of the Jews was written as Jerusalem, not "Jerusalim" <note>The author refers to the difference between the written form (Jerushalem) and the later pronunciation (Jerushalayim) reflected in marginal points.</note>. The same can be said for the pronouns "he" <note>original: "himself"</note> and "she" <note>original: "herself"</note>. Later writers turned the letter *Vau* <note>The Hebrew letter 'Waw' or 'Vav' (ו)</note> into the letter *Yod* <note>original: "Jod"; the Hebrew letter 'Yod' (י)</note>—a change that occurs frequently in Hebrew—when they wanted to indicate the feminine gender. However, the ancients did not do this; they were not accustomed to distinguishing the masculine from the feminine except through vowel sounds. Thus, among the irregularities of certain words, some belong to the ancients and others to the moderns. Finally, the ancients in their time often used "paragrammatic letters" <note>Letters added to the end of a word that do not change its meaning, often used in ancient poetry for rhythm or emphasis.</note> with great elegance. 

I could illustrate all these points with many examples, but I do not wish to test the reader's patience any longer. However, if anyone asks how I know these things, I reply that I have often encountered these words and details in the most ancient writings—that is, in the Bible itself. The only reason words and phrases become antique and obsolete is that subsequent writers stop using them. The <term>marginal notes</term><note>original: "marginals"; these refer to the *Keri* (what is read) as opposed to the *Ketiv* (what is written) in the Hebrew Bible.</note> refer to doubtful readings. Some people ask: how does it happen that there are never more than two variations for a single word or phrase? Why aren't there occasionally three or more? But it is easy to answer these questions and suggestions. To the first point, I say that the variations were often many more than those noted in our <term>codices</term><note>original: "codices"; ancient manuscript books.</note>. In the <term>Talmud</term><note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, containing records of rabbinic discussions.</note>, there are many variations that were ignored by the <term>Masoretes</term><note>Jewish scholars between the 6th and 10th centuries who worked to standardize the text of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. He says, 

> "At this point, I do not know how to respond, except to repeat what I have already said: namely, that it is the habit of the Talmudists to contradict the Masoretes." 

Therefore, I cannot accept the assumption that there were never more than two variations for any one passage. However, I readily admit—and indeed, I believe—that no more than two are ever found in any single manuscript, and this is for two reasons:

**1st.** Because the main cause of these different readings is essentially two-fold. It is primarily due to the resemblance of one Hebrew letter to another. In fact, it is a recurring question, whenever there is room for doubt, whether **Beth** (ב) or **Kaph** (כ), **Yod** (י) or **Waw** (ו), **Daleth** (ד) or **Resh** (ר), etc., is the proper letter to use. Since these are among the most frequently used letters in the language, it often happens that either one will make tolerable sense within the context. Additionally, whether a syllable should be long or short is determined by the "quantities" of those letters which we have described as "quiescent" or "slurred" <note>Letters that are sometimes written but not pronounced, often acting as vowel indicators.</note>. We must also add that not all marginal notes refer to doubtful readings; many, we should say, were added from a sense of duty and, as has been mentioned, for the sake of explaining obsolete or antiquated words.

The fact that copies of the Hebrew Scriptures became extremely rare after the time of Ezra will no longer be surprising to anyone who reads the first chapter of the First Book of Maccabees, or the seventh chapter of the Twelfth Book of Josephus's *Antiquities of the Jews*. Given the long and terrible persecution the Jews endured, it is quite remarkable that they were able to preserve anything at all; I believe no one who pays the slightest attention to the history of their sufferings will question this truth. Therefore, we see enough evidence to explain why no more than two variants are preserved for any given passage. This fact provides no support for those who argue that the Bible was written intentionally obscurely in these famous passages to hide certain important mysteries.

As for certain passages written so incorrectly that they violate the basic rules of language of all times—and which should have been corrected completely rather than simply noted in the margin—I have nothing to say. I cannot imagine what sense of respect kept the scribes from fixing them. Perhaps it was due to a strict scrupulousness and a desire to pass down these ancient writings to future generations exactly as they had received them, noting the discrepancies in the originals as "various readings" rather than as matters of uncertain meaning. In addition to all these doubtful variant readings, the scribes have further noted many defective or truncated places—gaps in the middle of paragraphs, and so on—the number of which is recorded by the <term>Masoretes</term><note>original: "Masoretes"; Jewish scholars between the 6th and 10th centuries who standardized the Hebrew Bible's text, vowel signs, and accent marks.</note> as twenty-eight. I am not aware whether they connect anything mysterious with this number or not. The <term>Pharisees</term><note>A prominent Jewish social and religious movement; here, the author refers to their tradition of strict textual preservation.</note>, however, scrupulously preserve certain spaces in their transcriptions of the Scriptures. I will give a single example as an illustration. We find the eighth verse of the fourth chapter of Genesis written as follows: “And Cain said to his brother Abel . . . . and it came to pass, while they were in the fields, that Cain,” etc.* The blank space is left at the point where we would have expected to learn what Cain said to his brother. Including those we have already specifically discussed, the spaces left by the scribes are twenty-eight in number; however, many of the passages where they occur would not actually appear incomplete if the inserted spaces were omitted. But enough on these matters.

\* In the English version, where textual difficulties are often smoothed over, the omission in the verse quoted would not be noticed if it were not pointed out. It reads as follows: “And Cain talked with Abel, his brother: and it came to pass,” etc.—*Editor.*

# CHAPTER X.

## OF THE REMAINING BOOKS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT.

I pass on to the remaining books of the Old Testament. Regarding the two books of <term>Paralipomena</term><note>original: "Paralipomena"; from a Greek word meaning "things omitted," this is the traditional title for the books of 1 and 2 Chronicles in the Septuagint and Vulgate.</note> (1 and 2 Chronicles), I have nothing certain or important to say, except that they were written long after the time of <term>Ezra</term><note>A Jewish scribe and priest who led a group of Judean exiles from Babylon back to Jerusalem in the 5th century BCE.</note>, and perhaps even after the restoration of the temple by <term>Judas Maccabeus</term><note>A leader of the Jewish revolt against the Seleucid Empire in the 160s BCE; he is famous for rededicating the Temple in Jerusalem, an event celebrated during Hanukkah.</note>. In chapter 9 of the First Book, the historian informs us "which families first dwelt in Jerusalem" (with the word "first" referring to the time of Ezra), and in the 17th verse, he gives the names of the gatekeepers, two of whom are also mentioned by Nehemiah (11:19). This by itself is enough to show that the books were written long after the rebuilding of the city. 

Regarding their actual writer, the authority that should be granted to them, or their usefulness and doctrine, I have nothing to say. Indeed, I cannot wonder enough how these books came to be accepted as sacred by those who excluded the Book of Wisdom, Tobit, Esdras, and the rest—which are labeled as <term>Apocryphal</term><note>A group of books excluded from the Hebrew Bible but included in some Christian versions of the Old Testament.</note>—from the <term>canon</term><note>The official list of books recognized as genuine and inspired Holy Scripture.</note> of Holy Scripture. My purpose here, however, is not to defend the authority of those other writings; I am content to leave them as I find them regarded by the world at large.

The Psalms were also collected and divided into five books during the era of the <term>Second Temple</term><note>The period in Jewish history from the rebuilding of the Temple (c. 516 BCE) to its destruction by the Romans in 70 CE.</note>. ->THE OLD TESTAMENT.<-

King <term>Jehoiachin</term><note>original: "Jehoiachim"; the author likely refers to the king of Judah who was taken prisoner to Babylon and later released. Modern scholars distinguish between Jehoiakim and his son Jehoiachin.</note> was still held as a prisoner in Babylon, and **Psalm 89** <note>original: "Psalm lxxxix."</note> was written when he had obtained his liberty. I believe that <term>Philo</term><note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher whose writings often reflected contemporary Jewish traditions.</note> would not have said what he did if it had not been the accepted opinion of his time, or if he had not received the information from someone worthy of trust.

The *Proverbs of Solomon*, I believe, were also collected about the same time, or at least during the time of King Josiah. In the 25th chapter, verse 1, we read: “These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah, King of Judah, copied out.” At this point, I cannot remain silent regarding the boldness of the <term>Rabbis</term><note>original: "Rabbins"; the Jewish religious scholars and leaders responsible for codifying Jewish law and scripture.</note>. They would have excluded this book, along with *Ecclesiastes*, from the <term>Scripture canon</term><note>The official list of books recognized as divinely inspired and authoritative.</note> and placed them alongside those other writings whose absence we have just now regretted. Indeed, these books would certainly have been rejected if they had not been found to contain several passages in which the **Law of Moses** was praised. It is truly a great shame that such excellent and holy things should have depended on the choices of men like the Jewish Rabbis who settled the canon of the Old Testament. I am grateful to them, however, for choosing to share these books with us at all, although I cannot help but doubt whether they passed them down with entire good faith—a point which I am not inclined to discuss further here. I therefore proceed to the **Books of the Prophets**.

When I examine these writings attentively, I find that the prophecies they contain were collected from other books. They are not always set down in the same order as they were delivered by the prophets themselves, whether by word of mouth or in writing. Furthermore, they do not contain all the prophecies that were uttered, but only those that could be gathered here and there. Consequently, these books cannot be regarded as anything more than fragments. **Isaiah**, for instance, began to prophesy during the reign of <term>Uzziah</term><note>A king of Judah who reigned in the 8th century BCE.</note>, as the narrator himself declares in the 1st verse of the 1st chapter of the book. But when we turn to *Chronicles* (2nd Book, chapter 26, verse 22), we find that Isaiah not only prophesied at that time...

The Prophecies of Jeremiah, in like manner, which are narrated as history, are taken from various <term>chroniclers</term><note>original: "chronologers"; writers who record events in chronological order.</note>. Not only are they gathered without any arrangement—with no regard for the timeline—but we also find the same story repeated in different ways more than once. Thus, in the 21st chapter, we have an explanation for the prophet’s alarm: he had foretold the devastation of the city to Zedekiah, who had consulted him. The narrative breaks off suddenly here. Chapter 22 is occupied with the prophet's speech to <term>Jehoiakim</term><note>original: "Jehoiachim"; King of Judah (reigned 609–598 BCE) who preceded Zedekiah.</note>, who reigned before Zedekiah, and to whom he foretells an approaching captivity. 

Next, in a further display of disorder in chapter 25, we find things that were revealed to the prophet before this time, <term>namely</term><note>original: "viz.", short for the Latin *videlicet*.</note> in the fourth year of the reign of King Jehoiakim. Then follow events concerning the first year of this king’s reign, and so on. No order in the incidents or the dates is observed; instead, prophecies are piled <term>in a jumbled mess</term><note>original: "pell-mell"; in a confused or disorderly manner.</note> on one another. At length, in chapter 38 (as if the fifteen intervening chapters had formed one great parenthesis), we are brought back to the story the writer began to tell in the 21st chapter. 

The connecting word found at the beginning of the 38th chapter clearly refers to verses 8, 9, and 10 of chapter 21. ->THE OLD TESTAMENT.<-

The state of confusion in which these prophecies exist cannot be understood under any other assumption.

The other prophecies contained in the remaining chapters, where Jeremiah speaks in the first person, appear to come from the book that Baruch wrote at Jeremiah's own dictation. As we learn from chapter 36, verse 2, that book only contained what was revealed to the prophet from the time of Josiah to the fourth year of the reign of <term>Jehoiakim</term><note>original: "Jehoiachim"; King of Judah (reigned c. 609–598 BCE).</note>, which is indeed where this book begins. Similarly, everything found between the 2nd verse of the 45th chapter and the 59th verse of the 51st chapter also appears to be derived from that same volume.

The fact that the Book of Ezekiel is nothing more than a fragment is clearly shown by its opening verses. Anyone can see that the <term>conjunction</term><note>In Hebrew, the book begins with the word "vayehi" (And it came to pass), implying a connection to a previous, now-missing text.</note> with which it begins refers to matters that came before, serving as the bond between those events and what follows. It is not only the conjunction that leads to this conclusion; the entire context assumes other writings. For the "thirtieth year," which marks the start of this book, shows the prophet in the middle of his narrative, not beginning it. He even demonstrates this himself in a parenthetical remark in verse 3, where he says:

> "The word of the Lord came <term>expressly</term><note>original: "expressly"; Spinoza's Latin text used the word *sæpe* (often) here, suggesting a frequency of revelation rather than a single specific instance.</note> unto Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans," etc.

This is as if he had said that the words of Ezekiel up to this point refer to other things that were revealed to him before this thirtieth year. Furthermore, <term>Josephus</term><note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 CE), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> (in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 10, Chapter 9) relates how Ezekiel had foretold that <term>Zedekiah</term><note>The last king of Judah before the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem.</note> would not see Babylon. This is a specific detail we do not find mentioned in the Book of Ezekiel as we currently have it; on the contrary, we read there in chapter 17 that Zedekiah would be taken captive to Babylon.

Regarding Hosea, it cannot be said with certainty that he wrote more than what we find in the book that bears his name. Still, I cannot help wondering why we do not have more from his hand, considering that he prophesied for more than eighty-four years, according to the evidence provided by the author of the book. Of this at least we are generally sure: neither do the books we possess contain all the prophecies ever delivered, nor does the collection of prophetic books that has survived contain every work of that kind ever written. Of all the prophets who preached during the reign of Manasseh—of whom there is a general mention in 2 Chronicles (33:10, 18, 19)—we have absolutely no records. Nor do we have the complete works of the twelve minor prophets. For example, the only prophecies of Jonah we have are those he delivered to the people of Nineveh, even though it is known that he also prophesied to the Israelites (see 2 Kings 14:25).

The Book of Job, and Job himself, have been the subject of significant debate among writers. Some have argued that Moses wrote the Book of Job and that the entire story is nothing more than an <term>allegory</term><note>A story or poem that can be interpreted to reveal a hidden meaning, typically a moral or political one.</note>. This is the conclusion reached by the Rabbis in the <term>Talmud</term><note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism and the primary source of Jewish religious law and theology.</note>, and it is the view favored by Maimonides in his work titled *The Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: "More Nebuchim" (Moreh Nevukhim)</note>. Others, however, regard the book as true history, believing that Job lived during the time of Jacob and married Jacob's daughter, Dinah. But <term>Aben-Ezra</term><note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a distinguished Jewish scholar, poet, and philosopher.</note>, as I have previously mentioned in his commentaries on this book, concludes that it is a translation into Hebrew from another language. This is a conclusion I wish had been better supported than it is; for if it were true, we would be able to conclude that the <term>Gentiles</term><note>Non-Jewish peoples or nations.</note> also possessed their own sacred scriptures.* I, therefore, leave the question in—

Another reason for the appearance of the Books of Daniel, Ezra, Esther, and Nehemiah at that specific time may have been to show the people that the prophecies of Daniel were being fulfilled, and to strengthen their piety and faith in better times to come in the midst of so much misery.

However, despite their relatively recent date, I believe many errors have crept into these books due to the haste and carelessness of the <term>transcribers</term><note>scribes who copied manuscripts by hand</note>. In these, as in the other books of Scripture, we find many of the marginal notes that we have already discussed at length. We also find several places in such an imperfect state that it is impossible to explain them except by assuming carelessness. But I must first discuss the marginal notes in these books. Now, if we were to accept the Pharisees' claim that these annotations are as old as the text itself, we would have to say that the writers (if there was more than one) noted these specific passages because the <term>chronologies</term><note>historical records or annals organized by date</note> from which they took their data were not accurately written. But I do not need to revisit this subject or describe its specific application at greater length than I have already done. In verse 64, the total of all the <term>genealogies</term><note>lists of ancestors or family lineages</note> listed individually throughout the chapter is given as 42,360. However, if the specific items are added together, they only amount to 29,818. 

Clearly, there is an error here, either in the grand total or in the individual items. The total is likely correct, as it was probably remembered by everyone as a significant figure, while the various smaller numbers were less likely to be perfectly retained. If an error had been made in the grand total, it would have been obvious to everyone and quickly corrected. This view is confirmed by the Book of Nehemiah (7:5), where this chapter from Ezra is referenced as a "Register of Genealogy." There, the sum total matches Ezra's exactly, even though the specific numbers differ significantly—some are higher and some are lower—and only add up to 31,089. From this, there can be little doubt that many mistakes have crept into the partial sums in both the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. 

However, the commentators who have tried to reconcile these obvious <term>incongruities</term><note>original: "incongruities"; inconsistencies or contradictions</note> have all invented elaborate explanations to the limit of their creativity. While they imagined they were defending the excellence of the Scriptures, they actually brought the biblical writers into contempt. They made it seem as if the authors did not know how to express themselves in their own language or how to organize what they had to say. Those who explain these things differently are actually ignoring the plain sense of Scripture, and by doing so, they diminish its authority. They think it is pious, indeed, to reconcile or force one part of Scripture to match another! In truth, this is a childish piety that obscures light with darkness, tries to make the true agree with the false, and corrupts the healthy with the rotten. However, do not assume I am labeling as blasphemers those who had no intention to deceive—for truly, to err is human. I return to my subject.

# THE OLD TESTAMENT.

It is only fair to say that when commentators strive to reconcile conflicting passages, they usually do nothing more than point out the causes of the errors. I do not imagine any reasonable person believes that the sacred historians wrote in such a way as to constantly contradict themselves.

But some, perhaps, will interrupt here and say that I am clearly destroying the authority of Scripture by what I propose, for in this way the entire body of the Bible might come to be suspected as corrupt. On the contrary, I have shown that we can take comfort in this: that the clear and pure parts will not be twisted into agreement with the obscure and faulty parts, and thus be corrupted themselves. It is not reasonable to suspect the whole work just because certain parts are found to be erroneous; indeed, no book in this world has ever been found entirely free of faults. But I ask: should it therefore be said that any book was ever written that is entirely flawed? Certainly not—especially when the language used is simple and clear <note>original: "perspicuous"</note>, and the writer's purpose is obvious.

I here bring to a close what I had to say on the books of the Old Testament. I venture to conclude from all that has preceded that, before the time of the Maccabees <note>A Jewish rebel group that led a revolt against the Seleucid Empire in the 2nd century BCE, leading to a period of independence.</note>, there was no existing <term>canon</term><note>An official list of books considered to be authoritative Scripture.</note> of Holy Writ. Instead, the books we have were selected from among many others based solely on the authority of the Pharisees of the Second Temple, who also established the standard order <note>original: "formula"</note> for the prayers used in the Synagogue.* Therefore, whoever seeks to prove the authenticity and authority of the Hebrew Scriptures is obligated to show the specific authority upon which each of those books rests. It is not enough to prove the divinity of one book and then conclude that all the others are therefore divine. Furthermore, it would be necessary to show that the council of the Pharisees could not err in their selection of the books they admitted into the canon; and this, I think, no one will ever be able to demonstrate.

The Pharisees always refer to the authority of this body when they invoke what they call their "Traditions."

<header>THE OLD TESTAMENT.</header>

The primary reason that leads me to claim that the Pharisees alone chose the books of the Old Testament and included them in the official list <term>canon</term><note>The set of books considered uniquely authoritative and divinely inspired.</note> of Sacred Writings is this: in the second verse of the final chapter of Daniel, I find a prophecy regarding the resurrection of the dead—an event which the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect during the Second Temple period that rejected the idea of an afterlife and the oral traditions of the Pharisees.</note> denied. 

The opinion of the Pharisees on this matter is clearly shown in the Talmud <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism, containing records of rabbinic discussions on law, ethics, and tradition.</note>; in the second chapter, we read the following: "Rabbi Judah, known as 'the Rabbi,' said that certain scholars wanted to suppress the Book of Ecclesiastes because its statements contradict the Law of Moses. Why was it not suppressed? Because it begins and ends in accordance with the Law." He continues: "They also wanted to exclude the Book of Proverbs," and so on, concluding with: "I mention the name of Nehunyah <note>original: "Neghunja"</note>, son of Hezekiah, out of gratitude; for if it were not for him, the Book of Ezekiel would have been suppressed, as its words were considered contrary to the Law." 

From these passages, we can plainly see that a council of men learned in the Law determined which books should be accepted as sacred and which should be rejected as unholy. Therefore, anyone who wishes to be certain of the authority of all the Scriptures should examine them again and demand that each book justify its place in the collection.

It would now be appropriate for me to proceed to examine the books of the New Testament in the same way I have reviewed those of the Old Testament. However, I hear that this work is already being carried out by men well-versed in science and skilled in languages. Since I do not possess a sufficiently accurate knowledge of Greek to take on the task myself, and since we lack copies of the New Testament books in their original Hebrew, I do not intend to analyze them in detail. Instead, I will limit myself to discussing only those points that directly relate to the purpose of my work.

# CHAPTER XI.

### DID THE APOSTLES WRITE THEIR LETTERS IN THE CHARACTER OF APOSTLES AND PROPHETS, OR MERELY AS TEACHERS? THE NATURE OF THE APOSTOLIC OFFICE.

Anyone who reads the *New Testament* cannot doubt that the apostles were prophets. However, the *Old Testament* prophets did not always speak from direct revelations made to them; on the contrary, they did so very seldom, as was shown at the close of *Chapter 1*. Therefore, we may reasonably doubt whether the apostles wrote their *Letters* <note>original: "Epistles"</note> as prophets—acting from revelation and by the express command of God, like Moses, Jeremiah, and the others—or whether they wrote simply as private and learned individuals. 

This inquiry is especially necessary because Paul, in his First Letter to the Corinthians (14:6), points out two kinds of preaching: one from revelation and another from knowledge. Therefore, I say it is uncertain whether the apostles are prophesying or teaching in their letters. When we look at the style of these writings, we find it entirely different from the style of prophecy. The prophets were in the constant habit of insisting that they spoke according to the decrees of God; phrases like “Thus says the Lord,” “Thus says the Lord of hosts,” and “The word of the Lord came,” are used incessantly. 

This style was not only used in public gatherings; it was also followed in the letters that contained revelations. We see this in the letter from Elijah to Jehoram (see <note>original: "vide"</note> 2 Chronicles 21:12), where we have

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the difference between the authoritative style of the prophets and the argumentative style of the apostles, specifically Paul.</meta>

# OF THE APOSTLES.

[God is] introduced as the speaker, who does not reason, but instead decrees through the absolute authority of his nature. The vocation of the prophets was not based on reasoning; for anyone who attempts to support dogmatic decisions with logic effectively submits those decisions to the judgment <note>original: "arbitrament"</note> of everyone else. And Paul actually does this through his reasoning; for he says to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 10:15), "I speak to you as sensible men; judge for yourselves what I say." 

The prophets, however, did not grasp the things they revealed through their natural abilities—that is, by the power of their own intellect—as I demonstrated in Chapter 1. Although we find certain conclusions reached through inference in the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses</note>, a careful look at these passages reveals that they cannot be considered definitive or absolute arguments. 

For example, when Moses says to the Israelites (Deuteronomy 31:27), "If you were rebellious against God while I lived among you, how much more rebellious will you be after I am dead!" This should not be understood as if Moses intended to prove logically to the Jews that they would definitely abandon the worship of the true God after his death. Such a conclusion would be false, as shown in Scripture: the Israelites remained faithful to Jehovah during the lifetimes of Joshua and the Elders, and later during the eras of Samuel, David, Solomon, and others. 

Consequently, these words of Moses should be seen as a mere moral figure of speech <note>original: "moral locution"; a way of speaking intended to influence behavior rather than provide a logical proof</note>. In this passage, he uses rhetoric and vivid imagery to predict the people's future departure from the worship of the Lord God. 

The reason I do not say that Moses spoke these words on his own authority to make his prediction seem more likely is because verse 21 of that same chapter informs us that God Himself communicated this fact to Moses using different words. There was no need for logical arguments to make God’s prediction and decree more certain to Moses. However, there may have been a need for him to visualize the event more vividly in his imagination, which he could best achieve by framing it...

It uses Moses’s warnings in Deuteronomy to illustrate that prophetic "arguments" are often rhetorical devices rather than logical proofs.</summary>

# OF THE APOSTLES.

In this way, I believe, all the arguments of Moses scattered through the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Hebrew Bible</note> are to be understood; they are not derived from the "sanctuary of reason," but are mere modes of expression by which he announced the decrees of God more sharply, while he himself imagined them more vividly.

I would not, however, want to be seen as denying that the prophets could show themselves to be possessed of argumentative powers through revelation; I only affirm that the more logically they reason, the more closely the matter they reveal aligns with natural knowledge. It is especially by the absolute dogmas <note>Established beliefs or doctrines</note>, decrees, or opinions they utter that the prophets are distinguished as having had supernatural knowledge. 

Therefore, it was for this reason that Moses, the greatest of the prophets, never made use of formal logic; meanwhile, the lengthy arguments and deductions of Paul, such as those found in the Epistle to the Romans, can in no way be imagined as coming from supernatural inspiration. The way the apostles address their readers, as well as their style of discussion in their Epistles, clearly proves that these were not written from revelation and by divine command, but entirely from their own natural understanding and experience. They contain nothing more than brotherly warnings <note>original: "fraternal admonitions"</note> mixed with certain courtesies or politeness (which the old prophetic authority completely rejects), such as where Paul applies a bit of flattery to his readers:

> "And I myself," he says, "am convinced of you, my brothers, that you also are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge," etc.;

And then he goes on to excuse his own boldness in writing to them as he does:

> "Nevertheless, brothers, I have written the more boldly to you in some ways, as if reminding you," etc. (see Epistle to the Romans 15:14, 15).

# OF THE APOSTLES.

Miracles <note>original: "signs"</note> were absolutely necessary to convert the nations to the religion of Christ and to confirm them in the faith, as Paul himself states clearly in the Epistle to the Romans (1:11): "For I long to see you, so that I may share some spiritual gift with you, to the end that you may be strengthened."

However, one might object that based on this, we could conclude the apostles did not even preach in the manner of prophets. When they traveled to preach here and there, they did not do so like the prophets of old, who acted by the express command of God. In the Old Testament, we read of Jonah going to Nineveh to preach or prophesy, and we see that he was sent there specifically; it was revealed to him exactly what he was to say. Similarly, it is related in great detail how Moses went into Egypt as God's messenger, and exactly what he was to say to the people of Israel and to Pharaoh, and what signs and wonders he was to perform in order to convince them to believe in his mission. Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel were all expressly ordered to preach to the Israelites. Indeed, none of the prophets ever preached anything that the Scriptures do not declare to have been received directly from God. 

But it is only on very rare occasions in the New Testament that we read of anything like this when the apostles went preaching in different places. On the contrary, we find clear indications that they chose the locations for their work themselves. Paul and Barnabas went so far as to argue about their assistants and to part company, choosing different fields of operation from those they had originally intended. "Barnabas was determined to take with them John, surnamed Mark, but Paul did not think it good to take him; ... and the disagreement <note>original: "contention"</note> was so sharp between them that they parted from one another" (Acts 15:37, 38, 39). They also sometimes attempted to go where they desired but were unsuccessful, as Paul testifies in the 13th verse of the 1st chapter of Romans, where he says, "Oftentimes I intended to come to you, but was hindered <note>original: "let hitherto"</note> until now"; and in the last chapter of the First...

# OF THE APOSTLES.

In his Letter to the Corinthians, he expresses himself this way: "As for our brother Apollos, I strongly encouraged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come at this time; however, he will come when he has a convenient opportunity." From such statements, from the disagreement between the apostles previously mentioned, and from the fact that Scripture never records a direct command from God for them to go and preach in one specific place or another (as it does with the ancient prophets), I must conclude that the apostles preached and taught not as prophets, but simply as teachers.

However, we can easily resolve this question when we consider the different callings <note>original: "vocations"</note> of the prophets and the apostles. The prophets were not commanded to preach and prophesy to all nations equally, but only to specific ones, and they required a special command <note>original: "mandate"</note> for each mission. But the apostles were called to preach to every nation without exception and to convert everyone to the faith. Therefore, wherever they went, they were fulfilling the general command of Christ. There was no need for what they were to preach to be revealed to them specifically before they set out on their mission. Even when they were brought before a judge's seat <note>original: "judgment-seat"</note> because of their teaching, they were told not to worry about how or what they were to say, "for what you are to say will be given to you in that very hour" (see <note>original: "vide"</note> Matthew 10:19). 

Let us conclude, then, that the apostles received through special revelation only those things which they preached immediately by word of mouth <note>original: "viva voce"</note> and confirmed with miracles (see the discussion at the beginning of Chapter 2). However, what they taught in writing or by speech without any sign or miracle to prove their mission was taught from their own natural knowledge (see <note>original: "vide"</note> 1 Corinthians 14:6). Nor should we hesitate to reach this conclusion. All the Epistles <note>formal letters written by the apostles</note> begin with a declaration of the writer's status as an apostle, and, as I will soon show, the apostles were given not only the power to prophesy but also the authority to teach. For this reason, let us acknowledge that they wrote their letters in their capacity as apostles, and

# OF THE APOSTLES.

For whatever I find in these letters <note>original: "Epistles"</note> regarding the calling of the apostles and the holy, divine spirit that inspired them, I see that it refers to their spoken discourses. The only exceptions are those passages where the "Spirit of God" or the "Holy Spirit" are used as synonyms for a mind that is at ease, happy, and dedicated to God (on these topics, see the discussion in Chapter 1). For example, in his First Letter to the Corinthians (7:40), Paul says, "But in my judgment, she is happier if she remains as she is, and I think that I, too, have the Spirit of God." Here, the context clearly shows that by "Spirit of God," the apostle means his own mental state; it is as if he had said, "The widow who chooses not to marry a second time is happy according to my view—and I, who live as a bachelor, consider myself happy." There are other similar passages that I think are unnecessary <note>original: "superfluous"</note> to cite here.

Since we conclude, then, that the letters were written using natural reason <note>original: "natural light"</note> alone, we must still ask how the apostles were able to teach things that go beyond natural knowledge. However, if we pay attention to what was argued in Chapter 7 of this work, we will find no difficulty in resolving this point. For even though the things contained in Scripture often far exceed our ability to understand them, we can still speak about them with confidence, provided we do not admit any other principles of interpretation except those derived from Scripture itself. This is exactly how the apostles worked: they took what they had seen, heard, and received through revelation and used it to reach conclusions, which they then shared with the people at the appropriate times. <meta>This page continues the discussion of how the apostles’ writings were produced.
