# OF THE APOSTLES.

The gospel, as it was preached by the apostles through simple stories of the life of Christ, does not fall strictly under the domain of pure reason. Since its core consists mainly of moral rules <note>original: "precepts"</note>—much like the rest of Christ's teachings—it can still be easily understood through our natural human abilities. Furthermore, the apostles did not need supernatural inspiration to adapt the religion—which they had already proven through miracles—to the understanding of ordinary people <note>original: "vulgar capacity"</note> so that everyone might accept it. Nor did they need such inspiration to advise humanity about their duties in whatever way each apostle saw fit; after all, that was the primary goal of their letters <note>original: "Epistles"</note>.

<margin>*</margin>We should also note that the apostles were given two distinct powers: first, the power to preach the story of Christ as prophets (that is, by confirming their teachings with miracles); and second, the authority to instill <note>original: "inculcate"</note> these teachings in whatever way seemed best to them, so they could strengthen their converts' devotion <note>original: "piety"</note> and virtue. Paul clearly points to both of these gifts in his second letter to Timothy (1:11), where he says, "For this gospel I was appointed a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher of the nations <note>original: "Gentiles"</note>." He says it again in his first letter to Timothy (2:7 <note>The original text cites 1:7, but the quote is from 1 Timothy 2:7</note>): "For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth in Christ and not lying), a teacher of the nations in faith and truth." 

These passages clearly show both types of authority: that of the apostle and that of the teacher. In the letter to Philemon (verse 8), we see even more proof of his authority to advise anyone at any time. He writes, "Therefore, although I have enough boldness in Christ to order <note>original: "enjoin"</note> you to do what is proper <note>original: "convenient"</note>, I prefer to appeal to you on the basis of love," and so on. It is important to notice here that if Paul had received a direct command from God to act as a prophet—and to teach specifically as a prophet—he would not have felt free to turn God's commands into mere requests. Therefore, we must understand that when he speaks of his freedom to give advice, he is speaking as a teacher, not as a prophet.

<meta>This page continues the argument that the apostles acted as independent teachers who used their own reason and judgment. # OF THE APOSTLES.

It is still not entirely clear whether the apostles were free to choose the method of teaching that each thought best, or if they were merely teachers by virtue of their role as apostles—unless, of course, we use our own reason and conclude that whoever has the authority to teach also has the authority to choose the manner of teaching they prefer. However, it will be more satisfying to explain the whole subject using Scripture, from which it clearly appears that each of the apostles chose his own way of teaching.

For instance, Paul says in his Epistle to the Romans (15:20): "Striving eagerly to preach the gospel not where the name of Christ was already known, so that I would not build on another person’s foundation <note>original Latin: *alienum fundamentum*</note>."* If all the apostles had followed the same method of preaching and built the Christian religion on the exact same foundation, Paul would have had no reason to call the foundations of another apostle "strange" or "foreign" <note>original: *alienum*</note>, since they would have been the same as his own. 

Because he uses the word "foreign," we must conclude that each of the apostles built his religious structure on a different foundation. In their capacity as scholars or teachers <note>term: "doctors" — from the Latin *doctor*, meaning a teacher or learned person, rather than a medical professional</note>, they were affected in the same way as teachers in the world at large: each has his own method of teaching, which he prefers when instructing the uneducated or those who have not yet begun to study the arts and sciences under someone else (this even applies to mathematics, the truth of which no one doubts). 

Furthermore, when reading the Epistles <note>The letters written by the apostles in the New Testament</note> with some attention, we see that the apostles agree well enough on the substance of their religion, but differ considerably regarding its basic principles <note>original: "fundamentals"</note>. For example, to strengthen the faith of the brothers and to show them that salvation depends on the grace of God alone, Paul taught that no one could be glorified because of their works, and that no one could be justified by their good deeds, but only through their faith (Epistle to the Romans 3:27, 28).

# OF THE APOSTLES.

Even more evidence for this point is found throughout Saint Paul’s doctrine of **election** <note>original: "election"—the theological concept that God chooses specific individuals for salvation</note> or **predestination**. Saint James, on the other hand, teaches that **justification** <note>original: "justification"—the process by which a person is declared righteous before God</note> comes through good works, and not through faith alone (General Epistle of James 2:24). Setting aside all of Paul’s reasonings and arguments, James declares that the whole of religion consists of a few simple elements. 

There can be no question that these different foundations, selected by each of the apostles for their religious structures <note>original: "edifice"</note>, led to endless disputes and divisions <note>original: "schisms"</note> that severely shook the Church even in the time of the apostles. The Church will continue to be torn by these disagreements until the time comes when religion—finally separated from theological and philosophical debates—is reduced to the few simple truths that Christ taught to his disciples. 

Such a simple approach, however, was impossible for the apostles because the gospel was still unknown to the world. <note>Editor's Note: The earliest writings in the New Testament are some of the Epistles. The Gospels were written much later than these—perhaps 60 or 100 years afterward, or even more. The first three are likely different versions of one original source; the fourth was derived from other sources and was written by a Platonist <note>a follower of the philosopher Plato</note>.</note> Therefore, fearing that the novelty of their teachings might shock the public too much, they did what they could to adapt their teaching to the spirit <note>original: "genius"</note> of their age. They built upon the foundations that were best known and most commonly accepted at the time (see 1 Corinthians 9:19, 20). 

We see, then, that none of the other apostles used philosophy as much as Paul did. This was because Paul's calling was to preach to nations like the Greeks and Romans, who were more or less familiar with philosophy. Meanwhile, the other apostles—who preached to the Jews, who looked down on philosophy—adapted themselves to the state and temperament of their audience and taught religion stripped of all philosophical speculation (see Galatians 2:11, etc.). How fortunate our own age would be if we could see religion finally freed from every form of superstition!

## CHAPTER 12.

### CONCERNING THE TRUE COVENANT OF THE DIVINE LAW; WHY THE SCRIPTURES ARE CALLED SACRED, AND WHY THEY ARE SAID TO BE THE WORD OF GOD. THE HEBREW SCRIPTURES, TO THE EXTENT THAT THEY CONTAIN THE WORD OF GOD, HAVE COME DOWN TO US UNCORRUPTED.

Those who believe the Bible, exactly as it stands, is the literal hand-writing of God—sent directly from heaven to humanity—will undoubtedly cry out that I am guilty of the "sin against the Holy Spirit" <note>The "unforgivable sin" mentioned in the Gospels, often interpreted here as heresy or blasphemy against divine revelation.</note>. # WHY THE SCRIPTURES ARE STYLED SACRED

3.  And finally, I shall show that the doctrines of Scripture, so far as they are necessary for obedience and salvation, cannot have been corrupted.

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the definition of sacredness. It concludes the sentence from the previous page, explaining that things are called sacred only in relation to their use in devotion.</meta>

-> WORD OF GOD. <-

...devotion, then these words will be sacred, as will a book written with words arranged in that way. But if these words fall into disuse over time, so that they eventually convey no meaning to the reader, or if the book they form falls into almost complete disuse—whether through ill will or because it is no longer needed—then the words and the book will be useless and possess no sanctity. 

Finally, if the same words are arranged differently, or if through usage they come to have a different or opposite meaning, then the words and the book—which were previously sacred—will become impure and profane. It follows from this that nothing outside of the mind—taken absolutely or on its own—is either pure or impure, sacred or profane. 

This principle is illustrated by many parts of Scripture. To quote one or two: Jeremiah (7:4) says that the Jews of his time falsely called Solomon's temple the "Temple of God." For, as he goes on to explain, the title "Temple of God" could only be properly applied as long as it was entered by people who worshipped Him in truth and acted justly. But once it was frequented by murderers <note>original: "homicides"</note>, idolaters, and other wicked people, it became instead a "den of transgressors." 

Scripture never tells us what happened to the Ark of the Covenant, which has often surprised me. This much only seems certain: that it perished or was destroyed along with the Temple, even though there was nothing the Jews held more sacred or revered more highly. For this reason, Scripture is sacred and its doctrines are divine only as long as it moves people to devotion <note>original: "piety"</note> toward God. But if it is almost entirely neglected—as it once was by the Jews—it is nothing more than ink and paper. It may then indeed be profane and liable <note>original: "obnoxious"—in this period, the word meant "subject to" or "exposed to" rather than "annoying."</note> to corruption. 

If it is corrupted or destroyed under such circumstances, it is incorrect to say that it is the "Word of God" that is corrupted or destroyed. <header>WHY THE SCRIPTURES ARE CALLED SACRED</header>

"Why do you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us'? Instead, he broke only the stone tablets. These tablets were sacred before because they bore the covenant that bound the Jews in obedience to Jehovah <note>original: "Jehovah," the Hebrew name for God</note>; however, they lost all their sanctity once the people broke that agreement by worshipping a golden calf. 

In the same manner and for the same reason, the tablets of the second covenant, as well as the Ark of the Sanctuary, can be said to have perished. It is not surprising, then, that the original writings of Moses no longer exist, nor that the Scriptures we have—which I discussed in the previous chapters—have reached us in their current state. This is to be expected when the original document of the divine covenant, the most sacred of all objects, has completely perished. 

Therefore, let those who accuse us of lack of faith <note>original: "impiety"</note> stop their attacks. We have not spoken a word against God’s message and have been extremely careful not to change or corrupt it. Instead, they should direct their anger—if anger can ever be justified—against the people of old. It was their wickedness and neglect that dishonored the Ark, the Temple, and the law of God, allowing the sacred items entrusted to them to be altered and corrupted. 

Finally, if they wish to be "recognized as a letter from Christ, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on the tablets of human hearts" <note>original: "fleshy tables of the heart"</note> (as stated in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians 3:3), they must stop worshipping the literal text <note>original: "the letter"</note>, which kills. Instead, they should show themselves more eager to pursue the spirit, which gives eternal life.

# WORD OF GOD.

...to show what is correctly meant by the Hebrew phrase *Dabar Jehovah* <note>original: "Dabar Jehovah," meaning the Word of the Lord</note>, translated as "word of God" or "word of the Lord." The word *dabar* <note>original Hebrew: "word," "matter," or "thing"</note> has several meanings besides "word"; it can also mean a discourse, a decree, or a thing. We have already shown in Chapter 1 how, in Hebrew, a thing is described as being "of God" or is referred to God. From this, it is easy to understand what is meant in Scripture when the words, sayings, or commands of God are mentioned. 

It is therefore unnecessary to repeat what has already been said on this point, nor is it necessary to return to what was argued in Chapter 3 regarding miracles. It will be enough here to bring this matter back to the reader’s attention so that my next point may be better understood: namely, that the expression "word of God"—when the subject being discussed is something other than God Himself—properly signifies that divine law which we discussed in detail in Chapter 4. 

In other words, it refers to that universal or truly catholic <note>original: "Catholic," here used in its original sense of "universal" or "all-encompassing" rather than referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note> religion common to the entire human family. The prophet Isaiah speaks of this in Chapter 1:16 and following <note>original Latin: "et seq."</note>, where he says it consists not of ceremonies, but of charity and holiness of life and mind; he refers to this indifferently as the "word" and the "law" of God. 

Furthermore, the expression "word of God" is used metaphorically to describe the order of nature and fate, or the necessary sequence of events in creation. This order, in fact, depends on and follows the eternal decrees of the divine nature. The phrase is especially used for the parts of this order and sequence that the prophets foresaw. This is because they did not perceive future events as the effects of natural causes, but rather as the special commands or decrees of God. 

Finally, the phrase is employed to describe the command of a prophet, provided it was conceived through his unique prophetic power and not through the force of his natural intellect. This occurred primarily because the prophets were accustomed to regarding God as a lawgiver, as was shown in Chapter 4. Consequently, Scripture is called the "Law of God" for these three reasons: 

1. Because it teaches absolute religion, of which the eternal God is the author;

Although there are many other things in Scripture that are simply matters of history, or ideas derived from our common human logic, the title "Word of God" is taken from the dominant characteristic of the biblical writings. In this way, we can easily see how God is to be understood as the author of the Bible. This also helps us understand why the Bible is divided into the books of the Old and New Testaments. Before the coming of Christ, the prophets used to preach religion to the Jews as the law of their own nation, based on the covenant <note>term: a formal agreement or contract, in this case between God and the Israelites</note> made in the time of Moses. After Christ appeared in the world, however, the apostles preached religion as a universal law for all humanity, based solely on the Passion <note>term: the suffering and death of Jesus Christ</note> of Christ. 

But this does not imply that there is any difference in the doctrines of the Old and New Testaments, nor that they are the tools of two separate covenants. Finally, it does not mean that this universal religion—which is also the most natural religion—is anything new, except to those who did not know it before. "It was in the world," says John the Evangelist (John 1:10), "and the world knew it not."

Even if we had fewer books of both the Old and New Testaments than we currently possess, we would not be without the word of God. As already stated, by "Word of God" we mean the true or universal religion. Similarly, we do not believe we are without God's blessed word just because we lack many other precious writings, such as *The Book of the Law*, which was religiously preserved in the temple as the legal instrument of the covenant between God and the Jews. This is not to mention *The Book of the Wars*, *The Chronologies*, and many others from which the books we have were compiled.

<header>THE WORD OF GOD</header>

The books we now possess, which make up the Old Testament, were selected and compiled from a larger body of writings. This view is confirmed by several other points:

1. The books of both Testaments were not written by a direct command to serve all ages at one single time. Instead, they were written almost by chance <note>original: "fortuitously"</note> for specific individuals, according to the needs of the time and the authors' own particular state of mind. This is clearly shown by the calling <note>original: "vocation"</note> of the prophets, who were summoned to warn the wicked people of their own era. The same is true for the Epistles <note>term: the letters written by the apostles to early Christian communities</note> of the apostles.

2. Understanding the literal text of Scripture and the minds of the prophets is one thing, but understanding the mind of God—that is, understanding the actual truth of a thing in itself—is quite another. This follows from what was already discussed in Chapter 2, which deals with the nature of a prophet. We have shown that this same distinction must be made regarding the historical narratives and the miracles (see <note>original: *vide*</note> Chapter 6). However, no such distinction is necessary for the parts of the Bible where true religion and true virtue are discussed.

3. The books of the Old Testament are a selection from a great number of writings and were finally compiled and approved by a council of Pharisees, as shown in Chapter 10. Similarly, the books of the current New Testament were accepted into the Canon <note>term: the official list of books recognized as authoritative Scripture</note> by specific councils. By the decrees of these councils, many other books were rejected as false <note>original: "spurious"</note>, even though many people had previously held them to be sacred. The members of these councils, however, were not prophets; they were simply scholars <note>original: "doctors"</note> and learned people. We should acknowledge that they used the word of God as a standard when making their selection, meaning they must have had a knowledge of the word of God before they could approve the books they chose.

4. The apostles did not write as prophets, but as teachers. They chose their own methods of instruction, naturally considering the circumstances and the capacity of the people they were teaching. It follows from this that there must be many things in the writings of the apostles that are not essential to religion and could be set aside <note>original: "dispensed with"</note>.

<header>WORD OF GOD.</header>

It remains established, therefore, that Scripture has always taught this doctrine, and that no error has crept in here to corrupt the meaning of the text. This includes truths such as: that God exists; that he is all-knowing <note>original: "omniscient"</note>, foreseeing all; that he is all-powerful <note>original: "omnipotent"</note>; and that by virtue of his eternal decree, it is well with the good but ill with the wicked, and that our salvation depends on his grace alone. 

Such, in brief, is the teaching of the whole of Scripture; otherwise, everything else it contains would be empty and without significance. Nor are the other moral precepts of Holy Scripture <note>original: "Writ"</note> to be regarded as less free from corruption <note>original: "taint"</note>, seeing that they all obviously rest on the broad foundation of love for God and love for our neighbor. The commands to act justly, to help <note>original: "succour"</note> and assist the poor and oppressed, to not commit murder, to not commit adultery, to not covet our neighbor’s goods, and so on—these are precepts which the wickedness of man could never corrupt, and of which no length of time can lessen the excellence. # OF SCRIPTURAL TEACHINGS <note>original: "OF SCRIPTURE DOCTRINE"</note>

From these facts, it follows that the teachings of Scripture contain no lofty <note>original: "sublime"</note> speculations or philosophical problems. Instead, they contain only simple things that can be understood even by the most slow-witted <note>original: "dullest"</note>. Therefore, I am constantly amazed at the cleverness of those I mentioned earlier. They claim to see such deep mysteries in Scripture that no human language is capable of explaining them. Based on this assumption, they have introduced so much philosophical speculation into religion that the Church now looks like a university <note>original: "academy"</note>, and religion looks like a science—or rather, a constant argument. 

But why should I be surprised? These men boast of having supernatural light, yet they are unwilling to admit they know less than the philosophers who rely only on their natural human reason <note>original: "natural understanding"</note>. I would be truly surprised if they taught anything new, even as a matter of pure theory, that had not already been thoroughly debated by the ancient <note>original: "Gentile"</note> philosophers—the very people they accuse of being spiritually blind. When these so-called "mysteries" are examined closely, they turn out to be nothing more than Aristotelian, Platonic, or other philosophical ideas. A fool might find such things in his dreams, but a rational person would never find them in the Holy Scriptures. 

By saying this, I do not mean to claim without exception that Scripture contains nothing theoretical. On the contrary, in the previous chapter, I mentioned certain matters of this kind as fundamental parts of scriptural teaching. I only mean to argue that these points are few and simple. I will now explain what they are and how to identify them. This will be easy for us, since we have already established that Scripture was not intended to teach the sciences. From this, we can see that God only requires obedience from humanity. It is stubbornness and contempt that are condemned, not a lack of knowledge <note>original: "ignorance"</note>.

# OF SCRIPTURAL TEACHINGS <note>original: "OF SCRIPTURE DOCTRINE"</note>

Since the Apostle Paul states that whoever loves others fulfills the law (Romans 13:8), it follows that Scripture does not promote any branch of knowledge <note>original: "science"</note> except what is necessary for humanity. This knowledge exists so that by obeying God through the command to love one's neighbor, people may show themselves obedient to Him. If they ignore this, they necessarily prove themselves to be rebellious <note>original: "contumacious"</note>, or at the very least, lacking the discipline of respectful submissiveness.

Other theoretical <note>original: "speculative"</note> matters that do not lead directly toward this goal—such as abstract ideas about God or the study of the natural world—do not actually concern Scripture. Therefore, these topics should be distinguished and separated from revealed religion. Even though these points are easily understood by everyone, as I have already said, the entire way we judge religious matters depends on them. Therefore, I intend to explore this subject more fully and explain it thoroughly.

To achieve this, it is first necessary to show that having an intellectual or precise understanding of God is not a gift given to all believers in common, as the gift of obedience is. Next, I will show that the knowledge of God which the prophets require of all people—and which everyone is obligated to have—is nothing more than the knowledge of His divine justice and mercy. These are qualities that are easily demonstrated from Scripture.

First, this follows most obviously from Exodus 6:2-3, where God, in order to show the singular grace showered upon Moses, says to him: "I revealed myself to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as *El Shaddai* <note>original: "El Sadai"</note>, but by my name *Jehovah* <note>original: "Jehovah"; modern scholars often use "Yahweh"</note> I was not known to them." 

To better understand this text, we should observe that *El Shaddai* in Hebrew signifies "the God who suffices," because He gives to everyone what is sufficient for them. Although *Shaddai* is often used for "God" in an absolute sense, there is no question that *El*, the earliest proper title of the Supreme Being, is always understood to be part of it. Furthermore, it should be observed that no name for God except *Jehovah* is ever found in Scripture when referring to the absolute essence of God without...

It is a truth that the other names of God are essentially nouns or adjectives—attributes, in short—which seem appropriate to God when he is viewed in relation to created things, or is revealed through them. *El* <note>original: "El" (Hebrew: אֵל), meaning "might" or "power."</note>, or with the letter *he* <note>original: "ha"</note> added, *Eloha* <note>original: "Eloha" (Hebrew: אֱלוֹהַּ), the singular form of Elohim.</note>, signifies nothing more than "the powerful," as already mentioned. It is only applied to God to indicate supreme excellence, in the same way that we speak of Paul as ***The Apostle***. Therefore, *El* indicates the grand attributes of God as we conceive them: *El* the powerful, the great, the awful, the just, the merciful, and so on.

The word is also often found in the plural form, *Elohim* <note>original: "Elohim" (Hebrew: אֱלֹהִים)</note>, but with a singular meaning; in that case, it implies all the attributes of God collectively. This form is very frequent in *Scripture*. But since God informs Moses that he was not known to the patriarchs <note>The biblical fathers, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> by his name of Jehovah, it follows that they did not know any attributes of God that explain his absolute essence. Instead, they knew only his influences and his promises—in other words, his power, as far as it was made manifest by visible things. 

Now, God does not tell Moses that the patriarchs did not know him by the name of Jehovah in order to accuse them of any lack of faith or unworthiness. On the contrary, it was to praise their faith and belief. Although they did not possess the unique knowledge of God that Moses had, they still believed firmly in his promises. Unlike the great prophet Moses—who, despite his more sublime ideas of God, still doubted or questioned the divine word—the patriarchs never objected to God. They did not complain, as Moses did, that instead of the promised safety, God had brought the Jews into greater misery than before. 

Since the patriarchs were ignorant of the proper name of God, and since God informs Moses of this to commend their simplicity and faith—while also highlighting the special favor shown to Moses—it follows most obviously, as we stated above, that people in general are not required to know the attributes of God as a commandment. * Even a brief reading shows that the early part of the Book of Genesis was compiled from at least *two* different sources. The first chapter and the first three verses of the second chapter form a complete unit—a grand, simple history of creation. In the English version, the Great First Cause is always simply called "God" here. Biblical scholars have referred to this as the *Elohistic* <note>From "Elohim," the Hebrew word for God used in this section.</note> portion of Genesis. From the fourth verse of chapter 2, the history of creation begins again, focusing more specifically on humanity. Here, the simple word "God" is replaced by the more elaborate "Lord God." It is also interesting to note that in the first history of creation—which is undoubtedly much older—the gift of the plant kingdom to man is given without any restrictions: "And God said, 'Behold, I have given you *every herb* bearing seed which is upon the face of all the earth, and *every tree* in which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat.'" It is only in the second, or *Jehovistic* <note>From "Jehovah" (Yahweh), the Hebrew name for God used in this section.</note> account, as it has been called, that we find the *restriction regarding the tree of the knowledge of Good and Evil*. Furthermore, in the ancient Elohistic account, God creates man in His own image: "*male and female He created them.*" In the more recent history, man is at first alone, and the Lord God decides that "it is not good for the man to be alone" and resolves "to make a helper suitable for him." Then follows the story of the rib from which woman was fashioned. All of this is linked to the name of Him who said, "Let there be light, and there was light," as if biological sex were not a universal and primary law of the Almighty. It is in this fictional story <note>original: "romance"</note> of creation, too, that the story of the serpent occurs: "Now the serpent was more subtle than any beast of the field which the Lord God had made." "And he said unto the woman," etc., as if clear speech were not the unique property <note>original: "apanage"</note> of humans, involving a level of mental ability not found in creatures as low on the scale of being as reptiles. This entire section of the Bible cannot be taken literally; it is imagination, poetry, and allegory, for which various interpretations have been offered. For instance, some say it represents how humans lived without worry during the summer half of the year, followed by autumn and its fruits, which leads into the winter half—whose astronomical symbol is the serpent or dragon, and so on. The relationship between astronomy and mythology is thoroughly explained by M. Dupuis <note>Charles-François Dupuis (1742–1809), a French scholar who argued that all religions originated from ancient astronomy.</note> in his scholarly work titled *The Origin of All Religious Worship* <note>original: "Origine des Cultes"</note> (6 volumes, Paris). After this, the Elohistic and Jehovistic elements are often mixed together, though not so much that they cannot be identified by their unique characteristics. — *Editor*

# OF SCRIPTURE DOCTRINE

...attributes of God that humans can easily imitate through a certain rule of life. This is explicitly taught by Jeremiah; for when speaking of Shallum, the son of King Josiah, he says (Jeremiah 22:15):

> “Did your father not eat and drink, and practice judgment and justice? Then it went well with him. He defended the cause of the poor and the needy; then it went well with him. Was this not what it means to know me? says the Lord.”

The meaning is equally clear in chapter 9:24:

> “But let those who boast, boast in this: that they understand and know me—that I am the Lord, who exercises loving-kindness, justice, and righteousness on the earth; for I delight in these things, says the Lord.”

Similar sentiments are also found in Exodus (34:6–7), where God—answering Moses' request to see and know Him—reveals no attributes other than those showing His divine justice and mercy. Finally, we must note what John says, though we will discuss it more fully later; since no one has seen God, he explains God to be Love or Charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to *caritas*, or divine, selfless love.</note>, and concludes that whoever has charity in their heart truly knows and possesses God.

We see, therefore, that Moses, Jeremiah, and John all agree that a knowledge of God consists of just a few principles that everyone should be required to know and follow. The sum and substance of these is this: that God is perfectly righteous and merciful, and the only true model <term>original: "exemplar"</term> for human life. Scripture provides no explicit definition of God, nor does it demand that we know any attributes other than those just mentioned as necessary for imitation. 

From all of this, we conclude that the intellectual concept of God—which involves debating the nature of the Supreme Being as He is in Himself—has nothing to do with a perfect rule of life, with faith, or with revealed religion. Humans are incapable of imitating God's absolute nature in their daily lives, and therefore cannot use it as an example to follow. Consequently, it is plain that people may hold mistaken intellectual ideas about God's inner nature in every possible way without committing a sin.

# OF SCRIPTURE DOCTRINE

It is therefore not surprising that God adapted his revelations and the methods by which they were revealed to the imaginations and preconceived ideas of the prophets. Because of this, pious people have often held different opinions about God, as we have shown with many examples in our second chapter. Furthermore, there is no reason to be surprised that God is constantly described so inaccurately in Scripture—that eyes, ears, hands, feet, senses, a mind, and physical proportions are attributed to him, not to mention emotions such as anger, jealousy, mercy, and so on. He is even depicted as a monarch or judge sitting on a royal throne in heaven, with Christ at his right hand and the heavenly host surrounding him. 

All of this is simply an act of meeting the common people <term>original: "the vulgar"</term> at their level of understanding; Scripture's goal is to make people obedient, not to make them scholars. Typical theologians, however, have concluded that whenever their natural reason <term>original: "natural understanding"</term> encountered something that did not match their higher concepts of divine nature, it should be interpreted metaphorically. Conversely, they decided that whatever went beyond their understanding should be taken literally. 

But if every passage of this type in Scripture had to be interpreted and understood metaphorically, then Scripture would have been written only for the most learned philosophers, not for the unrefined and illiterate public. Moreover, if it were wicked to think and believe these things about God with a pure and simple mind, then the prophets should have been especially careful to avoid such phrasing. Out of concern for the weaknesses of the common people, they should have spoken clearly about God’s attributes in a way that ordinary men could easily understand and remember; but they never did this. 

We should therefore not believe that opinions, when considered on their own and without looking at a person’s actions, are inherently pious or impious. Instead, let us say that a person is good or bad based on whether their opinions lead them to obedience and a pure life, or conversely, lead them toward immoral behavior and rebellion against God’s

# CHAPTER XIV.

## ON FAITH, THE GROUNDS OF FAITH, AND THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN FAITH AND PHILOSOPHY.

To have a right understanding of the nature of faith, it is especially necessary to know that Scripture was adapted to the level of understanding not only of the prophets, but also of the common and fickle <note>original: "thoughtless and inconstant"</note> Jewish people. It was written so that no one, even with the slightest attention, could fail to understand it. However, anyone who blindly accepts everything contained in the Scriptures as the universal and absolute doctrine of God does not truly understand what was merely adapted to popular thinking <term>original: "common apprehension"</term>. Such a person cannot avoid confusing common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> opinions with divine doctrine; they will inevitably present the ideas and inventions of men as sacred commands and thereby abuse the authority of Scripture.

It is easy to see that this is the primary reason why different religious factions <term>original: "sectarians"</term> promote so many conflicting opinions as essential articles of faith, which they always try to prove using scriptural texts. Indeed, this has become a proverb in the Netherlands <note>original: "the Low Countries"</note>: "There is no heretic without a text" <note>original: "geen ketter sonder letter"</note>.

The sacred books of the Jews were not written by a single hand, nor even in the same era. This definition follows so plainly from what has already been proven that it seems to require no further explanation. Nevertheless, I shall expand upon a few details that follow from it:

1. Faith in itself is not saving <note>original: "salutary"</note>; it is only so regarding the obedience it implies. As James says (*General Epistle 2:17*), "faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead." It follows that anyone who is truly obedient necessarily possesses a true and saving faith; for if obedience is granted, then faith (as we have said) is necessarily granted as well. This same apostle goes on to declare (*ibid. 18*), "Show me your faith without your works, and I will show you my faith by my works." 

John also writes (*1st Epistle 4:7, 8*), "Everyone who loves (God and his neighbor) is born of God and knows God; he who does not love does not know God, for God is love." From this, it follows again that we can judge no person as faithful or unfaithful except by their works. That is to say, if a person’s works are good, even if they differ in the specific points of their creed from other believers, they are to be considered faithful. On the contrary, if their deeds are evil, though they may agree with the words of the truly pious, they are still an unbeliever <term>original: "infidel"; in this context, Spinoza means someone lacking the internal moral commitment of faith, regardless of their religious label</term>. For where obedience exists, faith necessarily exists, and faith without works is dead, as John also expressly teaches (*ibid. 13*), where he says, "By this..."

<meta>This page continues Spinoza’s argument that faith is not defined by the intellectual truth of one's beliefs, but by their practical effect on a person's conduct. # OF FAITH.

...the simple definition of faith we have provided, all the elements of which must be sought in the broad foundation we have adopted and in the overall purpose of the Scriptures—unless we wish to mix our own imaginations with sacred teachings. Now, these teachings do not require dogmas that are absolutely true, but only those that are necessary for obedience and for strengthening the mind in love for one's neighbor. It is in this sense alone that any person can be said to be "in God, and God in him," as the Apostle John describes it.

Since, therefore, every person's faith should be considered good and beneficial (or the opposite) based on whether it leads to obedience or disobedience—rather than whether it is true or false in itself—and since no one denies the great variety of human temperaments (that not everyone can naturally agree on everything, and that the same opinions affect people differently, moving one to piety and devotion while moving another to laughter and contempt), it follows that a "catholic" <note>In this context, "catholic" refers to its original meaning: universal or all-encompassing.</note> or universal faith must not contain any dogma that could be a subject of controversy among reasonable and fair-minded people. In the nature of things, a dogma that is pious and profitable to one person may be impious and useless to another; therefore, all dogmas are to be judged by their effects—by the actions they produce and the way of life <note>original: "conversation," which in the 17th century referred to one's conduct or social dealings rather than just speech.</note> to which they lead.*

To a universal faith, therefore, belong only those dogmas which obedience to God absolutely demands, and without which obedience is impossible. Regarding all other articles of faith, everyone should be allowed to think as they please, based on what they know about themselves and what they find best helps them grow in love for God and their neighbor. If such a course were followed, there would be no room left, I believe— <note>The text ends here due to the page break; the catchword "me-" suggests the next word is "methinks" or "me-believe."</note>

1. GOD, the Supreme Being, the just and merciful, exists, and is the example of the true life. He who does not know GOD, or does not believe that GOD exists, cannot obey him, nor know him as his judge.
2. GOD is one. No one doubts that this belief is absolutely necessary for the highest devotion, admiration, and love of GOD; for devotion, reverence, and love arise from the idea of supreme excellence in one over all.
3. GOD is omnipresent, and all things lie open before him. If anything were believed to be hidden from GOD, or if he were held not to see everything, doubts might arise regarding the impartiality of his justice, which governs all, or his justice might even be denied.
4. GOD has sole dominion and right in all things. Uninfluenced by anything beyond himself, he acts and wills by his own sovereign pleasure and unique <note>original: "peculiar"</note> grace; for all are bound to obey him, but he is bound to obey none.
5. The worship of GOD consists of, and obedience to him is shown through, justice and charity alone; in other words, in the love of our neighbor.
6. All who obey and worship GOD in this way are saved; while those who live under the rule <note>original: "empire"</note> of sensuality are lost. If people do not firmly believe this, there is no reason why they should prefer obedience to GOD over indulgence in sensual pleasures.

# OF FAITH.

...affinity and nothing in common. This, I think, no one will deny who considers for a moment the scope and foundations of these two departments of human knowledge, which indeed differ **completely** <note>original: "toto cœlo"; literally "by the whole heaven," meaning diametrically opposed</note>. The scope of philosophy is nothing but truth, while that of faith—as we have abundantly shown—is nothing but piety and obedience. Furthermore, the foundations of philosophy are common ideas <note>original: "notiones communes"; universal concepts or logic shared by all people</note> and must be sought for in nature alone. By contrast, the foundations of faith are laid in history and language, and must be sought in Scripture and revelation only, as has been already shown in Chapter VII. Faith, therefore, grants everyone the fullest liberty to philosophize and to come to whatever conclusions they please about the nature of things and ideas without any charge of sin. It considers as heretical and divisive <note>original: "schismatic"</note> only those who teach views that lead to hatred, anger, strife, and disobedience; on the other hand, it regards only those as faithful who, according to the limit of their powers and intentions, encourage and practice justice and charity.

To conclude, as the subject I have just been engaged with is the main part of all I proposed for myself in this treatise, I am anxious—before proceeding further—to entreat the reader most earnestly to read over the last two chapters again, and to weigh and ponder their contents again and again. I trust the reader will then be convinced that I have not written with any purpose of introducing revolutionary new ideas <note>original: "novelties"</note>, but with a wish to correct imperfections and to amend erroneous views—in which I venture to hope the reader will allow I have sometimes been successful.

# CHAPTER XV.

->THEOLOGY DOES NOT ASSIST REASON, NOR DOES REASON AID THEOLOGY. ON THE GROUNDS OF OUR BELIEF IN THE AUTHORITY OF THE SACRED SCRIPTURES.<-

Those who do not know how to distinguish between philosophy and theology debate whether Scripture should support reason or reason should serve Scripture. That is to say, they wonder whether the meaning of Scripture ought to be made to harmonize with reason, or if reason should be forced to bend to Scripture. Of these two views, one is held by the skeptics, who deny the certainty of reason, and the other by the dogmatists <note>Dogmatists here refers to those who assert certain religious or philosophical doctrines as unquestionable truths</note>. However, it is apparent from what has already been said that both are greatly mistaken. Indeed, regardless of which opinion is adopted, either reason or Scripture must necessarily be misused. 

We have shown that Scripture does not teach philosophy, but piety; and that the entire content of the Bible is adapted to the capacity and preconceived opinions of the common people <note>original: "the vulgar"; referring to the general public or those without specialized education</note>. Consequently, anyone who tries to make Scripture harmonize with philosophy will have to attribute many things to the prophets which they never even imagined, and will often grossly misinterpret their meaning. ### REASON AND THEOLOGY.

[Anyone who makes philosophy the servant of] theology will find himself forced to recognize the prejudices of the common people <note>original: "the vulgar"; referring to the general public or those without specialized education</note> of ancient times as divine truths, and with these, he will fill and cloud his understanding. Consequently, both—those who use reason and those who reject it—will seem to speak irrationally.

The first among the Pharisees <note>Pharisees: A prominent social and religious movement in ancient Judaism; here used to refer to traditional Jewish scholars</note> who openly argued that Scripture should be harmonized with reason was Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar</note> (whose opinion we reviewed in Chapter VII and refuted with many arguments). Although he enjoyed a great reputation among them as a writer, most of his fellow believers disagree with him on this point. Instead, they follow a certain Rabbi Judah Alpakhar,* who, in his eagerness to avoid Maimonides' error, falls into the opposite mistake. This Rabbi maintained that reason ought to be helpful and, indeed, subordinate to Scripture. He does not think that anything in Scripture should be understood metaphorically simply because the literal sense is contrary to reason, but only because it contradicts Scripture itself—that is, because it is at variance with commandments or dogmas <note>dogmas: core religious principles or doctrines</note> clearly expressed elsewhere. 

He therefore establishes a universal rule: whatever Scripture teaches as a doctrine and affirms in express words must be accepted as absolutely true on its own authority alone. He believes no doctrine can be found in the Bible that directly contradicts another, but only seems to do so by implication. The style of language in Scripture often appears to suggest something contrary to what is actually taught; only for this reason should such texts be interpreted as metaphorical. For example, Scripture clearly teaches that God is One (Deuteronomy 6:4). Nowhere is it found directly stating that there are several Gods, even though there are many places where God speaks of himself, and where the prophets speak of God, using the plural number. In these cases, we should assume this is merely a specific style of speaking; the purpose of the language is not to declare that there are multiple Gods. Therefore, all such passages are to be explained metaphorically. To be clear, this is not because the idea of multiple Gods is contrary—

Therefore, in obedience to his own rule, he would be forced to simultaneously accept each as true and reject each as false. Furthermore, what does it matter if one passage contradicts another indirectly (by logical consequence) rather than directly, provided that the consequence is clear? What if the context of the passage and the nature of the subject do not allow for a metaphorical interpretation?

Therefore, we declare the views of both this writer and Maimonides <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Aristotelian reason with Hebrew Scripture.</note> to be untenable. We maintain our unshaken position that theology is not subject or subordinate to reason, nor is reason subject to theology. Instead, each reigns supreme in its own proper sphere: the sphere of reason is truth and knowledge, while the sphere of theology is piety and obedience. 

The power of reason does not extend so far as to be able to determine whether people may be saved by obedience alone, without any knowledge of things. Meanwhile, theology asks for nothing and prescribes nothing but obedience; it neither desires nor achieves anything that goes against reason. For the dogmas of faith, as we have shown in the preceding chapter, are determined by theology only as far as is necessary for obedience. However, the precise understanding of these dogmas—regarding their truth and so forth—theology leaves to the decision of reason, which is truly the light of the soul.

# REASON AND THEOLOGY.

Here, I will take the opportunity to say that by "theology," I mean revelation, specifically in how it shows the goal of Scripture—namely, the way and manner of obedience, or the principles of true piety and true belief. In other words, I am referring to what is properly called the Word of God, which does not consist merely of a specific number of books labeled as "sacred" (see Chapter 12). 

Theology, in this sense, will be found to agree with reason if its commands and rules for living are considered. If its ultimate goal is kept in view, it does not differ at all from what reason dictates; therefore, it is universally applicable and common to everyone. Regarding the actual text of Scripture, we already showed in Chapter 7 that its meaning must be determined solely from its own historical context <note>original: "history"</note>, not from the general study of nature, which is the foundation of philosophy alone. 

We should not be discouraged if, after investigating the true meaning of Scripture in this way, we find it occasionally contradicting reason. Whatever contradictions of this type are found in the Bible—or whatever a person may ignore without harming their love for others <note>original: "charity," referring to the moral obligation to act with kindness and justice</note>—we know for certain does not affect theology or the Word of God. On these matters, everyone may think as they please without sinning. Let us conclude definitively, then, that Scripture should not be forced to conform to reason, nor should reason be made subject to Scripture.

However, the very foundation of theology—namely, that a person is blessed or saved through obedience alone—cannot be proven true or false by reason. Because of this, we might be asked critically: why do we believe in it? If we accept it without reason, like blind people, we are acting foolishly and without judgment. If, on the contrary, we try to prove this foundation through reason, theology would then become a part of philosophy and could not be separated from it. To these objections, I reply that I have definitively shown that this fundamental dogma <note>A "dogma" is a set of principles or beliefs held to be incontrovertibly true by a particular group.</note> of theology cannot be investigated using natural understanding <note>The "natural understanding" refers to the innate human capacity for logic and reason, independent of divine revelation.</note>; at least...

I believe, therefore, that those who seek to prove the authority of Scripture by using mathematical formulas or logical demonstrations are making a serious mistake. The authority of the Bible rests upon the authority of the prophets; consequently, it can be supported by no arguments more powerful than those the ancient prophets used to convince the people of their right to be heard. Our own assurance of that authority can rest on no other foundation than the one on which the prophets built their own certainty and authority. 

We have found that the prophets' entire sense of certainty relied on three things:
1. A clear and vivid imagination;
2. Signs or miracles;
3. And finally—most importantly—a mind dedicated to justice and goodness.

The prophets relied on no other foundations than these. They could not prove their authority by any other means, whether they were addressing the crowds in person in former times, or are communicating with us now through written characters. Regarding the first principle—that they possessed a vivid imagination—this could only be known to the prophets themselves. Therefore, our own certainty regarding revelation must and should rest on the remaining two: signs and doctrine <note>original: "doctrine"; here referring to the moral teachings of justice and charity</note>.

It follows, therefore, that the Scriptures have been a great source of comfort to mankind. While every person without exception is capable of obedience, there are very few indeed who could achieve virtuous habits under the guidance of reason alone. Consequently, without the Scripture, we might despair for the moral well-being of almost all of humanity.

## CHAPTER XVI.

### ON THE FOUNDATIONS OF A COMMONWEALTH: THE NATURAL AND CIVIL RIGHTS OF INDIVIDUALS, AND THE RIGHTS OF THE RULING AUTHORITY.

Until now, our goal has been to separate philosophy from theology and to assert the right to free thought and expression <note>original: "free thought and free discourse"</note> which both fields grant to everyone. Now, it is time to investigate how far this freedom of opinion and speech extends in a well-organized state. To discuss this topic systematically, we must examine the foundations upon which a commonwealth <term>commonwealth: A self-governing community or state, often referring to a republic.</term> is built. First, we must consider the natural rights of individuals, without yet referring to general political systems <note>original: "polity"</note> or religion.

By the "right and law of nature," I mean nothing more than the rules of nature that apply to each individual thing, through which every creature is naturally inclined to exist and act in a specific way. For example, fish are naturally inclined by nature to live in water, and the large to eat the small. Therefore, fish inhabit the water by supreme natural right, and the large live off the small by that same right. 

It is certain that nature, viewed in its entirety, has an absolute right to do everything within its power; in other words, the right of nature is as broad as its power. The power of nature is simply the power of God, who possesses the supreme right to everything and over everything. But—

<summary>Spinoza defines natural right not as a moral or legal principle, but as the inherent power of any being to exist and act according to its nature, equating the power of nature with the power of God.</summary>
<keywords>natural rights, commonwealth, power of God, Spinoza, political philosophy, law of nature</keywords>

--- Page 283 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the foundations of natural right, arguing that it is determined not by human morality, but by the actual power an individual possesses within nature.</meta>

# NATURAL AND CIVIL RIGHT.

Since the power of nature as a whole is nothing more than the combined power of every individual thing in nature, it follows that each individual thing has the supreme right to everything it can reach or achieve. Therefore, the rights of individuals are equal to their power. 

It is the supreme law of nature that every individual thing should strive to remain in its own natural state, focusing on itself alone without regard for anything else. From this, it follows that every individual has a supreme right to its own state—that is, as I have said, to exist and to act exactly as its natural makeup determines. In this regard, we do not recognize any difference between humans and the rest of creation. Nor do we distinguish between humans who use reason and those who know nothing of reason, nor between the sane, the insane, or the foolish <note>original: "fatuous"</note>. 

Whatever a being does, it acts according to the laws of its own nature and by supreme right, because it is acting as nature designed it to, and it is incapable of acting any other way. Therefore, among humans—as long as they are considered to be living under the rule <note>original: "empire"</note> of nature alone—those who do not yet know reason or who have not yet formed the habit of virtuous conduct have a perfect right to live by the laws of mere desire <note>original: "appetite"; referring to instinctual or physical drives</note>. This is just as much a supreme right as that of the person who regulates their life according to the dictates of reason. 

In other words, just as the wise person has a supreme right to everything that wisdom commands (to live according to the laws of reason), the foolish or ignorant person has a full right to live according to the laws of desire. This is what the Apostle Paul teaches when he acknowledges that there was no sin before the law was proclaimed <note>original: "promulgation"</note>; that is to say, as long as people lived under the rule of nature, they were not living in sin.*

# NATURAL AND CIVIL RIGHT.

The natural right of every person, therefore, is determined by desire <note>original: "appetite"</note> and power, not by sound reason. For not everyone is naturally designed <note>original: "constituted"</note> to act according to the rules of reason. On the contrary, everyone is born ignorant of everything; before they can learn the true rules of life and develop virtuous habits, a large part of their lives must already have passed. In the meantime, however, they are still meant to live and, as much as they are able, to preserve their state of being. But they must do this solely by the impulses of appetite or desire; for nature gives nothing else as a guide to a person in their natural state, and does not grant them the power to live by the rules of sound reason. Humans are therefore no more bound to live by the rules of absolute right than a domestic cat is bound to live by the laws of a lion's nature.

Therefore, whatever anyone who is considered to be under the rule <note>original: "empire"</note> of nature alone considers useful to himself—whether led by right reason or by the impulse of desire—he seeks by a supreme law of nature. It is lawful for him to obtain it by force, by cunning, by pleading—in short, in any way possible—and to treat as an enemy whoever opposes him in satisfying his desire.

From this, it follows that the law or principle of nature—under which all are born and for the most part live—prohibits nothing except what no one desires and no one can desire. It does not forbid conflict, disagreement, anger, hatred, deception, or trickery, nor indeed anything that passion prompts. This is not surprising; for nature is not confined within the narrow limits of the laws of reason, which serve humans only and are meant solely for their guidance. Instead, nature embraces an infinity of other matters regarding the eternal order of creation as a whole, in which a human is a mere atom. By the necessity of nature, for instance, every individual thing is designed to exist and to act in a specific, determined way. Thus, whatever appears evil or absurd to us only seems so because we have only partial knowledge and are ignorant of the order and interconnection <note>original: "concatenation"</note> of nature at

It suggests that perceived "evils" are merely the result of our limited understanding of the vast, interconnected order of the universe.</summary>

It is unquestionable that it is beneficial for humans to live according to the laws and specific instructions of reason, which, as previously stated, are designed solely for their benefit. Everyone desires to live in peace, safety, and freedom from fear. However, this would be impossible if everyone were allowed to do whatever they liked, and if reason were given no more authority than passions like hatred and revenge. No one can live among enemies, hatred, and deception <note>original: "wiles"</note> without constant anxiety, and everyone will do their best to escape such conditions. 

Furthermore, if we consider that those who live without mutual help and the necessary development <note>original: "culture"</note> of reason live very miserable lives (as shown in Chapter 5), it becomes clear that to live in comfort and security, people must join together. They must agree that the natural rights each individual possesses should be held collectively. Individuals must stop living only for themselves through force and impulse <note>original: "appetite"</note>; instead, everything should be determined by the will and consent of the entire community. 

This attempt, however, would be in vain if everyone chose only to follow their impulses (since the laws of impulse pull everyone in different directions). Every person must be firmly resolved—and indeed obligated—to govern themselves in all things by the dictates of reason alone. No one dares to openly oppose reason, for fear of appearing to have lost their mind <note>original: "understanding"</note>. People must restrain their impulses or emotions when these urge them to act against the interests of others. They must follow the rule of doing nothing to another person that they would not want done to themselves, and, finally, they must defend the rights of others as if they were their own.

To make this point clearer, imagine a robber forces me to promise that I will hand over my property at a location of his choosing. Now, although my natural right is determined only by my power (as I have already explained), it is certain that if I can escape from this robber through trickery <note>original: "guile"</note> or a clever plan <note>original: "stratagem"</note>—promising him everything he asks—it is legally within my natural right to do so. 

Or, consider another example: suppose that without any intent to deceive, but simply by acting recklessly, I promised someone I would go without food and drink for twenty days. Later, I realize I have made a foolish promise that I either cannot keep at all or could only keep by causing myself great harm. Since by natural right I may choose the lesser of two evils, I am perfectly free to break that promise and treat the agreement as if it had never existed. I say this can be done by natural right, whether I realize that my promise was reckless and wrong based on <term>right reason</term> <note>right reason: the use of logic and intellect to determine the best course of action for preservation</note> or just personal opinion. Regardless of whether I see what I promised as good or bad, right or wrong, because I deeply fear evil, I strive by nature’s decree <note>original: "ordinance"</note> to avoid it in every way possible.

Consequently, whoever possesses supreme power also possesses the supreme right, which they can enforce using the full strength of the law. # NATURAL AND CIVIL RIGHT.

[...in other] words, a ruler holds his authority by a precarious tenure <note>precarious tenure: an insecure or uncertain grasp on power that could be lost at any moment</note>, and no one more powerful than himself will be bound to obey him unless they choose to do so.

In this way, then, a state can be established without the slightest infringement of <term>natural right</term> <note>natural right: the individual's inherent power to act according to their own nature and for their own survival</note>, and all agreements can be kept with the most perfect faith. This is possible if each individual transfers the whole of the power he has over himself to the community of which he is a member. That community then comes to possess supreme natural right in everything—in other words, it holds the supreme authority which every individual, whether out of choice or out of fear, will then be required to obey. 

A state or community established in this way is called a democracy. It is defined as a general assembly of people who collectively hold the highest right to everything that each person previously possessed individually. Therefore, it follows that the supreme authority itself is bound by no law, while everyone else is required to obey it in whatever it ordains. Everyone must consider themselves pledged to this—whether they agreed to it silently <note>original: "tacitly"</note> or openly—when they transferred their common natural right to a collective supreme power. 

If the individual members of a democracy therefore desire to keep any specific rights for themselves, they must take special care to also keep the power to defend those rights. If they have not taken such precautions, and a stand cannot be made for the right in question without creating a division in the state—and perhaps even endangering its existence—then they have subjected themselves unconditionally to the ruling authority, and they have no choice but to obey. 

Because this is the case, and because reason and necessity alike demand submission, it follows that we are bound to obey the commands of the highest power, even if they seem absurd to us. If we do not, we would be considered enemies of the <term>commonwealth</term> and would be acting against reason, which strongly encourages us to support the supreme authority with all our might. After all, reason also teaches us that in a difficult situation <note>original: "in a strait"</note>, we should choose the lesser of two evils. Add to this the fact that the danger of having to submit unconditionally to the will and authority...

# NATURAL AND CIVIL RIGHT.

[...the power] of another is then very imminent <note>imminent: likely to happen very soon; in this context, the threat of being subjected to someone else's will</note>; for we have seen that ruling powers have the right to command whatever they please, so long as they possess the power to enforce their commands, or are, in fact, the head of the state. For if they once lose their power of compelling obedience, they at the same time lose their power of commanding, which then falls to those who have been strong enough to acquire it. 

It only happens very rarely, therefore, that the highest powers in a state exert their authority in an absurd way. It is especially necessary for them—based on simple self-interest and the desire to stay in power—to consult the common good and organize everything according to the dictates of discretion and right reason. As Seneca says, "No one maintains violent power for long" <note>original: "Violenta nemo imperia continuit diu" — a quote from the Roman philosopher Seneca’s tragedy, *Troades*</note>. 

Furthermore, such absurdities are even less to be feared in a democracy. It is nearly impossible for the majority of an assembly, especially a large one, to give in to the whims of one foolish person or to agree to anything foolish or harmful <note>original: "pernicious"</note>. Besides, the very basis and goal of a <term>policied state</term> <note>policied state: a society organized under a formal system of government and laws</note> is to escape the rule of raw passions and to restrain humanity within the bounds of reason and social propriety, so that people may live together in peace and harmony. If this foundation is disturbed, the whole structure of society necessarily collapses. The duty of the supreme power or government, therefore, is to provide for these things, and the duty of subjects <note>subjects: individuals living under the authority of a government; in modern terms, citizens</note> is to obey, to carry out the commands of the chief authority, and to acknowledge as law and right only what the government declares to be so.

In speaking this way, however, some may suppose that I am turning subjects into slaves; for they may think that a slave is someone who only moves at the command of another, while a freeman is someone who lives and acts of his own free will. But this is not absolutely true. He who is mastered by his own appetites, and who can neither understand nor do what is truly for his own good, is the greatest slave of all. In contrast, the true freeman is the one who lives in all things according to reason. Therefore, acting by command—in other words, obedience—does not necessarily...

# NATURAL AND CIVIL RIGHT.

It is the motive or purpose of the action that makes a person either a bondservant or free. If the goal of the action is for the <term>behoof</term> <note>behoof: benefit or advantage</note> of the person giving the command and not for the person acting, then the agent is a slave and useless to himself. However, where the advantage of the community at large—and not the ruler—is the aim, as it is in a republic or constitutional state, then the person who obeys is no slave, but subject only to the laws of his country. Indeed, that <term>commonwealth</term> <note>commonwealth: an independent state or community, especially a democratic republic</note> is the freest whose laws are founded on the highest right and reason. In such a state, everyone who wishes to may be truly free, for there he may live in accordance with the dictates of reason.

In the same way, children are not to be considered slaves even though they are bound to obey the commands of their parents; for the commands of parents are assumed to be focused specifically on the advantage of their children. We therefore recognize a great difference between a *slave*, a *son*, and a *subject*, words which may be individually defined as follows: 

* **A slave** is one who is required to obey the commands of a master, where those commands refer only to the advantage of the person giving the orders. 
* **A son** does what is advantageous to himself at the command of his parent. 
* **A subject**, lastly, does what is useful to the community—and therefore to himself—by obeying the commands of the supreme power in the state.

Thus, I briefly present the foundations of democratic authority. I desired to treat this form of government in particular both because it seems to me the most natural form of government and because it accords best with the liberty which every individual has by nature. In a democracy, no one transfers his natural [right...]

As a general thesis, the question may be put this way: whoever holds supreme power—whether it is one person, a small group, or the whole population—has the right to command whatever they wish. We can also determine who is an ally, who is an enemy, and, finally, what constitutes the crime of treason.

By ***Private Civil Right***, we mean nothing other than the freedom each person has to protect their own property and status. This liberty is guaranteed by the laws of the supreme power and is defended by its authority alone. Wrong is committed when a citizen or subject suffers an injury to their person or estate <note>original: "estate"; referring here to property or land</note> from another, contrary to their civil rights or the decree of the supreme authority. "Wrong" cannot be conceived except in a social state; it cannot properly occur between the supreme authority and a subject, since everything is lawful for the ruling power. It occurs only between private individuals, who are bound by law not to injure one another.

Justice arises from a mindset that gives to everyone what belongs to them by civil right. *Injustice*, on the other hand, follows from a disposition to withhold or to take from another what properly belongs to them by right and law. Partiality and impartiality are equivalent terms for "unjust" and "just." This is because the person entrusted with the authority to settle disputes between citizens is expected to have "no respect of persons" <note>original: "no respect of persons"; a phrase meaning to show no favoritism or bias based on a person's status or identity</note>. Instead, they must regard all as equal and defend the rights of everyone with equal zeal and conscientiousness, neither favoring the rich nor trampling on the poor.

Confederates <note>original: "Confederates"; here referring to allied nations or states in a league</note> are the people making up two or more distinct states who enter into a <term>compact</term> <note>compact: a formal agreement, treaty, or contract between parties</note>. They do this for mutual defense, to escape the dangers of war, or for any other reason of perceived benefit to themselves. Under this agreement, they promise not only to avoid harming one another, but to provide mutual aid and assistance in case of need, while each state continues to retain its individual independence. 

This treaty or compact remains in force as long as the motive that led to its creation—whether fear of danger or the prospect of advantage—continues to be felt. No engagement is ever made except in the hope of some benefit or out of the fear of some evil. If the reason for the compact is removed, the agreement ends on its own, as is proven by everyday experience. For although different states often agree not to harm one another, each will still strive to the best of its ability to prevent its neighbor from becoming more powerful than itself. Nor are the

<page-num>281</page-num>

# NATURAL AND CIVIL RIGHT.

The terms of a treaty are rarely respected unless actions prove to be in conformity with them. If promises to provide aid or be useful are not kept—or if they are "kept only in words, but broken in reality" <note>original: "kept to the ear, are broken to the hope"; an allusion to Shakespeare's Macbeth, meaning a promise that is technically kept but fails its intended purpose</note>—then deceit and injury are feared, and with good reason. Indeed, who but a fool, ignorant of the rights of ruling powers, would trust the mere words and assurances of someone who possesses supreme authority, is armed with the power to do as they please, and for whom the glory and advantage of their own nation must be the supreme law! 

When we connect these facts with moral considerations, we see that no one who holds the chief authority could, without guilt, keep promises that would prove harmful to the interests of the state they rule. Whatever promise a ruler may have made, if they see it involves injury to the community over which they preside, it cannot be kept without breaking faith with their subjects. It is this faith—the protection of the people—that a ruler is most bound to observe; indeed, it is customary for rulers to bind themselves to this duty through solemn oaths.

An **Enemy** is defined as someone who lives outside the boundaries of a state and behaves in a way that shows they do not acknowledge its authority, either as a <term>confederate</term> <note>confederate: an ally or a member of a league of states</note> or as a subject. It is not hatred or animosity that makes someone an enemy of a state, but rather their legal status. The right of the state regarding someone who does not recognize its authority through a treaty or contract is the same as its right regarding someone who causes it damage. Therefore, the state may use every means at its command to compel such a person either to join it as an ally or to obey its commands as a subject.

The crime of **Treason**, lastly, occurs only among the subjects of states who, by silent or formal agreement, have transferred the whole of their rights to the ruling power. A person is said to be guilty of this crime if they attempt in any way to seize the sovereign authority for themselves or to transfer it from the current possessor to another. I say "makes the attempt" in this case because if the matter could not be brought to <term>adjudication</term> <note>adjudication: the formal act of making a judicial judgment or settling a legal dispute</note> until after the act was completed, the state would usually intervene too late, long after the supreme authority had already been lost.

Everyone agrees that this principle is properly applied in war. However, it is not as clearly understood by everyone that citizens are absolutely bound by the same rule, even though the reason for obedience is the same in both cases. Since the commonwealth should be watched over and directed by the supreme authority alone, and since citizens are absolutely committed to yielding this right to that authority, any person who takes it upon himself—on his own initiative and without the order and agreement of the supreme power—to start or interfere in any public business, violates the right of the ruling power. Even if a benefit to the state certainly follows from his actions, he has nevertheless committed treason and is properly condemned and sentenced to punishment.

The objection to this is that because everyone—whether they possess reason or not—is bound by the divine command to love their neighbor as themselves, it seems impossible to live according to mere instinct and not cause injury or injustice to others. At this point, it might still be argued that ruling powers, just like their subjects, are bound by divine law. This seems to contradict our earlier statement that the supreme authority of a state does not give up its natural rights, and that everything within its power is lawful for it to do. To resolve this difficulty—which arises more from questions about natural right than from political logic <note>original: "reason of state," the principle that the interests of the state justify any means used to maintain it</note>—I argue that in the state of nature, everyone is bound to live by revealed right for the same reasons they are bound to live by the dictates of reason. That is, it is beneficial and necessary for their own well-being to do so. If someone chooses not to live this way, they do so at their own risk.

In the natural state, a person lives according to their own path, not in obedience to someone else's commands. They do not recognize any earthly judge, nor do they fear anyone acting as a punisher <note>original: "avenger"</note> on behalf of religion. I maintain that the supreme power in the state keeps the right to live this way. While a ruler might seek advice from others, they are not bound to recognize anyone else as their judge. No one but the sovereign themselves can punish the violation of a right—unless, of course, a prophet were specifically sent by God and proved their mission with undeniable miracles. Even in that case, the sovereign would not be submitting to the man as a judge, but to God Himself. 

However, if the sovereign authority refuses to obey God’s revealed will, it does so at its own peril. There is no natural or social law to restrain it. As we have seen, social law depends entirely on the decrees of the supreme authority, while natural right depends exclusively on the laws of nature. These laws of nature are not organized solely according to religion (which focuses on human benefit), but according to nature in its entirety—that is, the eternal decrees of God.

### CHAPTER XVII.

->INDIVIDUAL RIGHT IS NEVER WHOLLY ABANDONED TO THE<-
