The idea developed in the previous chapter concerning the right of the supreme power in a state over everyone, and of the <term>natural rights</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "natural rights" often referred to the power or freedom an individual has in a state of nature before joining a society.</note> of individuals transferred to it, remains entirely theoretical in several ways, even though it agrees with experience in many respects. However, theory and practice can be brought very close together here. No one, for example, could ever transfer their power—and consequently their rights—to another so completely that they stopped feeling like a human being. Nor has there ever been any sovereign power in the world that could dispose absolutely, and at its own will and pleasure, of everything belonging to the state and the people. 

It would be useless to command a subject to hate someone who has served them, to love someone who has injured them, to feel no offense at being treated unworthily, or to stop caring about their own personal safety—along with many other things that follow necessarily from the constitution of human nature. I believe experience clearly demonstrates this; for people have never so entirely abandoned their rights, or so effectively surrendered <note>original: "ceded"</note> them to another, that they themselves no longer...

# THE HEBREW REPUBLIC.

These considerations must be kept in mind and feared by the person to whom power was entrusted, and who, by this trust, was raised to the sovereign power in the state. It is a known truth that despotic rulers have mostly lived in as much fear of their own subjects—even when those subjects were stripped of their rights—as they have feared foreign enemies. If people could indeed strip themselves of their natural rights so completely that they had no will or choice left except to do what the supreme power commanded, then governors could truly rule tyrannically and cruelly with <term>impunity</term> <note>Exemption from punishment or freedom from the injurious consequences of an action.</note>. But I believe no person in their right mind would ever consent to strip themselves of all natural rights and power. Everyone, under all circumstances, must still reserve some portion of these for themselves; consequently, those rights will not depend on someone else, but will belong to the individual alone.

To properly understand the extent of the right and power of the highest authority in a state, we must observe that a ruler's right does not consist simply in the ability to force subjects to obey through fear. Rather, it consists absolutely in the fact that his commands are followed. It is not the reason or motive for the obedience that matters, but the obedience itself which gives the sovereign authority its right and power to command. Whether subjects obey out of fear of punishment, hope for a reward, love for their country, or any other impulse, they still choose to obey of their own accord. In doing so, they act in accordance with the <term>decrees</term> <note>Official orders or laws issued by a legal authority.</note> or commands of the highest power in the state. 

Consequently, whatever a subject does that aligns with the commands of the sovereign power—whether he is moved by love, driven by fear, influenced by both at once, or by respect (a feeling made of fear and admiration), or, in short, by any other motive—he acts not only by his own right, but also by the right of the supreme power. This position is strongly confirmed by the fact that obedience relates more to an internal mental state than to an outward act. Therefore, the person most under the authority of another is the one who obeys all commands with a sincere and willing heart...

Both rulers and those they rule are equally human; they are disinclined to work and highly inclined toward physical pleasures. Those who have had much experience with the unpredictable and fickle nature of the masses have almost lost hope for humanity. This is because men are not governed by reason and higher ideals, but by their appetites and emotions alone. Always impulsive, they are easily led by their greed and their love of luxury. Arrogant, each person believes that he alone knows everything and desires to arrange everything in his own way. Selfish, he judges whether something is just or unjust, right or wrong, based only on whether he thinks it serves his own interests. Vain, <note>original: "vainglorious"</note> he looks down on his equals and refuses to be guided by them. Envious, he resents others for having more honor or better fortune than himself. Revengeful, he wishes harm on others and rejoices when it happens. 

But enough—it is unnecessary to go further. Everyone knows all too well the crimes and wickedness produced by dissatisfaction with the present and the desire for change. We know what blind rage and the hope of escaping miserable poverty have driven mankind to do, and how entirely personal concerns occupy and influence men’s minds. To foresee and prevent disturbances in a state arising from such causes—to leave no room for disorder to creep in, and to arrange matters so that everyone, whatever his personality or temperament, prefers the public good to his private advantage—this is the task undertaken and the work to be achieved by the patriotic ruler. 

Out of sheer necessity, much has been done to secure these great goals. However, I believe matters have rarely been arranged so successfully that governments were not in even greater danger from their own citizens than from foreign foes. Rulers have feared opponents <note>original: "unfriends"</note> at home just as much as enemies abroad. Let the great Roman Republic provide the proof of this fact. Although it was invincible against enemies from the outside, it was often defeated and miserably oppressed by its own citizens—perhaps never more cruelly than in the civil war of Vespasian against Vitellius (see Tacitus, *Histories*, Book 4 <note>original: "vide Tacitus, Histor. lib. iv."</note>). For this reason, and to make themselves more secure, we see that kings in the past who seized power <note>original: "usurped their state"</note> often tried to persuade the world that they were descended from the immortal gods. They assumed that if they could make their subjects view them not as equals or mere mortals like themselves, but as gods, the people would more readily submit to being ruled and prove more obedient in all things. Thus, Augustus Caesar persuaded the Roman people that he was descended from Aeneas, the son of Venus, and should therefore be ranked among the divinities. Consequently, he ordered temples to be raised in his honor, his bust to be enshrined in the likeness of a god, and divine honors to be paid to him by a body of priests dedicated to his service (Tacitus, *Annals*, book 1). 

Alexander, for his part, ordered that he should be greeted as the son of Jove. However, this seems to have been done out of political strategy <note>original: "policy"</note>, not vanity, as is proved by his answer to Hermolaus:

> “It was enough to provoke laughter,” he is reported to have said himself, “when Hermolaus wanted me to rebel against Jupiter, whose oracle had acknowledged me. In the Hebrew state, consequently, the civil government <note>original: "polity"</note> and religion—which consists essentially, as we have shown, in obedience to God—were one and the same. The dogmas of the Jewish religion were not mere doctrines, but established rights and commandments; piety was considered justice, while impiety was seen as injustice and crime. Anyone who abandoned the state religion ceased to be a citizen and, for this reason alone, was looked upon as an enemy. Likewise, anyone who died for his religion was held to have died for his country; in short, no distinction whatever was made between civil law and religious profession. On these grounds, the ancient Hebrew state might rightly be called a <term>theocracy</term> <note>A system of government in which God is recognized as the supreme civil ruler.</note>: its subjects were bound by no law except that revealed by God. All of this, however, was based more on perception than on reality; for the ancient Hebrews did, in fact, retain the absolute right of ruling in their own hands, as I shall immediately show by analyzing the way their state was administered.

Inasmuch as the Hebrews surrendered their natural rights to no one among themselves, but instead all equally—as in a <term>democracy</term>—transferred these rights to Jehovah, and with one voice proclaimed that they would do whatever God commanded without a mediator, it follows that by this arrangement everyone remained individually equal. They all had an equal title to consult God, to receive and interpret laws—in a word, to share in the administration of affairs. For this reason, everyone at first approached Jehovah themselves so that they might know His commands. But in their earliest interview, the people were so alarmed, and heard the voice of God speaking with such terror and amazement, that they thought the end of all things had come. If Moses had chosen a successor who, like himself, possessed the entire administrative power—including the right to consult God in the tabernacle and, consequently, the right to establish or abolish <note>original: "abrogating"</note> laws, decide on war and peace, send ambassadors, appoint judges, choose a successor, and handle all the duties belonging to a sovereign ruler—then the constitution of the state would have been a pure monarchy. In fact, there would have been no real difference, except that a typical monarchy is usually said to be governed by the "grace" or "will" of God, which is not clearly visible. In contrast, the Hebrew monarchy under Moses was ruled—or ordered to be ruled—by the decrees of God through direct and open revelation. 

This difference, however, does not reduce the ruler's authority in any way; if anything, it increases it. In other matters, particularly regarding the people, they are equally subjects whether in a typical monarchy or in the Jewish nation. In both cases, the people are unaware of divine decrees, for everything depends on the will of the monarch. What is right or wrong is simply what the ruler decides it to be. The people might believe that the sovereign only commands what has been revealed to him by God, but this does not make them less controlled. On the contrary, it places them even more firmly under the hand of authority.

Moses, however, as previously mentioned, chose no single successor. First, the people were commanded to build a house which should be, as it were, the palace of Jehovah—that is, the palace of the sovereign power of the state. This was to be done not at the expense of any one individual or group, but by the whole people, so that the building in which God was to be consulted should be common property. The Levites were the chosen administrators within this royal hall of audience, and Aaron, the brother of Moses, was made the chief among them. He was, in effect, the second in authority after Jehovah the King, and Aaron’s sons were to be regarded as his legitimate successors. Aaron, therefore, as the high priest <term>chief priest</term> and the person nearest to God, was the highest interpreter of the divine laws, the person who delivered the responses of the divine oracle to the people, and the intercessor with God for the nation. 

Now, if an officer with such powers had also possessed an equal right of civil command <term>political or secular authority</term>, there would have been nothing lacking to make him an absolute monarch. However, the priest of the temple was deprived of this right of civil command. Indeed, the entire tribe of Levi was forbidden from taking any part in the common affairs of life (to say nothing of the civil administration) by which they might earn a living. It was ordained that they should be maintained by the rest of the community so that, as it was said, they might be held in higher honor by the common people as a group solely devoted to the service of Jehovah.

Next, the military force <note>original: "militia"</note>, chosen from all the remaining twelve tribes, was commanded to invade the territory of the Canaanites and to divide it into twelve parts for allotment among themselves. For this business, twelve chiefs were selected, one from each tribe. Along with Joshua the captain and Eleazar the high priest, these chiefs were given the authority to divide the land of Canaan into twelve equal parts and to distribute them by lot. Once these answers were received, Joshua had absolute authority to proclaim God’s decrees and to enforce obedience to them. 

He also had the right to promote and honor any individuals he chose from the militia, to send ambassadors, and so on. In short, the entire administration of war rested with Joshua, as the commander-in-chief of the army. However, no one could naturally inherit <note>original: "legitimately succeed"</note> this important office; a successor could only be chosen directly by God when the nation’s needs required such an appointment. At all other times, all affairs of peace and war were managed by the tribal chiefs, as I will soon demonstrate.

Finally, every male between the ages of twenty and sixty was required to take up arms. Thus, the army was the people, and the people were the army. They swore loyalty <note>original: "fealty"</note> not to any commander or high priest, but to their religion and their God, Jehovah. Consequently, the army was called the "host" <term>a large group of armed men; an army</term> or the ranks of God, and among the ancient Hebrews, God Himself was called the "Lord of Hosts." 

This is why the Ark of the Covenant was always carried in the middle of the army during major battles, where the outcome would determine the nation's fate for better or worse. In the symbolic presence of their King and Ruler, it was believed the people would behave with greater bravery and exert all their strength.

From the laws <note>original: "ordinances"</note> delivered by Moses to his successors, we can see that he chose officials or administrators rather than absolute rulers of the state. He gave no one the right to consult God alone or in whatever place they chose. Consequently, he gave no one the same authority he had held: the power to establish or abolish <note>original: "ordaining and abrogating"</note> laws, to declare peace or war, or to choose ministers for both the temple and the state.

All of these are actions belonging to one who holds supreme or sovereign authority. The high priest himself had the right, indeed, of interpreting the laws and of delivering the responses of <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The personal name of God in the Hebrew Bible</note>. He did not do this, however, as <term>Moses</term> had done—whenever he chose—but only when asked to do so by the commander-in-chief of the army, the supreme council of the state, or those in authority. On the other hand, the commander-in-chief of the army and the council could choose to consult God whenever they wished, but they could only receive the answers He deigned to give through the high priest. Therefore, the words of God from the mouth of the high priest were not "commandments," as they had been when spoken by <term>Moses</term>, but were instead "responses" delivered to <term>Joshua</term> and the council. Nevertheless, these responses eventually acquired the force of commandments and decrees.

The high priest, who received the responses of God directly, possessed neither military nor civil authority. Conversely, those who held the legal right to the land did not have the legal right to establish laws. Furthermore, the first high priests, both <term>Aaron</term> and his son <term>Eleazar</term>, were appointed by <term>Moses</term>. Once <term>Moses</term> was dead, however, no one possessed the right to elect a <term>pontiff</term> <note>original: "pontiff"; here referring to the Jewish High Priest</note>; instead, the son legally succeeded the father in his office. 

The commander of the army was also chosen by <term>Moses</term>, not by the high priest. The chief command was first assumed by <term>Joshua</term> by virtue of a title granted to him directly by <term>Moses</term>. After the death of <term>Joshua</term>, however, the high priest did not appoint anyone in his place, nor did the tribal chiefs consult God again regarding a new commander. Instead, each chief oversaw the <term>militia</term> <note>a military force raised from the civil population</note> of his own tribe, and the chiefs of all the tribes met together in a council to handle the nation's military affairs. In doing so, they resumed the right of supreme command that had previously been granted to <term>Joshua</term>. 

It is clear, indeed, that there was no necessity for a single commander-in-chief except when the different tribes had to combine their forces against a common enemy. This situation was most notable under <term>Joshua</term>, when the various tribes did not yet have fixed settlements and all territory was held by common right. The other parties involved surrender the rights they previously held over that specific portion to the new possessor. For this reason, <term>Moses</term> chose tribal chiefs. His goal was that after the land was divided, each chief would have specific oversight of the territory belonging to his tribe and its internal affairs. Furthermore, the chief was not required to answer to any judge except <term>Jehovah</term> or someone whom God specifically sent as a prophet. Any chief who abandoned <term>Jehovah</term> was to be treated by the rest of the tribe no longer as one of their own, but as an enemy who had broken their treaty, and he was to be dealt with accordingly. 

Examples of this are recorded in Scripture. For instance, after the death of <term>Joshua</term>, the Israelites themselves—not a new supreme commander—consulted <term>Jehovah</term>. Since some duties were entrusted <note>original: "confided"</note> to one tribe, others to different tribes, and still others were administered with equal right by all the rest, it follows most obviously that the constitution of the Hebrew state after the death of Moses was neither a monarchy, nor an aristocracy, nor a democracy. Instead, as I have said, it was a theocracy <term>theocracy: a system of government where God is recognized as the supreme civil ruler and laws are interpreted by religious authorities.</term>. This is because: 

1. The royal palace was a temple, and the tribes were united as fellow citizens solely through their shared interest in this temple; 

2. All citizens were required to swear loyalty <note>original: "fealty"</note> to the Lord God as their judge, promising absolute obedience to Him alone in all things; 

3. And the commander-in-chief of the nation, when there was a need for such an officer, was chosen by **Jehovah** rather than by the people themselves. 

**Moses** expressly declares this in the name of God in Deuteronomy (19:15) <note>The author cites 19:15, though Deuteronomy 17:15, which discusses God choosing the nation's leader, is likely the intended reference.</note>, and the fact itself is proven by the election of **Gideon**, **Samson**, and **Samuel**. Therefore, there is no reason to doubt that the other faithful leaders were also chosen in the same way, even if this is not mentioned in their histories.

Now that these points are established <note>original: "premised"</note>, it is time to see what influence this constitution had in ensuring moderation for both the rulers and the subjects, so that the people did not rebel and the rulers did not become tyrants.

Those who rule or hold authority, regardless of what wrongdoing <note>original: "iniquity"</note> they commit, still strive to give their actions a veneer of justice. They try to persuade the people that everything they do is good and honest. They succeed in this easily enough when the entire interpretation of the laws lies with them. It is certain that rulers derive the greater part of their power to enforce their own desires and impulses <note>original: "appetites"</note> from the fact that they are the sole interpreters of the laws. On the other hand, they lose the greater part of their arbitrary power if the right to interpret the laws belongs to someone else, and if the administration of the law is handled so publicly that no one is in doubt about what is being done. The interpretation of the law was entrusted solely to the Levites (Deut. 21:5). They held no share with the other tribes in the general administration of affairs; instead, they derived their entire income, subsistence, and social standing from the impartial interpretation of the laws. Furthermore, the entire population was commanded to assemble in a specific place every seven years to be instructed by the high priest in the laws of their country. Every man was also ordered to read and re-read the Book of the Law with his utmost attention (Deut. 31:9 and 6:7). Therefore, for their own sake and if they wished to be honored by the people, the chiefs were bound to ensure that everything was done according to the prescribed forms familiarly known to all. Only by doing so could they hope to be revered as <term>vice-gerents: administrative deputies acting on behalf of a higher ruler, in this case, God</term> of God and ministers of His supreme authority.

By acting otherwise, they could not escape the hatred of the people, which in such cases is usually "theological"—that is <note>original: "i. e."</note>, unmitigated and intense in its character. To this end—to restrain the unrestrained desires of their chiefs—there was an additional important circumstance: the militia was composed of the people at large. No one from the age of twenty to sixty was exempt from service, and the chiefs were not authorized to have any foreign <term>mercenaries: professional soldiers hired to serve in a foreign army</term> in their ranks. 

This, I say, was of the greatest importance. It is certain that princes can only act as tyrants and oppress the people by using a soldiery they pay themselves; they dread nothing more than the freedom of the citizen-soldier, by whose bravery, endurance, and willing sacrifice the liberty and glory of the state were achieved. For this reason, when **Alexander** was about to engage in the second war against **Darius**, he took to heart the counsel of **Parmenio** (received through **Polyspercon**) and began to mix foreign elements heavily into his native army. **Quintus Curtius** informs us (Book 4, Chapter 3, Section 13 <note>original: "lib. iv. 3, 13"</note>) that Alexander, having shortly before been forced to reprimand Parmenio sharply, did not dare to reprimand him again or to infringe <note>original: "trench"</note> on the liberties of the Macedonians—which he greatly disliked—until after he had increased his strength with foreign recruits.

The chief was especially careful to avoid proposing any radical innovations so as not to oppose the high priest or let his own civil authority clash with the authority of the leader of the national religion. And then, poverty could have been more tolerable nowhere else than in the ancient Hebrew state, where neighborly charity was practiced without limit as an act of piety toward God their king, and as a means of making him favorable <note>original: "propitious"</note> toward them. The Hebrew citizen, therefore, within the limits of the state could scarcely find himself in any condition other than well-off and comfortable, although abroad he was vulnerable to the most shameful treatment <note>original: "unworthy usage"</note> and to every insult and indignity.

The feeling, indeed, that he had no equal abroad, that he had God alone for a master at home, and that charity toward and love of his fellow citizen was true piety, contributed significantly to the general hatred other nations felt for the Jew. His return of this hatred, while it proved a powerful motive for keeping him in his own country, was another reason for shunning all causes of conflict and avoiding civil war.

In addition to this, there was the discipline of perfect obedience in which the Jew was educated. All his actions, down to the smallest detail <note>original: "minutest tittle"</note>, were regulated by the requirements of the law. He was not at liberty to plow as he pleased; he could only do so at certain seasons, in certain years even, and with the same sort of cattle in the yoke. Neither could he sow or reap except at times and seasons predetermined <note>original: "foreordained"</note>. In short, the life of the ancient Hebrew was a constant cycle of obedience and observance, to which habit must have given the feeling of freedom rather than of constraint. Because of this, it also followed that no one desired things that were forbidden, but only those that were commanded. Finally, at certain seasons of the year, the Jew was required to dedicate himself to ease and enjoyment—and this was not to satisfy his own inclination, but to show hearty obedience to the commands of Jehovah. Every citizen was considered a guest of God <note>original: "the Jew was the guest of Jehovah"</note> (Deuteronomy 16). The seventh day of every week was a day of rest on which he performed no kind of work. Besides this Sabbath, other times were designated for celebrations where merriment and socializing were not merely permitted, but positively commanded. I do not imagine that anything could have been devised more likely to encourage general obedience than this specific law; for nothing takes such a strong hold of the mind as the joy and gladness that spring from devotion—that is, from a combination of love and admiration. 

The people were not likely to be bored or disgusted by repetition and familiarity, because the festival days occurred only occasionally and the services appropriate to each were different. To these various considerations must be added the extreme reverence for the Temple which distinguished the Jewish people. This was created by the unique nature of their religious rites, as well as by the purification ceremonies they were bound to observe—which were always most religiously followed before venturing to present oneself within the sacred grounds. Even today, it is never without the greatest horror that a Jewish person reads of the wickedness of King Manasseh <note>A king of Judah (7th century BCE) who, according to the Bible, abandoned monotheism and placed pagan idols in the Temple.</note>, who dared to set up an idol in the Temple of the Lord. 

The popular reverence for the scroll of the Law, preserved within the innermost sanctuary, was no less intense. In such a state of affairs, popular discontent and distaste were never to be feared; for no one dared to form or express any opinion of their own on divine matters. All people alike were held bound to give unquestioning <note>original: "unreasoning"</note> assent and obedience to whatever was commanded by divine authority, as received in responses within the Temple, or as written and contained in the laws established by God. The first kings among the Jews were bound by the laws like common subjects, not raised above them; they could not legally abolish <note>original: "abrogate"</note> old laws, nor could they establish new ones that held the same authority as the old. 

Furthermore, the law of the Levites forbade kings and subjects alike from interfering with sacred matters, labeling such actions as "unclean" and "profane." Since the security of royal power essentially depended on the approval of another person—namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, the high priest, who was regarded as a prophet—it is obvious that there was a power in the state greater than that of the king. Consequently, the king necessarily reigned with an uncertain grip on power. 

We have evidence of this on several occasions. With what boldness, for instance, does Samuel the priest address and command King Saul? # CHAPTER XVIII.

## CONCERNING CERTAIN POLITICAL AXIOMS DERIVED FROM THE CONSTITUTION OF THE HEBREW REPUBLIC AND THE HISTORY OF THE JEWISH PEOPLE.

Although the Hebrew state, as described in the preceding chapter, could have lasted forever, it cannot be imitated today; nor indeed would it be desirable to do so. Anyone who wishes to transfer their rights to God must reach a clear understanding and agreement with God, just as the ancient Hebrews did. This requires not only the person’s own consent but also the consent of the Supreme Being to make the contract complete. 

However, God has revealed to humanity through the apostles that covenants with Him are no longer recorded in ink or engraved on stone tablets <note>original: "tables"</note>; instead, they are written by the Holy Spirit upon the heart. Furthermore, a political system <note>term: "polity"</note> like that of the ancient Hebrews might have suited them in their isolation in Judea, where they lived without trade or communication with the rest of the world. However, it would never be sufficient for modern nations that must engage in commerce with others. The constitution of the Hebrew state could only satisfy the needs of a very few nations.

# POLITICAL AXIOMS.

Once they had acquired the power to interfere in the business of the state and had combined princely roles with their proper priestly <note>original: "pontifical"</note> duties, each began to seek fame and reputation, not only within the sphere of his religious duties but beyond them. Wherever they could, they connected their names with state affairs. From this arose a clear desire to determine everything by priestly authority and to constantly issue decrees on subjects such as new ceremonies and new articles of faith. They intended for these to be held no less sacred, and with no less authority, than the laws of Moses. 

Because of this, religion eventually declined into a type of fitful <note>original: "spasmodic"</note> superstition, and the law became corrupted against all reason and sensible interpretation. To this, we must add that while the priesthood was paving the way to civil power at the beginning of the restoration <note>term: "the restoration" refers to the return of the Jewish people to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the Temple after the Babylonian exile</note>, they agreed to everything that could win the people to their side. They approved of the people's actions, even the most blameworthy, and twisted Scripture to align with all their immoralities. The prophet Malachi testifies to this shameful conduct in the most direct manner; attacking the priests of his day, he describes them as those who despise the name of God and continues with these words:

> “The priest’s lips should preserve knowledge, and the people should seek the law from his mouth; for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts. But you have departed from the way; you have caused many to stumble at the law; you have corrupted the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7, 8).

He goes on to accuse them of interpreting the laws arbitrarily and of having no respect for God, being swayed only by personal interests. It is certain, however, that the priests could never act so cautiously that they were not challenged in their innovations by some of the more clear-sighted and bold members of the community. These critics subsequently grew bolder and argued that no laws were binding except for those that were written. They contended that no other decrees were valid—specifically those that the Pharisees (who mostly rose from the common people) called the "traditions of the ancestors" <note>original: "traditions of the patriarchs"</note>.

# POLITICAL AXIOMS.

Once they changed the first form of their government to a monarchy and were ruled by kings, there was scarcely any end to the civil wars that followed. In these conflicts, battles were so bloody that the accounts of their cruelty almost surpass belief. In one battle, we read of 50,000 Israelites slain by the Judeans <note>The people of the southern Kingdom of Judah</note>; in another, by contrast, the Jews were slaughtered in vast numbers by the Israelites (though the Bible does not give the exact number of the slain). 

In this particular battle, the King of Judah was taken prisoner, the walls of Jerusalem were almost entirely demolished, and the Temple itself was stripped of all its treasures—as if to show that the victors placed no limits on their rage. Loaded with the spoils taken from their own brothers and satisfied by their blood, the Israelites finally agreed to take hostages. Leaving the king in his now-ruined empire, they sheathed their swords, feeling secure not because of Judah’s good faith, but because of its weakness. 

After only a few years, once the Judeans had rebuilt their strength, we find them again at war with the Israelites. The Israelites were again the victors, reportedly killing 120,000 Judeans and taking 200,000 women and children into captivity, along with an enormous amount of loot. Exhausted by these and other bloody wars (which the Bible mentions only briefly), the Hebrew nation as a whole was so weakened that it eventually became easy prey for foreign enemies.

When we examine the different periods in which the Hebrew people enjoyed the blessings of peace, we find a great difference between the various eras of their history. Often, before there were kings in Israel, we read of 40—and once (though this is highly improbable) 80—years passed happily without a foreign or civil war. But after the kings had seized supreme power, the goal was no longer peace and liberty, but rather glory and conquest. We read that all the kings, with the sole exception of Solomon—whose wisdom and interests were better suited to peace than war—were addicted to conflict. Added to this was the restless desire for power...

Kings, on the other hand, whose tempers are always equally prideful <note>original: "elate"</note> and who cannot yield without disgrace, cling stubbornly to every flaw in their system of rule; rather than bend, they would perish in the ruins of their country.

From what has just been stated, we see:

1. How disastrous it is both to religion and the state <note>original: "commonwealth"</note> to grant the ministers of religion the right to pass decrees or handle the business of the state. On the contrary, things go much more smoothly if the religious body is only heard on worldly affairs when their counsel is requested; their proper duty is to teach and to act in accordance with established ideas and accepted custom.

2. For a government is certainly a tyranny where opinions—which are the individual right of everyone and which no one can surrender by their own will—are regarded as crimes. Where such a state of things prevails, the rage of the multitude is usually found

4. Finally, we have seen how disastrous it was for a people who were not used to living under a monarchy <note>original: "kingly rule"</note>, and who already had established laws for their government, to be given the power to elect a king <note>original: "sovereign"</note>. The people could not handle such a heavy responsibility <note>original: "load of power"</note>, nor could the royal authority tolerate existing laws and privileges among the people that had been established by others with less authority than the king himself. Furthermore, a king could hardly be persuaded to sincerely defend these laws and privileges; this is because when they were first created, no one was thinking about a king, but only about the people or a council holding the highest power. 

A king who acted merely as a defender of the ancient rights and privileges of the community would look more like a servant than a master. Therefore, a new monarch would naturally focus on creating new laws and introducing reforms that benefit himself. He would try to put the people in a position where it would be harder for them to reduce the king’s power than it would be for him to expand it.

# POLITICAL AXIOMS.

If he wishes to be a true king and not have the people acting as his judges—if he wants submissive subjects and is not content to rule based on the unstable foundation <note>original: "slippery tenure"</note> of popular approval—he will avenge the death of the previous sovereign. By making examples of the leaders of the revolt, he will deter the people from committing such a crime again. However, he cannot effectively avenge his predecessor's death simply by killing any number of citizens, unless he also defends the predecessor's cause entirely, approves of his actions, and follows in his footsteps in every way. 

As a result, it has frequently happened that people change their tyrants but never succeed in getting rid of tyranny altogether; nor has a monarchy ever been permanently replaced by any other form of government in these cases. The people of England provided a memorable example of this fact when they deposed and, with a display of legal process <note>original: "show of justice"</note>, put their king <note>Charles I (1600–1649)</note> to death. Once the king was removed, they felt compelled to attempt a change in their form of government. However, after much bloodshed, disorder, and partisan disagreement, it resulted in a bold soldier <note>Oliver Cromwell (1599–1658)</note> being hailed as a new monarch under a different title—as if the entire issue had only been about names! 

But this arrangement could not possibly last. Soon after the death of the Protector, there seemed to be only one desire in the public mind: the restoration of the old royal family. The restoration was consequently carried out under the leadership <note>original: "auspices"</note> of another clever <note>original: "astute"</note> soldier <note>General George Monck (1608–1670)</note>, and England was once more officially ruled by a king, just as it had been in the past.*

<header>POLITICAL AXIOMS.</header>

At this point, however, someone might object by pointing out examples from Roman history where the people truly managed to get rid of their tyrants. However, I believe that any example cited from that history will actually confirm my view. Although the Roman people could remove a tyrant and change their form of government more easily than most—since they held the right to choose their kings and appoint successors, and had not yet become accustomed to long-term kingly rule—they still faced the same struggle. Even though they put to death three of their first six kings, they never accomplished more than replacing one tyrant with several. These new rulers kept the people miserably engaged in a constant series of foreign and domestic wars until, at length, the government reverted to a monarchy—merely under a different name—just as happened in England.

Regarding the States of Holland, as far as we know, they never had kings as rulers, but rather <term>counts</term> <note>original: "counts"; titles of nobility who acted as regional rulers</note>, who never actually held any kind of absolute sovereign right. The "High and Mighty States of Holland," in a document written during the time of the Earl of Leicester, explicitly declared that they have always kept the supreme authority in their own hands. They reserved the right and power to direct these counts in how they exercised their authority. Furthermore, to defend civil liberty and to free themselves from their officers should they degenerate into tyrants, they declared all the counts' acts and ordinances null and void unless they were reviewed and approved by the general council of the States. From this, it follows that supreme power has always belonged to the <term>States-General</term> <note>the representative assembly of the Dutch provinces</note>. When the last of the counts of Holland actually attempted to seize this power for himself, the people could not be said—

### CHAPTER XIX.

->**ALL AUTHORITY IN SACRED MATTERS RESTS EXCLUSIVELY WITH THE CIVIL POWER; AND RELIGIOUS WORSHIP MUST BE IN HARMONY WITH THE INSTITUTIONS OF THE STATE IF GOD IS TO BE RIGHTLY OBEYED.**<-

When I stated earlier that those entrusted with the administration of public affairs were the sole arbiters of what is right, and that all legislation depended on them, I did not intend for this to apply only to civil matters. I also meant it to apply to sacred matters. I maintain that the government of a country should also be the guardians and interpreters of these religious concerns. 

My purpose in this chapter is to reinforce this principle. Many people deny this right to civil rulers and refuse to acknowledge them as the interpreters of divine decrees <note>original: "decretals"; historically, these were papal letters or decrees that formulated decisions in church law</note>. Furthermore, these people take the liberty of condemning, vilifying, and even excommunicating their rulers from their position of religious authority <note>original: "ex cathedra"; literally "from the chair," referring to authoritative or dogmatic pronouncements made by a religious leader</note>, just as Saint Ambrose did to the Emperor Theodosius <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD) was the Bishop of Milan who famously forced the Roman Emperor Theodosius I to perform public penance, setting a precedent for church authority over secular rulers.</note>. 

However, I will show that such individuals seek opportunities to divide the state against itself and even to seize supreme power for themselves. First, I will demonstrate that a religious system only acquires the force of law through the decree of those who lead the state and hold the right to command. I will also show that God has no specific reign among humanity except through those who govern. Moreover, religious worship and pious practices should be organized in harmony with the peace and well-being of the commonwealth. Consequently, these matters are to

It is certain that devotion to one’s country is the highest virtue that can be shown. Without it, nothing good can remain; everything falls into confusion, and lawlessness <note>original: "licence"</note> and impiety take over, to the terror and harm of everyone. From this, it follows that nothing can be beneficial to an individual if it is bad in itself—that is, if it proves injurious to the community at large. On the contrary, no act can be wrong—it is actually absolutely good—if it is done for the benefit of the state <note>original: "commonwealth"</note>. 

For example, it has been considered a religious duty <note>original: "pious"</note> to give your coat to someone who attacks you and tries to steal your cloak. However, when this decision is judged by the standards of right and reason, and the action is seen to be harmful to the public as well as to the individual, it becomes an act of religious duty to bring the robber before a judge. This is done so that the criminal may be punished and the community protected. Manlius Torquatus <note>A Roman consul famous for his extreme discipline; he executed his own son for engaging the enemy against orders, even though the son won the skirmish.</note> is renowned because the safety of the republic was more important to him than pity and compassion for his own son. 

If this view is well-founded, it follows that the safety of the state is the supreme law <note>This refers to the Latin legal maxim: *Salus populi suprema lex esto* ("Let the safety of the people be the supreme law").</note>, to which all laws, both divine and human, must submit. But since it is the duty of the government to determine what is for the good of the whole community and necessary for the safety of the state—and to command those things to be done—it follows that it is also the responsibility of the supreme power alone to determine how every person should behave toward their neighbor. In other words, the state determines how every person is required to obey God. 

These considerations give us the key to a right understanding of how the ruling power of the state acts as the interpreter and regulator of its religious system. It also explains why no one can truly obey God if they do not align their religious observances with the public good, and consequently, if they do not obey the commands of the governing authority. ### CHAPTER XX.

#### IN A FREE STATE, EVERYONE IS FREE TO THINK WHAT THEY WISH AND TO SAY WHAT THEY THINK.

If ruling people’s thoughts were as easy as controlling their speech, rulers would always reign securely, and there would be no such thing as government by force. Everyone would then live according to the opinions of their governors, and by their decisions alone would decide what was good or bad, true or false, and just or unjust. But this is impossible, as has already been shown (Chapter XVII), since no one can yield their mind and understanding absolutely to another. No one can surrender—nor can they be forced to surrender—their natural right or ability to reason freely and to judge for themselves in certain matters. 

Consequently, any authority exerted over the mind is considered tyrannical. A ruler oppresses their subjects and appears to seize <note>original: "usurp"</note> their rights when they attempt to dictate what should be accepted as true or rejected as false, or what ideas should inspire devotion toward God. These are the natural and inalienable rights of all people. I admit, certainly, that a person’s judgment may be influenced <note>original: "preoccupied"</note> in so many incredible ways that, while it cannot be said to be directly under someone else's authority, it depends so entirely on their will that it almost seems to belong to them. However, despite everything that political cunning <note>original: "craft"</note> has been able to achieve in this area,

<page-num>343</page-num>

# FREEDOM OF THOUGHT AND SPEECH IMPERATIVE.

Things have never reached such a point that people have not felt they were their own masters regarding their judgment and emotions, or that there was not as great a diversity of opinions as there is of tastes in the world. Even Moses—who secured the confidence of his nation in a remarkable way, not through deceit or trickery <note>original: "craft or guile"</note> but by the divine power within him—could not escape the suspicious and hostile interpretations of the common people <note>original: "multitude"</note>, even though he was believed to be more than mortal and to speak and act under the inspiration of God <note>original: "Deity"</note>. It was even harder for the rulers who came after Moses to avoid suspicion. If it were possible under any circumstances for rulers to escape suspicion, it would certainly be in a monarchy; in a democracy, it is clearly impossible, for reasons that I assume must be obvious to everyone.

Therefore, although the ruling powers are considered to have a right to everything and to be the interpreters of law and religion, this can never prevent people from having their own views on things in general, or from being influenced by this or that opinion or emotion. It is true, indeed, that governments may legally <note>original: "rightfully"</note> treat all those who do not think or feel as they do as enemies; but we are not currently discussing legal rights, we are speaking only of what is practical <note>original: "useful"</note>. I acknowledge that rulers <note>original: "princes"</note> often exercise their right through extreme violence and sentence citizens to death for very minor reasons; however, everyone would agree that such things cannot be done while any regard is shown for sound reason. Because such actions cannot be carried out without great danger to the state, we can also argue that rulers have no true right to commit such acts, and consequently, no absolute right at all. As we have shown, the rights of ruling powers are determined by their actual capacity to enforce obedience.

Therefore, since no one can surrender their right to judge and to think as they please <note>original: "lists"</note>, and because everyone is, by the supreme law of nature, the master of their own thoughts, it follows that any attempt to force all people to speak the same way will have disastrous consequences for the state <note>original: "commonwealth"</note>. This is true even though people are naturally possessed by the most varied and even opposite sentiments; they cannot be forced to utter—

...not a word, except by the command of their governors; for not even the most cautious and educated—let alone the common people—will be able to hold their tongues at all times. Indeed, it is one of the most common human weaknesses that people share their views and opinions with others even when silence is most necessary. A government <note>original: "regimen"</note> would therefore be of the most oppressive kind if all freedom of speech and public discussion were denied. Conversely, a government is moderate where such freedom is granted to everyone. 

Nevertheless, it is undeniable that the authority of the state may be attacked by words as well as deeds. Since freedom of speech cannot be completely denied to subjects, it would be very problematic if such freedom were granted without any limits. It is therefore necessary to inquire to what extent freedom of speech can and should be allowed while still maintaining the peace of the state <note>original: "commonwealth"</note> and the rights of those in power. As I stated at the beginning of my sixteenth chapter, this inquiry is a central goal of my work.

Based on the foundations of the state already explained, it clearly follows that its purpose is not to dominate or to coerce people through fear, nor is it intended to make them act according to the arbitrary will of others. On the contrary, its purpose is to ensure that everyone is free from fear and can live securely as far as possible—that is, that they may fully enjoy their natural right to exist and to benefit from their own hard work. The goal of the state is not to turn rational beings into mindless animals or **automata** <note>original: "autómatons"</note>. On the contrary, its goal is to allow their minds and bodies to function unimpeded, to ensure that everyone can freely use their reason, and to put an end to hatred, anger, deception, and conflict among its citizens. In fact, the ultimate goal of the state is **LIBERTY**. 

However, to establish a governed <note>original: "policied"</note> state or commonwealth, we have seen that one condition was essential: namely, that the right and authority to pass laws must belong to all citizens collectively, to a small group of them, or to a single individual. For since...

<summary>This page argues that because humans are naturally inclined to speak their minds, a stable government must allow freedom of speech. It concludes that the true purpose of a state is not to instill fear, but to protect the natural rights and liberty of its citizens so they may live by reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 344 regarding the limits of state power over the individual. <page-num>345</page-num>

# FREEDOM OF THOUGHT AND SPEECH IMPERATIVE.

...Since the opinions of free people are so diverse, and each person commonly believes that they alone know what is best, it is impossible for everyone to think alike on any subject or to speak with a single voice. Consequently, it would be impossible for people to live together in peace unless each individual gave up the right to act solely according to the decision of their own mind. While the right to act on one’s own judgment ceases in a society, this applies only to physical actions—not to the right of reasoning and judging. 

Because the authority of the government must be respected, no one may take any action that goes against its laws <note>original: "decrees"</note>. However, everyone is free to think and judge for themselves and, by extension, to express their views. This is permitted as long as the person expresses themselves simply and rationally, without anger, malice, or deceptive intent, and does not craftily attempt to force their own private views over the general consensus. 

For example, if someone can demonstrate that a certain law is contrary to common sense and argues that it should therefore be repealed <note>original: "abrogated"</note>, while simultaneously submitting their views to the government (which holds the exclusive right to make and repeal laws) and doing nothing to break that law in the meantime, that person deserves credit from the state <note>original: "republic"</note> and is a good citizen. 

On the other hand, if their purpose is to accuse the authorities <note>original: "magistracy"</note> of injustice and make the government hated by the people, or if they rebelliously <note>original: "seditiously"</note> seek to overturn a law against the will of the ruling power, they must be considered a disturber of the public peace and a rebel. 

We see, then, how a person can speak and make their views known while still respecting the rights and authority of the government—that is, the peace of the state <note>original: "commonwealth"</note>. This is achieved if the individual leaves the final decision of what should be done to those in power and takes no personal action against their laws. This remains true even if the citizen must occasionally act in opposition to what they personally believe is right, or do what they clearly see should not be done. A person can submit to this without violating their integrity; indeed, they may occasionally have to do so if they wish to prove themselves a loyal and peaceable subject...

<summary>This page argues that while citizens must surrender their right to act independently to maintain social peace, they must retain the right to think and reason. A good citizen may argue for the repeal of laws they find irrational, provided they continue to obey those laws and respect the government's ultimate authority.</summary>
<keywords>freedom of speech, social contract, civil obedience, rule of law, dissent, citizenship, Spinoza, political philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the duties of a citizen within a state. It completes the sentence from the previous page, defining a "valuable citizen" and explaining why obeying the law is both a pious and rational act, while defining what truly constitutes seditious speech.</meta>

<page-num>346</page-num>

# FREEDOM OF THOUGHT AND SPEECH IMPERATIVE.

...able citizen. We have already shown that since justice depends entirely on the decisions of the supreme authorities, no one can be truly just or pious unless they live in accordance with those authorities' commands. In fact, the highest form of piety is that which is directed toward securing the peace and prosperity of the state <note>original: "republic"</note>. These benefits could not be maintained if every person chose to live according to their own personal whims. Therefore, it is a crime for a subject to act against the decree of the supreme power on their own initiative, because the ruin of the state would inevitably follow if everyone allowed themselves such lawlessness <note>original: "licence"</note>. 

Furthermore, a person does nothing against the requirements of reason when they act in conformity with the decrees of the state's supreme authority. This is because, guided by reason, they have already surrendered <note>original: "ceded"</note> the right to live according to their own private judgment to their rulers. 

This reality can be confirmed by looking at experience. In the legislative bodies <note>original: "councils of the greater as well as of the less estates of a realm"</note>, it rarely happens that any resolution is passed by the unanimous consent of the members. Nevertheless, every action is considered to be done by common consent; this applies to those who voted *against* the resolution just as much as those who voted *for* it. But I return to my subject.

We have seen from the way a state is constituted how every person may use their right of private judgment within the limits of reason without harming the rights of the ruling powers. Based on these same principles—the very foundations of the state—we can easily determine which opinions are seditious. Seditious opinions are those that, by their very expression, work to nullify the social contract in which every person surrendered the right to act on their own private views. 

For example, if someone were to maintain that the supreme state power did not exist independently or by its own right, or that promises should never be kept, or that everyone should live however they desired without regard for others, they are promoting ideas that the aforementioned contract directly rejects. Such a person is seditious, not so much because of their private views and opinions, but because of the actions that such views and opinions involve.

<summary>This page argues that true piety and reason require citizens to obey state laws, as the social contract demands the subordination of individual whims to the collective peace. It defines sedition as the expression of ideas that fundamentally undermine the legal and social foundations of the community.</summary>

<keywords>social contract, justice, piety, supreme power, state authority, sedition, private judgment, common consent, civil obedience</keywords>

<page-num>347</page-num>

<header>FREEDOM OF THOUGHT AND SPEECH IMPERATIVE. 347</header>

...namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, because in the fact that he thinks as he does, he either explicitly or implicitly <note>original: "expressly or tacitly"</note> breaks his promise to the supreme authority. It is for this reason that other mental states which do not involve any breach of the political contract <note>The theoretical agreement where citizens trade some freedoms for state protection</note>—such as anger, revenge, and so on—are not considered seditious. Such passions, indeed, only become dangerous in corrupt states where reason is distorted, and where superstition and personal ambition have gained such power that they have more influence among the people than the government does. 

I would not, however, deny that there are other opinions which, while they seem only to concern what is true or false, are nevertheless proposed and spread with malicious intent. But these have already been discussed in Chapter 15, where we have shown that reason nevertheless remains free. Furthermore, if we consider that loyalty to the state—just like faith in God—can be known only by a person's actions (such as charity toward neighbors and similar deeds), we shall have no reason to doubt that the best republic <note>original: "republica," referring to a well-ordered state</note> grants the same rights to philosophy as we have shown are granted to the religious faith of its members. 

I admit, indeed, that several problems <note>original: "inconveniences"</note> arise from such liberty; but was anything ever so wisely organized that no trouble could follow from it? Anyone who tries to regulate and control everything by law will provoke the world’s vices rather than correcting them. What cannot be prevented must be tolerated, even though harm often results from it. For how many are the evils that follow from luxury, envy, greed, drunkenness, and the like? Yet these, though they are vices, are endured because they cannot be prevented by legal decrees. 

But freedom of opinion—which is a positive virtue and which cannot be controlled anyway—should be encouraged all the more. When we see that no problem can arise from such freedom that cannot be immediately addressed by the authority of the magistrate <note>A civil officer or judge who administers the law</note> (as I shall soon show), and that it is essentially necessary for progress in the arts and sciences—which are only successfully cultivated where the mind is free and unrestricted—I think enough has been said to show the supreme importance of freedom of thought and freedom of opinion in every well-ordered commonwealth <note>A state or independent community</note>.

<summary>This page argues that while states must regulate actions, they should not attempt to control thoughts or opinions, as free inquiry is essential for the progress of the arts, sciences, and a healthy society.</summary>

Suppose that this freedom could be suppressed, and men so oppressed that they dared not even whisper anything except what was permitted or dictated by rulers. Even then, things could never reach such a state that subjects would not have their own thoughts. It would then inevitably follow that men would daily think one thing and say another. Consequently, trust <note>original: "faith"</note> in the commonwealth, which is so essential, would be destroyed. Hateful betrayal <note>original: "perfidy"</note> and brown-nosing <note>original: "sycophancy"</note> would be encouraged, leading to cunning, deception, and the corruption of all kind and social feelings. 

However, it is far from possible for men to be forced to speak only within certain prescribed limits. In fact, history shows that the more strictly freedom of speech is denied, the more resolutely people struggle against the restraint. This resistance does not come from flatterers and sycophants, nor from the other weak-willed spirits of the world whose main goal in life is to live in the shadow of the powerful, to possess titles and honors, and to have money in their purses and full bellies. Rather, it comes from those whom a refined <note>original: "liberal"</note> education and integrity of life have made truly free. 

Generally, people are naturally built so that they find nothing more intolerable than to see opinions they believe to be true treated as crimes. They hate seeing the values that move them to devotion toward God and kindness toward man labeled as wickedness. Because of this, such laws are detested. Whatever can be dared <note>original: "adventured"</note> against authority is seen not as shameful or wrong, but as brave and praiseworthy—a mindset that is soon followed by rebellion <note>original: "sedition"</note>, riot, and revolution. 

Since human nature is built this way, it follows that laws against opinion do not affect the worthless, but rather the virtuous. Such laws seem designed not to restrain the wicked, but to provoke the honest and respectable. Therefore, these laws cannot be defended or enforced without great danger to the public peace. Furthermore, they are completely useless. Those who believe the opinions condemned by the law are true will be unable to obey it; and those, on the contrary, who reject these opinions as...

Men have never fought with such bitterness, nor surrendered to such deadly passion and committed such cold-blooded acts of cruelty, as when they succeeded in making governments their partisans in matters of faith and doctrine. This is shown clearly by repeated experience, and reason also dictates that it must be so. 

Laws that decree what everyone must believe and forbid anyone from speaking against certain opinions have too often been enacted only to protect or increase the power of those who did not dare allow free investigation <note>original: "suffer free inquiry"</note>. By a misuse of authority, they have turned the superstition of the mob into violence against their rivals. But surely it would be more reasonable to take measures to restrain the rage and fury of the multitude, rather than to make laws that can only be broken by those who love virtue, the arts, and the sciences. Such laws bring the state <note>original: "commonwealth"</note> into such difficult straits that intelligent people cannot endure them. 

For what greater evil can be imagined for a state than that honorable men—men who live the most virtuous lives—should be driven into exile because they hold unique views on philosophical matters <note>original: "speculation"</note> and do not know how to hide their true feelings <note>original: "dissemble"</note>? If they do not flee, they face even worse treatment: the dungeon, or perhaps even the stake <note>original: "execution by fire"</note>! What, I say, can be more detestable <note>original: "execrable"</note> than for men to be regarded as criminals for no crime or wickedness, but simply because they have an independent <note>original: "liberal"</note> mind? It is a tragedy when the scaffold, which should be the terror of evildoers, becomes a stage for the display of courage and endurance on the part of...

<meta>This page concludes the argument that persecuting virtuous people for their beliefs creates martyrs and undermines the law, transitioning into a discussion on why freedom of opinion is essential for a stable democracy and the "natural state" of humanity.</meta>

<page-num>350</page-num>

<header>FREEDOM OF THOUGHT AND SPEECH IMPERATIVE.</header>

...suffering virtue, to the infinite scandal of all law and authority! These men know they are sincere; they do not fear death like common criminals, and they would rather suffer the most extreme punishment than degrade themselves by hiding or denying <note>original: "gainsaying"</note> their opinions. Their minds are never tortured by remorse for any shameful or wicked act. On the contrary, they still see themselves as honest men, and they do not view it as a tragedy to die for a good and glorious cause. What example is set by the death of such men—whose cause the careless and unethical ignore, the tyrant hates, and the good and great admire? It is an example that the truly noble will always seek to follow and praise.*

Therefore, so that trust and confidence may prevail instead of deception <note>original: "dissimulation"</note> and mere compliance, and so that the sovereign power may rule in the most beneficial way for everyone—without ever feeling forced to give in to rebellious protests <note>original: "seditious clamour"</note>—freedom of opinion must necessarily be granted. People must be governed in such a way that, even though they openly think differently from one another, they can still live together in peace and friendship. There can be no doubt that this method of governing is the best, as it is most in harmony with human nature.

In a democracy (which comes closest to the natural state), we have shown that everyone agrees to act according to a shared arrangement, though they do not agree to reason or judge on shared grounds. Because it is impossible for all people to think alike, they have agreed to abide by the decision of the majority. Thus, whatever the majority decides has the force of law for everyone, while the minority meanwhile keeps the right to propose the repeal of that law at some future time. In places where people are granted less liberty, there is a greater departure from the natural state, and consequently, the government must be more restrictive <note>original: "stringent"</note>. I could quote many examples to show that no inconvenience arises...

<page-num>351</page-num>

<header>FREEDOM OF THOUGHT AND SPEECH IMPERATIVE.</header>

...no danger is likely to arise from this liberty that cannot be addressed and managed by the authority of the government, and that people, though they hold opposite opinions, may live in peace with one another. I shall select the city of Amsterdam as a sufficient example for my purpose. Here, the fruits of this liberty of thought and opinion are seen in the city's wonderful growth and are praised by every nation. In this most flourishing republic and noble city, people of every nation, faith, and sect live together in the utmost harmony. In their business transactions with one another, the only questions asked are whether the parties are rich or poor, and whether they are accustomed <note>original: "wont"</note> to act in good faith or not. There is never a question of religion or creed, for in the presence of a judge, these have no part in the proceedings and neither protect nor condemn a person. Here, there is no sect, however disliked or despised, whose ministers do not find support and protection from the government <note>original: "magistrate"</note>, provided they do no harm to anyone, give everyone their due, and live respectably. 

In contrast to this, consider what happened in earlier times when the religious controversies of the Remonstrants and Counter-remonstrants <note>The Remonstrants and Counter-remonstrants were rival theological factions in the Dutch Reformed Church in the early 1600s. Their dispute over predestination led to a major political crisis in the Netherlands.</note> were taken up by politicians and the nobility. After much discord, the result was a schism <note>original: "schism"; a formal split or division within a group or church.</note>. It was then discovered from many instances that laws made on behalf of religion—intended to reduce controversy—actually made the strife worse rather than calming it. Such laws became the cause of lawlessness and misdeeds rather than order and good conduct. 

Moreover, a schism does not always arise from a sincere study of truth—which is the source of humanity and gentleness—but often from a desire for power <note>original: "lust of dominion"</note>. From this, it is as clear as the sun at noonday that the real "schismatics" are those who condemn the writings of their opponents and unfairly stir up the uneducated masses <note>original: "unlettered vulgar"</note> against the authors. This is far more true of those critics than of the writers themselves, who mostly write only for the learned and make no appeal except to reason and calm reflection. Therefore, the true disturbers of the state are those who, in a free commonwealth, refuse to allow that liberty of opinion which cannot be suppressed.

<summary>Using Amsterdam as a model, the author argues that religious tolerance leads to economic prosperity and social harmony, while government attempts to regulate religious thought only cause civil unrest.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the argument that freedom of thought and speech is essential for a stable society, summarizing the main points of the preceding chapters and warning against the dangers of religious interference in civil law.</meta>

<page-num>352</page-num>

<header>FREEDOM OF THOUGHT AND SPEECH IS IMPERATIVE.</header>

In the preceding pages, I hope I have shown the following:

1.  That it is impossible to strip people of the freedom to say what they think.
2.  That this freedom can be granted to everyone without affecting the rights and privileges of the sovereign authority <note>original: "supreme power"</note>. Furthermore, everyone can exercise this freedom while respecting that same authority, as long as care is taken not to turn this freedom into lawlessness <note>original: "licence"</note>, not to force new laws onto the state, and to do nothing against established laws.
3.  That everyone may enjoy this freedom while keeping the peace of the republic sacred, and that any inconvenience arising from it can be easily addressed and prevented.
4.  That everyone may enjoy this same freedom with full respect for piety and religion.
5.  That laws created to regulate theoretical or abstract beliefs <note>original: "speculative matters"</note> are useless.
6.  Finally, that freedom of thought and speech is not only consistent with the peace of the state, the authority of its government, and the maintenance of its religious institutions, but is actually necessary for their safety and preservation. 

Whenever an attempt is made to take this freedom away—when the opinions of debaters are put on trial rather than their intentions <note>original: "minds"</note> (which are the only things capable of sin)—the best and most noble people are inevitably made into examples. These individuals are then viewed as martyrs; their punishment irritates the nation and moves the people to pity or even revenge, rather than to fear. 

As a result, peaceful arts and mutual trust disappear. Flatterers and hypocrites are encouraged. Dogmatism <note>Rigidly following a set of rules or beliefs without question.</note> begins to claim authority for itself because concessions have been made to it, and because rulers have taken sides in religious disputes. These dogmatists then shamelessly boast that they are the "elect of God" and the direct interpreters of His divine decrees. They argue that the civil government, being merely human, should be forced to yield to the divine—in other words, to them and their decisions. Everyone knows that such a situation is completely incompatible with the peace and prosperity of a well-ordered state.

<summary>This page summarizes the author's argument that freedom of speech and thought are not only harmless to the state but essential for its survival, preventing the rise of religious extremism and social unrest.</summary>
<keywords>freedom of speech, liberty of thought, sovereign authority, religious dogmatism, martyrdom, civil power, state peace</keywords>

<page-num>353</page-num>
<header>FREEDOM OF THOUGHT AND SPEECH IS IMPERATIVE.</header>
<sig>23</sig>

Therefore, in this place and once again—as I have already argued in Chapter 18—we conclude that there is nothing safer for the public welfare <term>common weal</term> than for religious devotion and faith to be centered entirely on the practice of charity and justice. Furthermore, the authority of the government, regarding both sacred and secular <note>original: "lay"</note> affairs, should be limited only to people's actions. As for everything else, the freedom to think as they please and to say what they think should be granted to everyone without restriction.

And now I have completed what I had proposed for myself in this formal study <note>original: "Treatise"</note>. I have only to add that I have written nothing which I have not most carefully considered and submitted to the chief authorities of my native country. However, if anything that I have said violates the law or seems opposed to the common good, I would have it challenged and corrected. I am fully aware that I am only human and prone to making mistakes, but I have taken great pains not to fail. I have been especially anxious that everything I have written should be found consistent with the laws of my country, with religious duty, and with moral conduct.

->THE END <note>original: "FINIS"</note><-

# APPENDIX.

***

The Editor cannot resist the desire to introduce the reader to the following appropriate and characteristic letter by Spinoza. It was written in response to a hostile criticism of this work, which a mutual friend of the critic and Spinoza had sent to him. This translation is somewhat free <note>The editor suggests it is not a literal word-for-word translation</note> to enhance the pleasure the Editor himself experienced in translating it into English, and for the sake of the reader; however, I believe there is no expression here that Spinoza’s views do not justify, and which he would not have allowed to pass. The original is Letter 49 <note>original: "Epist. 49"</note> of the *Posthumous Works* <note>original: "Op. Posth." or "Opera Posthuma"</note>.

***

<margin>* Isaac Orobio, M.D., a Jewish physician of Amsterdam.</margin>

->*Spinoza to Isaac Orobio <note>original: "I. O."</note>*<-

> “Distinguished Sir,
>
> “You are undoubtedly surprised that I have kept you waiting so long for a reply to your last letter. In truth, it is with difficulty that I have brought myself to notice the libelous letter <note>original: "libellous epistle"</note> you enclosed; indeed, I only write now to fulfill my promise to answer it. To remain as true as possible to my own principles <note>original: "do as little violence as possible to my proper sentiments"</note>, I shall be brief. I will content myself with showing how your correspondent misrepresents <note>original: "falsifies"</note> both my views and my intentions—whether he does so intentionally and out of spite, or through ignorance, I cannot easily say. But to the matter at hand.

> “Your correspondent says at the beginning of his letter, ‘That it is of no consequence to know to what people I belong, or what manner of life I lead.’ If he had been properly informed on both these points, he would not have so easily concluded that I teach atheism <note>original: "inculcate atheism"</note>. Atheists, for the most part, are worldly people <note>original: "wordlings"</note> who seek eagerly after wealth and fame; yet everyone who knows me is aware that I have always held these things in very little regard. He then chooses to say that ‘I must be a man of no average ability,’ apparently for the purpose of sharpening his next assertion: that ‘I have, at best, skillfully, craftily, and with the worst intentions, defended the fundamentally bad and harmful <note>original: "pernicious"</note> cause of the Deists <note>Deists: people who believe in a God who created the universe but does not interfere with it, relying on reason rather than revelation</note>.’ This in itself is enough to show that the writer has not understood my arguments. For who could possibly be so crafty and hypocritical as to present a series of the most persuasive and convincing arguments in favor of a conclusion which he himself believed to be false? Of whom would your correspondent believe that truth and sincerity guided their pen, if he thought that falsehood in disguise could be enforced with the same straightforwardness of purpose as truth itself? But, indeed, I ought not to be surprised here; for even in this same way was Descartes slandered by Voet <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676) was a Dutch Calvinist theologian who famously attacked the philosopher René Descartes</note>. This is how the best men in the world are usually met by their opponents.

> “The writer next goes on to say, ‘It seems as though I had thought it necessary to strip away all religion just to avoid the suspicion of being superstitious.’ I do not claim to guess what he means by religion and what by superstition in this context, but I ask: Does a person cast off religion when they base everything they have to say on the fact that God is to be recognized as the Supreme Good? When they say He is to be loved as such with total sincerity of soul? And that our greatest happiness, our highest privilege, and our most perfect freedom consist in loving God? Furthermore, that the reward of virtue is virtue itself, and the penalty for weakness and immorality <note>original: "baseness"</note> is ignorance and a wretched spirit? Moreover, that everyone is required to love their neighbor as themselves, and to obey the laws and authorities of the land where they live? Now, I have not only emphasized all of this as powerfully as I could in words, but I have also provided the most persuasive arguments I could find to support my conclusions.

> “But I think I can see the source of my critic’s hostility…”
