This person finds nothing in a virtuous life or in right reason themselves that satisfies or delights him; it seems as though he would rather live under the rule of his passions, yielding to his appetites and lusts, if it were not for one consideration that holds him back—the fear of punishment. He must keep himself from doing wrong <note>original: "doing amiss"</note> like a slave; he cannot follow the divine commandments of his own free will, but instead cowers before them with a confused and unsatisfied soul. He tries to strike a bargain with the Almighty, and in exchange for good behavior, he looks for a much larger and more tangible <note>original: "sensible," meaning perceptible by the senses</note> reward than he expects to find in divine love. Indeed, he expects a greater reward the more he feels an inward aversion to doing good, as he reluctantly and by force compels himself to perform whatever good he actually does. This is the basis of his belief: that anyone not restrained by the same fear he feels must surely live without any check on their lusts and cast religion out of their hearts. But I will leave this unpleasant topic and proceed to the conclusions of my critic <note>original: "censor"</note>, and to this one in particular: that "I, with deceptive <note>original: "glozing"</note> and crafty arguments, instill <note>original: "inculcate"</note> Atheism."

> “The basis for this conclusion seems to be his thought that I strip God of all freedom and subject the Supreme Being to fate. This is utterly false; I do nothing of the sort. On the contrary, I maintain that everything follows by inevitable necessity from the very nature of God. It is universally admitted that God, by His very nature, knows Himself, and that this knowledge follows necessarily from the divine nature; yet I assume no one thinks that God is therefore controlled by fate. On the contrary, all reasonable people believe that God knows Himself both freely and necessarily at the same time. In fact, freedom and necessity are synonymous terms when the nature of the Deity is concerned: God, as the creator of all, is Himself fate, freedom, and necessity. In this I can see nothing which everyone may not understand, and nothing which anyone can find fault with. But if my critic nevertheless believes that what I say is said with an evil intention, what, I would ask, must he think of his own Descartes <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher whose ideas Spinoza often engaged with</note>, who maintains that nothing happens through our own actions that God has not already pre-ordained? Indeed, Descartes claims that in every moment of our lives we are, in a sense, created anew by God, and yet we still act freely according to the power given to us—a state of affairs which Descartes himself admits is completely incomprehensible.

> “The necessity of things for which I argue does not abolish <note>original: "abrogates"</note> either

<summary>Spinoza defends himself against charges of atheism by arguing that God’s nature involves both freedom and necessity, noting that his critic’s own preferred philosopher, Descartes, held even more paradoxical views on divine pre-ordination.</summary>
<keywords>Spinoza, Descartes, God, free will, necessity, fate, atheism, divine nature, punishment, virtue</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Spinoza’s letter defending his philosophical work, specifically answering the charge that his belief in "necessity" (the idea that everything happens by the nature of God) undermines morality and the need for divine commandments.</meta>

<page-num>357</page-num>

-> # APPENDIX. <-

...divine or human laws. The moral precepts—whether they take the form of commandments from God or not—are still divine and beneficial <note>original: "salutary"</note>. Furthermore, the good that comes from virtue and godly love is no less desirable, whether it is received from God acting as a ruler and lawgiver, or if it arises from the essential nature <note>original: "constitution," meaning the inherent necessity</note> of the Divine Nature itself. On the other hand, the evils resulting from wickedness are not less to be feared and mourned just because they follow naturally from the actions performed. Finally, whether we act out of free will or out of necessity, we are always accompanied by hope or fear in everything we do.

Therefore, my critic <note>original: "censor"</note> falsely claims that I place the question of morals and religion on such a footing that commands and instructions are no longer recognized. Or, as he puts it: "That there can be no expectation of reward and no fear of punishment if everything is subject to fate or follows by necessity from the nature of God."

Here I will not stop to ask whether it is the same thing, or something very different, to maintain that everything happens necessarily from the nature of God versus holding that the Universe is God. However, I ask you to notice how the critic offensively <note>original: "odiously"</note> and unjustifiably adds that "I intend <note>original: "am minded"</note> for people to lead virtuous lives not because of the instructions and commands of God, or moved by the hope of reward or fear of punishment, but," etc. In the whole of my treatise <note>original: "Tractate," referring to Spinoza’s *Theological-Political Treatise*</note>, I assert <note>original: "aver"</note> that you will find no such statement. 

On the contrary, I expressly declare (see <note>original: "vide," Latin for "see"</note> Chapter IV) that the core of the divine law—the law written on our hearts and minds by the hand of God (see <note>original: "vide"</note> Chapter II)—consists primarily in this: that we love God as our supreme good. We should do this not through fear of punishment (for love knows nothing of fear and cannot come from fear), nor even out of love for something else we might wish to enjoy, but entirely and solely out of devotion to the Supreme Being. If this were not the rule, we would be loving God less than the thing we desired. 

I have further shown in that same passage that this is the very law that God revealed to the prophets. If I now maintain that this law takes its character as a "commandment" from God, or if I understand it the same way I understand God's other decrees—as involving an eternal truth and an eternal necessity in itself—it still remains an ordinance of the Almighty and is a doctrine wholesome to humanity. Likewise, whether I love God of my own free will or by the necessity of a divine decree,

<summary>Spinoza defends his philosophy against the charge of atheism, arguing that moral laws and the love of God remain essential and "divine" even if they arise from the necessity of God's nature rather than from a traditional lawgiver.</summary>

<page-num>358</page-num>
<header>APPENDIX.</header>

I still love the Creator and find myself blessed. Therefore, I could reasonably maintain that this critic belongs to that class of men I mentioned at the end of my preface. I said there that I would much rather they left my book unread than have them provide perverse interpretations of its views; by doing so, they gain no benefit from reading it themselves and only prove to be hindrances to others who might have profited from its contents.

“Although I believe I have already said enough to explain my views and answer my critic <note>original: "censor"</note>, I still think it is worth making a few further observations. I say, then, that he is mistaken when he imagines I was following that established principle <note>original: "axiom"</note> of theological writers which draws a distinction between the formal religious teachings <note>original: "dogmatic doctrine"</note> and the simple storytelling <note>original: "narrative discourse"</note> of a prophet. If he really understands what I say in my 15th chapter, when I quote Rabbi Judah Alpakhar, how could he believe that I agreed with the Rabbi? In that chapter, I was actually busy pointing out the errors in his conclusions. If my critic intended any other principle than the one I referred to, then I admit that I am not familiar with it and therefore could not have been following it.

“Furthermore, I cannot see why my critic should say I believed that ‘all would agree with my views who deny that reason and philosophy are the proper interpreters of Scripture.’ In fact, I have pointedly rejected those conclusions, as well as the people who dismiss reason entirely—such as Maimonides [who tries to reconcile Scripture with reason by arbitrarily twisting <note>original: "torturing"</note> the text into whatever shape he desires].

“It would take too long to list everything argued by my critic in which I can see he does not approach his task with a fully confident spirit. Therefore, I proceed at once to the passage where he says that ‘I have no grounds for my opinion that Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> was not a true prophet.’ He strangely tries to prove this singular conclusion of his by using the general statements and opinions I proposed, despite the fact that everything I say about Muhammad plainly shows I regard him as an impostor. This is because he denies throughout the Quran <note>original: "Koran"</note> that very liberty which the universal religion—revealed by natural reason as well as by prophetic insight—allows: the right to worship God in spirit and in truth. I have maintained that this right must be granted to mankind under all circumstances. And had I happened not to have done so, I would ask whether I were

<meta>This page concludes Spinoza’s letter defending his "Tractatus Theologico-Politicus." He addresses accusations of atheism and expands on his view that salvation is available to those outside the Christian faith who act with love and justice.</meta>

<page-num>359</page-num>
<header>APPENDIX.</header>

Am I really bound to prove that everyone who spoke like an oracle was a false prophet? The prophets of the Old Testament were required to prove they were true prophets—and this was done not only through signs, but also through the excellence of their teachings. If I am answered by the claim that Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> taught divine principles and gave reliable signs of his mission, then my critic himself would have no reason to deny that Muhammad was a true prophet.

<margin>*</margin>
> "Regarding the 'Turks' <note>A term commonly used in the 17th century to refer to Muslims or the people of the Ottoman Empire.</note> and other nations outside the bounds of Christianity, I freely admit my belief that if they worship God in love and truth and act justly toward their neighbors, they possess within themselves the equivalent of the Spirit of Christ. Their salvation is certain, regardless of whatever ideas they might ignorantly hold regarding Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> and his revelations.

> "You can see, therefore, my dear friend, that my critic misses the truth by a wide margin. Yet I also perceive that he does me far less injustice than he does himself when he dares to claim that I 'promote atheism through hidden tricks and deceptive <note>original: "glozing"</note> arguments.'

> "In closing, I hope that you do not find anything in the preceding pages to be too harsh, or anything that my critic <note>original: "censor"</note> did not fully deserve. However, if you find anything of that sort, I ask you to cross it out, or soften and change it however you see fit. It is not my intention to upset or irritate him, whoever he may be; nor is it my goal, in my desire to remain in your good graces, to make even a single enemy elsewhere. Indeed, since such negative criticisms are common enough, I would hardly have bothered to reply to this particular one—as I mentioned at the start of my letter—if I hadn't promised you that I would. Farewell! I leave this letter to your good judgment <note>original: "prudence"</note>, and ask you to believe that I am yours, etc.,

->“B. DE SPINOZA.”<-

Professor Newman <note>Francis William Newman, a prominent scholar and brother of Cardinal John Henry Newman</note> has kindly permitted Mr. Chapman to print the following letter addressed to him:—

> "Mr. Leigh Hunt's little book has been very acceptable to me. I think there is in it all that tenderness of wisdom which is the peculiar possession and honor of advanced years. I presume he regards his book as only a *contribution* to the Church of the Future, and the liturgical part of it as a mere sample. I feel with him that we cannot afford to abandon the old principle of a 'public recognition of common religious sentiments;' and I rejoice that one like him has taken the lead in pointing out the direction in which we must look.
> (Signed) F. W. NEWMAN."

> "To the class of thinkers who are also feelers—to those whose soul is larger than mere logic can grasp, and who habitually endeavor, on the wings of Imagination, to soar into regions which transcend reason—this beautiful book is addressed. . . . It cannot be read even as a book (and not accepting it as a ritual) without humanizing and enlarging the reader's mind."—*Leader.*

> "The 'Religion of the Heart' is a manual of aspiration, faith, and duty, conceived in the spirit of natural piety. . . . It is the object of the book to supply one of those needs of the popular mind which speculative rationalism is apt to neglect: to aid in the culture of sound habits and of reasonable religious affections. If the time has not yet arrived for the matured ritual of natural religion, the present endeavor will at least be regarded as a suggestion and help in that direction."—*Westminster Review.*

> "This volume deserves to be read by many to whom, on other grounds, it may perhaps prove little acceptable, for the grave and thoughtful matter it contains, appealing to the heart of every truthful person. . . . Kindly emotions and a pure morality, a true sense of the beneficence of God and of the beauty of creation, a heightened sensibility that shuns all contact with theology, and shrinks only with too much dread from the hard dogmas of the pulpit—make up the substance of this book, of which the style throughout is exquisitely gentle and refined. . . . Mr. Hunt never, on any occasion, discredits, by his manner of stating his beliefs, the comprehensive charity which sustains them. The most rigidly orthodox may read his book, and, passing over diversities of opinion, expressed always in

->THEISM, ATHEISM, AND THE POPULAR THEOLOGY.<-
Sermons by THEODORE PARKER, author of "A Discourse of Matters pertaining to Religion," etc. A portrait of the author engraved on steel is included at the beginning. Price 9 shillings.

The aim of this work is defined by its author at the beginning of the first Discourse as follows:—"I propose to speak of Atheism, of the Popular Theology, and of pure Theism. Of each first, as a Theory of the Universe, and then as a Principle of Practical Life; first as Speculative Philosophy, then as Practical Ethics."

> "To real thinkers and to the ministers of the Christian gospel, we emphatically say—Read them (Parker's books) and reflect on them . . . there are glorious bursts of eloquence, flashings of true genius"—*Nonconformist*.

> "Compared with the sermons which issue from the majority of pulpits, this volume is a treasure of wisdom and beauty."—*Leader*.

> "The method of these discourses is practical, addressing their argument to common sense. Atheism and the popular theology are exhibited in their repulsive relations to common life, while from the better conception of divine things, of which the writer is the chief apostle, there is shown to arise, in natural development, the tranquil security of religious trust, guidance, and comfort in all social duty, and the clear hope of the world to come."—*Westminster Review*.

### Atkinson and Martineau.
LETTERS ON THE LAWS OF MAN'S NATURE AND DEVELOPMENT. By HENRY GEORGE ATKINSON, Fellow of the Geological Society, and HARRIET MARTINEAU. Post octavo <note>original: "Post 8vo"</note>. Pages xii and 390, cloth binding. 1851. 5 shillings.

> "Of the many remarkable facts related in this book we can say little, but what strikes us is the elevating influence of an acknowledgment of mystery in any form at all. In Mr. Atkinson's thoughts there is, for all of us who live in slavery to dogmatic notions, an awful sense of freedom. However wildly he has wandered in search of it, truth is all for which he has cared to live. If he is drying up the fountain of life, yet to him life is living on the fountain of life itself. He does not care for fame, for reputation, for anything except to find truth and to live beautifully by it; and all this because he feels the unknown and marvelous existence, which is busy at the warp and woof of the world, is awe-inspiring to contemplate and beautiful to express our entire dependence thereon."—*Fraser's Magazine*.

> "A book from whose reasonings and conclusions we are bound to express our entire dissent, but to which it is impossible to deny the rare merit of strictest honesty of purpose. It is an investigation into a subject of the highest importance, about which the wisest of us is almost entirely ignorant, begun and pursued with a brave resolve to penetrate the mystery and ascertain the truth, and to state them, whatever results that inquiry might lead to, and to shrink from no consequence, and to avoid no difficulty, and to state them, whatever reception they might have from the world."—*Critic*.

> "A curious and valuable contribution to psychological science, and one we regard with much interest, as containing the best and fullest development of the new theories of mesmerism, clairvoyance, and kindred hypotheses. The book is replete with profound reflections thrown out incidentally, is distinguished by a peculiar elegance of style, and, in the hands of a calm and philosophical theologian, may serve as a useful summary <note>original: "precis"</note> of the most formidable difficulties he has to contend against in the present day."—*Weekly News*.

> "The letters are remarkable for the analytical powers which characterize them, and will be eagerly read by all those who appreciate the value of the assertion that 'the proper study of mankind is man.' The eloquence they embody is no less conspicuous than the sincerity, as well as depth of thought and earnestness in the search after truth, which are their principal features. Without affectation or pedantry—those faults of pretension—they are marked by simplicity of diction, and an ease of language and expression that give to a subject, for the most part intricate and perplexing, an inexpressible charm."—*Weekly Dispatch*.

> "A work of profound science, marked with great acuteness of reasoning, and conspicuous for qualities of intellectual power."—*Edinburgh Review*.

> "The *Course of Positive Philosophy* <note>original: "Cours de Philosophie Positive"</note> is at once a comprehensive encyclopedia of science and an original scientific method. It defines rigorously the characteristics of the several orders of which the particular sciences consist, ranges them in an ascending scale of complexity and specialization—beginning with mathematics and ending with social physics or sociology—and assigns to each science its proper method in accordance with the nature of the phenomena to be investigated. . . . Because it is not merely a comprehensive encyclopedia of scientific facts, but an exhibition of the methods of human knowledge and of the relations between its different branches, Mr. Mill, following the author himself, calls Comte's work philosophy, or he terms it positive philosophy."—*Spectator*.

**FOXTON.** *POPULAR CHRISTIANITY; its Transition State, and Probable Development.* By FREDERICK J. > "Few writers are bolder, but his manner is singularly considerate towards the very opinions that he combats—his language singularly calm and measured. A prototype for his volume may be found in that of the American, Theodore Parker—the 'Discourse of Religion.' He often touches a deep and fruitful truth with a power and fullness that leave nothing to be desired."—*Prospective Review, November* 1849.

> "It contains many passages that show a warm appreciation of the moral beauty of Christianity itself, which is most ably written, and evinces a spirit at once earnest, enlightened, and liberal; in a small compass he presents a most lucid exposition of views, many of them original, and supported by arguments which cannot fail to create a deep sensation in the religious world."—*Observer*.

**Newman. PHASES OF FAITH; or Passages from the History of My Creed. By FRANCIS WILLIAM NEWMAN. Sewed <note>A pamphlet or book with a paper cover stitched together rather than bound in hard boards</note>, 2 shillings; post octavo, cloth binding, 3 shillings, 6 pence.**

> “Besides a style of remarkable fascination, resulting from its perfect simplicity and the total absence of self-conscious writing, the literary character of this book arises from its display of the writer’s mind and the narrative of his struggles. . . . In addition to the religious and metaphysical interest, it contains some more tangible biographical matter, in individual pictures of the

<column-break/>

writer’s career, and glimpses of the alienations and social persecutions he underwent as a consequence of his opinions.”—*Spectator*.

> “Altogether, this is a most remarkable book, and is destined, we think, to acquire all the notoriety that was attained a few years ago by the ‘Vestiges of Creation’ <note>An 1844 book that anonymously proposed a theory of biological evolution, causing great public controversy</note>, and to produce a more lasting effect.”—*Weekly News*.

> “No work in our experience has yet been published that is so capable of grasping the mind of the reader and carrying him through the winding labyrinth of religious controversy; no work so energetically clears the subject of all its ambiguities and distortions; no work is so capable of making a path for the new reformation to tread securely upon. In this history of the conflicts of a deeply religious mind, courageously seeking the truth and conquering for itself, bit by bit, the right to speak with authority on that which it had previously accepted through tradition, we see reflected, as in a mirror, the history of the last few centuries. Modern spiritualism has reason to be deeply grateful to Mr. Newman: his learning, his piety, his courage, his candor, and his thorough mastery of his subject render his alliance doubly precious to the cause.”—*The Leader*.

> “Mr. Newman is a master of style, and his book, written in plain and vigorous <note>original: "nervous"; meaning forceful or spirited</note> English, treats a subject too important to fail in commanding the attention of all thinking men, and particularly of all ministers of religion.”—*Economist*.

> “As a narrative of the various doubts and misgivings that beset a religious mind when compelled by conviction to deviate from orthodox views, and as a history of the conclusions arrived at by an intelligent and educated mind, along with the reasons and steps by which such conclusions were gained, this work is most interesting and of great importance.”—*Morning Advertiser*.

**Collection of Words and Phrases** <note>original: Collecção de Vocabulos e Frases</note> used in the Province of Saint Peter of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil. 16mo. pages 32, sewed, 2s. 6d.

**Aztec (or Mexican) Gospel-book, Book of Epistles, and Lectionary,** <note>original: Evangeliarium, Epistolarium et Lectionarium Aztecum</note> drawn from an Ancient Mexican Codex recently discovered; edited with a preface, translation, notes, and glossary by BERNARDINO BIONDELLI. Folio. Pages l. and 574. 1858. (Only 400 copies printed, on stout writing-paper. Bound half Morocco, gilt top, uncut edges). £6 6s.

The very interesting Codex of which the above is a careful reprint, was discovered in Mexico by Beltrami in the year 1826. It is composed in the purest and most elegant Nahuatl that was ever written, by Bernardino Sahagun, a Spanish Franciscan, assisted by two princes of the royal house of Anahuac—one the son of Montezuma, the other the son of the Prince of Tezcuco. It purports to be a "postilla" (meaning "after those," specifically the words of the text) <note>original: post illa scilicet textus verba</note> on the Gospels and Epistles. Sahagun arrived at Mexico in the year 1529, and lived and labored with great success in that country for fully sixty years. Mr. Biondelli has accompanied Sahagun's text with a Latin version and has added a copious Nahuatl and Latin Vocabulary. Through his introductory observations, he has thrown considerable light not only upon the Nahuatl language, its affinity to other families of languages, and its grammatical peculiarities, but also upon the traditions, institutions, and monuments of the Aztecs—thus forming a complete treasury of everything appertaining to the ancient Aztecs.

**Contents:**—The Black Death—The Dancing Mania—The Sweating Sickness—Child-Pilgrimages.
This volume is one of the series published by the Sydenham Society, and, as such, was originally issued to its members only. The work having gone out of print, this new edition—the third—has been undertaken by the present proprietors of the copyright. This was done with the view not only of meeting the numerous demands from the medical profession to which it was primarily addressed by its learned author, but also for extending its circulation to the general reader. To the general reader, it had previously been almost inaccessible owing to the restricted mode of its publication. It is believed it will be very acceptable to them on account of the great and growing interest of its subject matter, and its elegant and successful treatment. The volume is a word-for-word reprint from the second edition; however, its value has been enhanced by the addition of a paper on “**Child-Pilgrimages**,” never before translated. This edition is therefore the *first and only one* in the English language which contains all the contributions of Dr. Hecker to the history of medicine.

# Catalogue of Important Works.

**Caxton.** THE GAME OF CHESS. A reproduction of WILLIAM CAXTON'S *GAME OF CHESS*, the first work printed in England. Small folio, bound in vellum <note>a fine parchment made from animal skin</note>, in the style of the period. Price £1 1s.

Frequently as we read of the works of Caxton and the early English printers, and of their "black letter" <note>a heavy, ornate typeface used in early printing</note> books, very few persons have ever had the opportunity of seeing any of these productions or forming a proper estimate of the ingenuity and skill of those who first practiced the "Noble Art of Printing."

This reproduction of the first work printed by Caxton at Westminster, containing 23 woodcuts, is intended, in some measure, to supply this deficiency and bring the present age into somewhat greater intimacy with the *Father of English Printers.*

The type has been carefully imitated, and the illustrations traced from the copy in the British Museum. The paper has also been made expressly for this edition, as near as possible to the original.

**Ludewig (HERMANN E.)** THE LITERATURE OF AMERICAN ABORIGINAL LANGUAGES. With Additions and Corrections by Professor WILLIAM W. TURNER. Edited by NICOLAS TRÜBNER. Octavo, flyleaf and general Title, 2 leaves; Dr. Ludewig's Preface, pages v–viii; Editor's Preface, pages iv–xii; Biographical Memoir of Dr. Ludewig, pages xiii, xiv; and Introductory Bibliographical Notices, pages xiv–xxiv, followed by List of Contents. Then follow Dr. Ludewig's *Bibliotheca Glottica* <note>Linguistic Library</note>, alphabetically arranged, with Additions by the Editor, pages 1–209; Professor Turner's Additions, with those of the Editor to the same, also alphabetically arranged, pages 210–246; Index, pages 247–256; and list of Errata <note>corrections</note>, pages 257, 258. One volume, handsomely bound in cloth, price 10s. 6d.

This work is intended to supply a great need, now that the study of Ethnology <note>the study of different peoples and their cultures</note> has proved that foreign languages are not mere curiosities, but essential and interesting parts of the natural history of man. They form one of the most curious links in the great chain of national affinities, defining as they do the relationship existing between man and the soil he lives upon. No one can venture to write the history of America without a knowledge of her aboriginal languages. Unimportant as such researches may seem to men engaged in the mere bustling occupations of life, they will at least acknowledge that these records of the past, like the stern-lights of a departing ship, are the last glimmers of "savage" life as it becomes absorbed or recedes before the tide of civilization. 

Dr. Ludewig and Professor Turner have made most diligent use of the public and private collections in America, access to all of which was most liberally granted to them. This has placed at their disposal the labors of the American Missionaries, which are so little known on this side of the Atlantic that they may be looked upon almost as untrodden ground. But English and Continental libraries have also been ransacked; and Dr. Ludewig kept up a constant and active correspondence with scholars of "the Fatherland" <note>Germany</note>, as well as with men of similar tastes and pursuits in France, Spain, and Holland, determined to leave no stone unturned to render his labors as complete as possible. The volume, perfect in itself, is the first of an enlarged edition of Vater's "*Index of the Languages of the Whole World*" <note>original: "Linguarum totius orbis Index"</note>. The work has been noticed by the press of both continents, and we may be permitted to refer particularly to the following:

### OPINIONS OF THE PRESS.

> "This work, mainly the production of the late Mr. Ludewig, a German naturalized in America, is devoted to an account of the literature of the aboriginal languages of that country. It gives an alphabetical list of the various tribes of whose languages any record remains, and refers to the works, papers, or manuscripts in which such information may be found. The work has evidently been a labor of love; and as no pains seem to have been spared by the editors, Professor Turner and Mr. Trübner, in rendering the work as accurate and complete as possible, those who are most interested in its contents will be best able to judge of the labor and diligence bestowed upon it by author, editors, and publisher."— *Athenæum*, 5th April, 1858.

> "This is the first installment of a work which will be of the greatest value to philologists <note>scholars of language</note>; it is a compendium of the aboriginal languages of the American continents and a digest of all the known literature bearing upon those languages. Mr. Trübner's hand has been engaged throughout <note>original: "passim"</note>, and in his preface he lays claim to about one-sixth of the..."

<header>Trübner & Co., 60, Paternoster Row.</header>

The purpose of compiling this book, the author states, is twofold: "On the one hand, to suggest the necessity of a more perfect work of its kind by an American, surrounded, as he necessarily would be, with the required resources; and, on the other, to supply Europeans with a guide to Anglo-American literature—a branch which, by its rapid rise and increasing importance, begins to force itself more and more on our attention." It is very modest of Mr. Trübner to treat his work as a mere suggestion for others. It is much more than this: it is an example which those who attempt to do anything more complete cannot do better than to follow—a model they would do well to copy if they wish to combine that admirable order and arrangement which so facilitates reference, and without which a work of this sort is almost useless.

> "All honor, then, to the literature of Young America—for young she still is, and let her thank her stars for it—and thank Mr. Trübner for taking so much pains to make us acquainted with it."—*The Critic*, March 19, 1859.

"This is not only a very useful, because well-executed, bibliographical work—it is also a work of much interest to all who are connected with the study of American literature. The bulk of it consists of a classified list, with date of publication, size, and price, of all the works, original or translated, which have appeared in the United States during the last forty years; and an alphabetical index facilitates reference to any particular work or author. On the merits of this portion of the work we cannot, of course, be expected to form a judgment. It would require something of the special erudition <note>original: "erudition"; deep knowledge or learning</note> of Mr. Trübner himself to say how far he has succeeded or fallen short of his undertaking—how few, or how many, have been his omissions. 

There is one indication, however, of his careful minuteness, which suggests the amount of labor that must have been bestowed on the enumeration of all the contents of the various Transactions and Scientific Journals. Thus, the *'Transactions'* of the American Philosophical Society, from the year 1769 to 1857—no index to which has yet appeared in America—are in this work made easy of reference, every paper of every volume being mentioned in order <note>original: "seriatim"</note>. The naturalist who wishes to know what papers have appeared in the Boston *Journal of Natural History* during the last twenty years (that is, from its commencement) has only to glance over the five closely-printed pages of this guide to satisfy himself at once."—*The Saturday Review*, April 2, 1859.

> "We have never seen a work on the national literature of a people more carefully compiled than the present, and the bibliographical introduction <note>original: "prolegomena"</note> deserves attentive perusal by all who would study either the political or the literary history of the greatest republic of the West."—*The Leader*, March 26, 1859.

"The subject of my letter today may seem to some readers to be of a purely literary character, but I feel justified in claiming a more general interest for it. Because the subject is connected with the good reputation of the United States abroad, it is likewise connected with the Government's interests. I have spoken of the friends and the antagonists of the United States among European society. I have stated that the antagonists are not only those of high birth, but 'of mind'—as it has been called—likewise; not only among the privileged classes and those connected with Government interests, but among those who live in the sphere of literature and art, and look down with contempt upon a society in which practical <note>original: "utilitarian"</note> motives are believed to be paramount. And I have asserted that, these differences in the opinions of certain classes aside, the Germans,

<column-break/>

as a whole, take a more lively and a deeper interest in American affairs than any other nation. Now, I am going to speak of a book just ready to leave the press of a London publisher, which is a remarkable instance of the truth of my assertion regarding the good reputation of American life to an uncommon degree.

"The London book trade has a firm, Trübner & Co., of whose business transactions American literature, as well as literature about America, forms a principal branch. It is the firm that has lately published this. Mr. Nicolas Trübner is a German who has never lived in the United States, and yet he risks his time, labor, and money in literary publications for which even vain endeavors would have been made to find an American publisher.

> "The new publication to which I have referred is a large octavo <note>original: "8vo."</note> volume with the title of 'Bibliographical Guide to American Literature: A Classified List of Books Published in the United States of America, from 1817 to 1857. With Bibliographical Introduction, Notes, and Alphabetical Index. Compiled and edited by Nicolas Trübner.'"
> —*New York Daily Tribune*, December 1858.

"This last remark has but too much truth in it. The United States, in the opinion of the great mass of even the well-educated people of Europe, is a country inhabited by a nation lost in the pursuit of material interest—a country in which the technically applicable branches of some sciences may be cultivated to a certain degree, but a country almost without any literature and art; a country not without newspapers—so much the worse for it—but almost without books. 

Now, here comes a list of American books, filling a thick volume, containing American publications only, from the year 1817 forward to the period of a more decided literary independence for the United States. Since no native-born, nor even any adopted American, has taken the trouble of compiling, arranging, digesting, editing, and publishing such a work, who else but a German could undertake it? Who else among the European nations would think American literature worth the money? And, let me add, that a smaller work of a similar character, 'The Literature of American Local History,' by the late Dr. Hermann Ludewig, was the work of a German as well. 

It may be that the majority of the American public will assign only an inferior degree of interest to works of this kind. The majority of people do the same, as it cannot be everyone's business to understand the usefulness of bibliography—of books containing nothing but the enumeration and description of other books. One thing, however, must be apparent: the deep interest taken by some foreigners in the more intellectual <note>original: "ideal"</note> spheres of American life. If it is true that a clear historical insight into its own development, intellectual as well as material, is one of the most valuable acquisitions of a nation, future American generations will acknowledge the good services of those foreigners who, by their literary dedication, contribute to prevent the national calamity of the origins of America becoming 'veiled in darkness.'"

> "It is remarkable and noteworthy that the most valuable manual of American literature should appear in London and be published by an English house. Trübner's Bibliographical Guide to American Literature is a work of extraordinary skill and perseverance, giving an index to all the publications of the American press for the last forty years."
> —*Harper's Weekly*, March 26th, 1859.

# Catalogue of Important Works.

> “Mr. Trübner deserves all praise for having produced a work that is in every way satisfactory. No one who takes an interest in the subject of which it treats can do without it; and we have no doubt that booksellers in this country will learn to consider it as necessary to them as a shop manual, and only second in importance, for the purposes of their trade, to the London Catalogue itself. That a foreigner, and a London bookseller, should have accomplished what Americans themselves have failed to do, is most creditable to the compiler. The volume contains 149 pages of introductory matter, containing by far the best record of American literary history yet published; and 521 pages of classified lists of books, to which an alphabetical index of 33 pages is added. This alphabetical index alone may claim to be one of the most valuable aids for enabling the student of literary history to form a just and perfect estimate of the great and rising importance of Anglo-American literature—the youngest and most untrammeled of all those which illustrate the gradual development of the human mind.”—*The Press, Philadelphia, Oct. 11, 1858.*

> “We do not so much express a wish by this notice that Mr. Trübner may not find the public ungrateful for his labor, as we congratulate American bibliophiles <note>original: "Bibliophiles"; book lovers or collectors</note> especially upon the advantage within their reach, by the acquisition and use of what Mr. Trübner has so opportunely supplied.”—*Washington National Intelligencer, March 22nd, 1859.*

> “This volume contains a well-classified list of books published in the United States of America during the last forty years, preceded by a tolerably full survey of American literary enterprise during the first half of the nineteenth century. The value of such a guide, in itself tolerably evident, becomes more so upon glancing over the five hundred and forty pages of close print which display the literary activity pervading the country of Prescott and Motley, of Irving and Hawthorne, of Poe and Longfellow, of Story and Wheaton, of Moses Stuart and Channing. This volume will be useful to the scholar, but to the librarian it is indispensable.”—*Daily News, March 24, 1859.*

> “There are hundreds of men of moderate scholarship who would gladly stand on some higher and more assured point. They feel that they have acquired much information, but they also feel the need of that subtle discipline, literary education, without which all mere learning is a *rude and undigested mass* <note>original Latin: "rudis indigesta moles"</note>, as much of a stumbling-block as an aid. To those in such a condition, works on bibliography are invaluable. For direction in classifying all reading, whether English or American, Allibone’s Dictionary is admirable; but, for particular information as to the American side of the house, the recently published Bibliographical Guide to American Literature, by Nicolas Trübner of London, may be conscientiously commended. A careful perusal of this truly remarkable work cannot fail to give any intelligent person a clear and complete idea of the whole state of American bookmaking, not only in its literary aspect, but in its historical, and, added to this, in its most mechanical details.”—*Philadelphia Evening Bulletin, March 5th, 1859.*

> “But the best work on American bibliography yet published has come to us from London, where it has been compiled by the well-known bibliophile, Trübner. The work is remarkable for condensation and accuracy, though we have noted a few errors and omissions, upon which we should like to comment, had we now space to do so.”—*New York Times, March 26th, 1859.*

> “Some of our readers, whose attention has been particularly called to scientific and literary matters, may remember meeting, some years since, in this country, a most intelligent foreigner, who visited the United States for the purpose of extending his business connections,

<column-break/>

and making a personal investigation into the condition of literature in the New World. Mr. Nicolas Trübner—the gentleman to whom we have made reference—although by birth a German, and by education and profession a London bookseller, could hardly be called a ‘stranger in America,’ for he had sent before him a most valuable ‘letter of introduction,’ in the shape of a carefully compiled register of American books and authors, entitled ‘Bibliographical Guide to American Literature,’ etc., pp. xxxii., 108. This manual was the germ of the important publication, the title of which the reader will find at the commencement of this article. Now, in consequence of Mr. Trübner’s admirable classification and minute index, the inquirer after knowledge has nothing to do but copy from the Bibliographical Guide the titles of the American books which he wishes to consult, dispatch them to his library by a messenger, and in a few minutes he has before him the coveted volumes, through whose means he hopes to enlarge his acquisitions. Undoubtedly it would be a cause of well-founded reproach, of deep mortification to every intelligent American, if the arduous labors of the learned editor and compiler of this volume (whom we almost hesitate to call a foreigner), should fail to be appreciated in a country to which he has, by the preparation of this valuable work, proved himself so eminent a benefactor.”—*Pennsylvania Enquirer, March 26th, 1859.*

> “The editor of this volume has acquired a knowledge of the productions of the American press which is rarely exhibited on the other side of the Atlantic, and which must command the admiration of the best informed students of the subject in this country. His former work on American bibliography, though making no pretensions to completeness, was a valuable index to various branches of learning that had been successfully cultivated by our scholars; but, neither in comprehensiveness of plan nor thoroughness of execution, can it be compared to the elaborate and minute record of American literature contained in this volume. The duty of the editor required extensive research, vigilant discrimination, and untiring diligence; and in the performance of his task we are no less struck with the accuracy of detail than with the extent of his information. The period to which the volume is devoted comprises only the last forty years; but within that time the literature of this country has received its most efficient impulses, and been widely unfolded in the various departments of intellectual activity. If we were permitted to speak in behalf of American scholars, we should not fail to congratulate Mr. Trübner on the eminent success with which he has accomplished his plan, and the ample and impartial justice with which he has registered the productions of our native authorship. After a careful examination of his volume, we are bound to express our high appreciation of the intelligence, fairness, and industry which are conspicuous in its pages; for exactness and precision it is no less remarkable than for extent of research; few, if any, important publications are omitted on its catalogue, and although, as is inevitable in a work of this nature, an erroneous letter has sometimes crept into a name, or an erroneous figure into a date, no one can consult it habitually without learning to rely on its trustworthiness, as well as its completeness.”—*Harper’s Magazine, April, 1859.*

> “Nor is the book a dry catalogue only of the names and contents of the publications of America. Prefixed to it are valuable bibliographical introductions <note>original: "prolegomena"</note>, instructive to the antiquary, as well as useful to the philologist. In this portion of the work, Mr. Trübner had the assistance of the late Dr. Ludewig, whose early death was a great loss to philological science. Mr. Moran—the assistant-secretary to the American Legation—has added to the volume a historical summary of the literature of America; and Mr.”

"Edward Edwards is responsible for an interesting account of the public libraries of the United States. To Mr. Trübner's own careful superintendence and hard work, however, the student must ever remain indebted for one of the most useful and well-arranged books on bibliographical lore <note>original: "lore" — knowledge or learning on a particular subject</note> ever published. In addition to this, it is right to congratulate Mr. Trübner on the fact that his present work confirms the opinion passed on his *'Bibliotheca Glottica'* <note>original: "Bibliotheca Glottica" — Library of Languages</note> that among the booksellers themselves, honorable literary eminence may exist without clashing with business arrangements. The booksellers of old were authors, and Mr. Trübner emulates their example." — *Morning Chronicle*, March 22, 1859.

"Mr. Trübner, who is not only a bibliopole <note>original: "bibliopole" — a bookseller</note> but a bibliophile <note>original: "bibliophile" — a book lover</note>, has, in this work, materially increased the claim which he already had upon the respect of all book-lovers everywhere, but especially in the United States, to whose literature he has now made so important and useful a contribution. So much larger than a former book under a similar title which he published in 1855, and so much more ample in every respect, the present constitutes a new tool for our libraries, as well as the most valuable existing aid for those students who, without libraries, have an interest in knowing their contents." — *Baltimore American*, April 2, 1859.

"Lastly, published only the other day, is *Trübner's Bibliographical Guide to American Literature*, which gives a classified list of books published in the United States during the last forty years, with a bibliographical introduction, notes, and an alphabetical index. This octavo volume has been compiled and edited by Mr. Nicholas Trübner, the well-known head of one of the great foreign publishing and importing houses of London, who is also the editor of Ludewig and Turner's *Literature of American Aboriginal Languages*. Besides containing a classified list of books with an alphabetical index, Mr. Trübner's book has an introduction in which, at considerable length, he treats the history of American literature, including newspapers, periodicals, and public libraries. It is fair to state that Mr. Trübner's *Bibliographical Guide* was published after Allibone's *Dictionary*, but printed at about the same time." — *Philadelphia Press*, April 4, 1859.

"This is a valuable work for book buyers. For its compilation we are indebted to a foreign bibliomaniac <note>original: "bibliomaniac" — here used playfully to mean an enthusiastic collector or expert of books</note>, but one who has made himself familiar with American literature and has gained access to the most ample sources of information. The volume contains: I. Bibliographical Prolegomena <note>original: "Prolegomena" — preliminary remarks or introduction</note>; II. Contributions to-

<column-break/>

-wards a history of American literature; III. Notices of Public Libraries of the United States. These three heads form the introduction and occupy one hundred and fifty pages. IV. Classified list of books; V. Alphabetical list of authors. This plan is somewhat similar to that adopted in Watts' celebrated *'Bibliotheca Britannica,'* a work of immense value whose compilation occupied some forty years. The classified portion of the present work enables the reader to find readily the names of all books on any one subject. The alphabetical index of authors enables the reader to ascertain instantly the names of all authors and of all their works, including the numerous periodical publications of the last forty years. Mr. Trübner deserves the thanks of the literary world for his plan and its able execution." — *New York Courier and Enquirer*, April 11, 1859.

"The author, in a ten-page preface, explains the ideas that led him to undertake his book and the plan he felt necessary to adopt. In a scholarly introduction, he provides a critical review of different works relating to America; he points out those which have contributed most to the establishment of a specifically American literature and provides its history. This part of his work is destined to bring him honor; it is methodically divided into the colonial period and the American period and contains very interesting information—which one is happy to find gathered together for the first time—regarding the progress of printing in America, authors' salaries, the book trade, and periodical publications. This introduction, which is no less than 150 pages, ends with a statistical table of all the public libraries of the various States of the Union. <note>original: French text from *Nouvelles Annales des Voyages*</note>

"The methodical and annotated catalogue of works occupies no less than 521 pages; it forms 32 sections, each devoted to one of the branches of human sciences. The section giving the list of works concerning geography and travel (section xvi.) includes nearly 600 articles, and among them one finds references to several works whose existence we did not even suspect in Europe. A general alphabetical index of authors' names at the end of the book allows one to shorten research that is often very painful. Mr. Trübner's bibliographical guide is a monument raised to American scientific and literary activity and, as such, it is worthy to take its place alongside works of the same genre published in Europe by Brunet, Lowndes, and Ebert. (V. A. Malte-Brun)." — *New Annals of Voyages*, April 1859.
